title: Find the Letter
desc: matching a spoken letter name to its printed form (12 cards, 6 uppercase and 6 lowercase)
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
key: Say: Here are twelve letter cards from the lantern shop. I will say a letter name. Point to the card with that letter.
Say: Point to the letter e. (top row, fourth card)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: First Sound Check
desc: saying the first sound of a pictured word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the first sound.
key: Model first: Moon. The first sound in moon is /m/. Now you try.
Point to the cat. Say: Cat. What is the first sound in cat? (/k/)

title: Rhyme Time
desc: making a rhyme for a given word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say a word that rhymes.
key: Model first: Night, light, kite. They rhyme. They sound the same at the end.
Point to the star. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with star. (car, far, jar, bar, gar)

title: Put It Together
desc: blending syllables and sounds into a word with picture support
dir: Listen to the slow, sleepy voice. Say the whole word.
key: Say: I am going to talk very slowly tonight. Put the parts together and tell me the word. The pictures can help you, but they are mixed up.
Say with a pause between the parts: lan ... tern. (lantern, the paper light in the first picture)

title: Rue Walks the Lantern Street
desc: questions about the character, the order of three events, and what happens next in a story read aloud
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Rue Walks the Lantern Street
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: This is a town at night. The people hang paper lanterns on a long rope over the street. A lantern is a little paper light you can
Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Rue comes to the bridge.

title: Find the Letter
desc: matching a spoken letter name to its printed lowercase form
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
key: Say: Every lantern has a tag with a small letter on it. I will say a letter name. Point to the lantern with that letter.
Say: Point to the letter l. (fourth lantern from the left)

title: Why the Sky Gets Dark
desc: making an inference, making a connection, and asking a question about an informational text read aloud
dir: Listen to your teacher read about day and night. Then answer out loud.
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture first. Say: The big round thing is the earth. That is what we live on. The sun is over here on the left. The side of the earth turned toward the sun is

Ask: The earth keeps turning all night long. So what will happen in the morning? (Your side will turn back toward the sun, and it will be day again. The text does not say this part, so the child has t

title: Write the Night Sounds
desc: writing the letter for a beginning sound (l, m, s, p)
dir: Listen for the sound. Write the letter on your paper and hold it up.
key: Point to the first picture. Say: This is a lantern. Lantern starts with /l/. Write the letter that makes the /l/ sound. Hold it up. (l or L)
Point to the moon. Say: Moon starts with /m/. Write the letter for /m/. (m or M)

title: The Phone Call
desc: asking questions to get missing information and to confirm understanding
dir: Your teacher is calling you. Ask questions until you know what to do.
key: Say: You are at home in the town. I will call you on the phone, but part of my message will be missing. Ask me questions until you know what to do.
Message 1. Say in a phone voice: Hello! Please bring the lantern down to the bridge. Look for: asks a question about which lantern or which bridge (there are lots of lanterns and two bridges). If the

title: Mystery Basket
desc: asking questions and follow-up questions to find out information
dir: Something is in the basket on the bridge. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
key: Your secret: a key is in the basket. Do not tell.
Say: One thing is packed in this basket. Ask me questions to find out what it is. You can ask things like: Is it alive? What do you do with it?

title: Name the Night Things
desc: naming objects, actions, and describing words from pictures
dir: Look at each picture. Answer out loud.
key: Picture 1. Say: What is this? (a lantern, a lamp, or a light. All three count.)
Picture 2. Say: What is this? (a bridge)

title: Bridge or Street
desc: sharing an opinion with a reason, a description, and an explanation
dir: Pick one. Tell your teacher why.
key: Say: Tonight you can watch the new year start from the middle of the bridge, with the whole river under you, or you can walk all the way down the lantern street, right under the lights. Which one woul
Look for: tells an opinion (picks one).

title: Label the New Year Page
desc: writing letters to label a drawing
dir: Draw one thing you want to try this year. Write letters to tell what it is. Hold it up.
key: Say: A new year is a fresh start. Draw one thing you want to try this year. Then write a word or some letters to tell what it is. Hold it up and tell me what you wrote.
Look for: writing that is separate from the drawing (letters or marks that look like letters, not only a picture).

title: Count the Lanterns
desc: counting 10 or more real objects one by one where the teacher can see, then counting groups of 10, 12, 14, and 11 objects one by one on the screen
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
key: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one

Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down

title: More Lanterns or More Stars?
desc: comparing two groups by counting (more, same, fewer)
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
key: Box 1. Say: Are there more lanterns or more stars? How do you know? (More lanterns. 9 lanterns and 6 stars.)
Box 2. Say: Are there more houses, more trees, or the same number of each? (The same. 5 houses and 5 trees.)

title: Window Shapes
desc: naming, describing, and drawing circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud. Then draw a shape on your paper.
key: Say: Here is a house at night, drawn with shapes. What shape is the purple roof? (triangle)
Say: What shape is the blue window? (square)

title: Sort the Lanterns
desc: sorting and classifying objects by color, by size, by two attributes at once, and making a rule
dir: Look at the tray and the pile. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the tray. Say: Here are the lanterns the town is about to hang up. How many lanterns are on the tray in all? (8)
Say: Sort them by color in your head. How many red? How many gold? (4 red and 4 gold)

title: Tallest Pole, Longest Rope
desc: ordering five objects by height and four objects by length
dir: Look at the poles and the ropes. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the poles. Say: The town has five lantern poles. Which pole is the tallest? (B)
Say: Which pole is the shortest? (A)

title: Where in Town?
desc: position words (on, next to, under, above, near and far, between)
dir: Look at the town. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Here is the town at night. Look at the bridge at the other end of the street. What is on the bridge? (the gold lantern)
Say: What is next to the house? (the park tree)

title: Number Cards
desc: naming the numerals 1 to 10
dir: Say the name of each number.
key: Say: The town wrote a number on every box of lanterns. What number is this? Click Next after each one.
The deck is 4, 9, 1, 7, 3, 10, 6, 2, 8, 5. It is out of order on purpose, so the child cannot count along to find a name.

title: What Comes Next?
desc: extending repeating patterns and naming the part that repeats
dir: Look at each row. Say what comes next.
key: Row 1. Say: Star, lantern, star, lantern, star, lantern, star. What comes next? (a lantern)
Row 2. Say: Look at this row. What comes next? (a pine tree. The pattern is pine, pine, star, star, and the row ends with the second star.)

title: The Town Chart
desc: reading, copying, and adding to a picture chart with two groups
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud. Then make marks on your paper.
key: Say: The children in town picked where they want to watch the first night of the new year, out on the bridge or down the lantern street. Each face is one child. How many children picked the bridge? (5
Say: Did more children pick the bridge or the lantern street? (The lantern street. 7 is more than 5.)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the most common sound for all 26 letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What sound does this letter make? Mark each correct sound.
For a, e, i, o and u the short sound is what is expected. The long sound is also correct.

title: Two Lines
desc: print concepts (where to start, where to go at the end of a line, counting words and letters)
dir: Look at the two lines. Answer out loud.
text: We walk down the street. The lantern is gold. The four pictures are a boot, a bridge, the moon, and a star.
key: Say: I want to read this. Ask: Where do I start, at the boot, the bridge, the moon, or the star? (the boot. Reading starts at the top on the left.)
Say: I read the top line and I stop at the bridge. Ask: Where do I go next? (to the moon, the start of the next line)

title: Book Parts
desc: print concepts (finding the title, where to start, which way to read, and the first and last word of a line)
dir: Look at the page. Point or answer out loud.
text: The Lantern Night A lantern is up high I see it glow
key: Say: This is a page from a book. Point to the title. (the big words in the banner at the top: The Lantern Night. If the student cannot point on the screen, they can tell you where it is.)
Ask: Where do I start reading? Point to it. (the first word of the top line, on the left: A)

title: Rhyme and Clap
desc: hearing rhymes, making a rhyme, and clapping syllables
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
text: A lantern is a little paper light you hang up.
key: Ask: Do night and light rhyme? (yes)
Ask: Do moon and star rhyme? (no)

title: Put It Together
desc: blending spoken sounds and saying the first, last, and all sounds in a word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Put these sounds together: /m/ /oo/ /n/. (moon)
Say: Put these sounds together: /s/ /t/ /ar/. (star)

title: Bo and the Lamp
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in a story read aloud to the student
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: Bo has a lamp. Bo sits on the bridge. The sky is dark. Bo sees a big star. A bridge sits on the river. You can walk on it.
key: Read the four lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Ask: Who is the story about? (Bo)
Ask: Where does Bo sit? (on the bridge)

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the sounds of letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: The student says the most common sound for each letter: t /t/, E as in egg, m /m/, p /p/, u as in up, S /s/, l /l/, g /g/, d /d/, n /n/. The letter name is not needed here.
The long sound for E or u is also fine. Write down any sounds that were missed.

title: Night Words
desc: reading high-frequency words and short vowel words
dir: Read each word out loud.
text: we go like at is sun log net hum
key: High-frequency words the student should know by sight: we, go, like, at, is
Sounds out or reads: sun, log, net, hum

title: Listen to the Town
desc: answering questions about key details in a text read aloud and asking for help
dir: Put your eyes on your teacher and listen. Then answer out loud.
text: Listening time. Your teacher will read you a report from the town by the river.
key: Ask: What do the people hang on the long rope? (paper lanterns)
Ask: Where does the rope go? (right across the main street, from one pole to the other)

title: Little Night Book
desc: reading a short emergent-reader book with purpose and understanding
dir: Point to each word and read it out loud.
text: I see a town. The sky is dark. I see a lamp. It is on. The lamp is red. I can see the lamp. It is not dim. I like the lamp. A lamp gives light. A lantern is a l
key: Count the words the student reads correctly, out of 32, and enter the number in the box. A word the student fixes without help counts. Write down the words that were missed.
Points or tracks under each word, left to right and top to bottom

title: Moon Watch
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in an informational text about the moon
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: The moon is in the sky. The moon is not hot. The moon has no light. The sun shines on it. That is why it looks bright. Some nights you see a bit.
key: Read the six lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Ask: Where is the moon? (in the sky. Line 1.)
Ask: Is the moon hot? (no. Line 2.)

title: Town Talk
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, question words, position words in complete sentences)
dir: Look at the picture. Listen to your teacher. Say your answer out loud.
key: Say: One lantern, two ____. (lanterns)
Say: One box, two ____. (boxes)

title: New Year Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write opinion piece about the bridge or the lantern street
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Would you rather watch the night sky from the bridge, or walk down the street under the lanterns? Draw the one you pick. Write or tell what you think and why.
key: Tells the reader what the choice is about: the bridge or the lantern street (W.K.1)
States an opinion, which one the student would pick. Drawing, telling, or writing all count (W.K.1)

title: New Year Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write informative piece about a lantern, an owl, or the moon
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Pick one: a lantern, an owl, or the moon. Draw it. Write its name. Then write or tell one true thing about it. An owl is a bird. It is awake at night. A lantern
key: Names what the drawing and writing are about: a lantern, an owl, or the moon. The student may say it, label the picture, or write a letter or word for it (W.K.2)
Gives at least one piece of true information about it, such as: A lantern glows. An owl is awake at night. The moon is in the sky (W.K.2)

title: New Year Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write story about a time outside in the dark, told in order with a reaction
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Think of a time you were outside when it was dark. Draw what happened. Then tell what happened first and what happened next. Tell how you felt.
key: Tells about one real thing that happened, not a list of facts (W.K.3)
Tells two parts, a first and a next, in the order they happened (W.K.3)

title: Night Walk List
desc: answering questions from a picture chart and from experience
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the chart. What hangs on the rope?
Look at the chart. What do we use to look at the stars?
key: The lantern. Uses the chart to answer.
The telescope. Uses the chart to answer.

title: Tell Me More
desc: describing a familiar thing you do, with details
dir: Tell your teacher out loud. Use lots of details.
text: Tell me about something you do right before bed.
key: Names the thing and tells something about it
Adds a detail when you ask: Where do you do it?

title: Up the Street
desc: counting out loud by ones
dir: Count out loud. Start at 1. Go as high as you can.
text: The town is hanging lanterns all the way down the main street. Count out loud as the lanterns go up.
key: Say: Start at 1 and count as high as you can. Check: counts 1 to 20 in order with no skips.
Keeps going from 20 to 40 and gets across each new ten (29 to 30, 39 to 40).

title: Ten to a Rope
desc: counting by tens
dir: Count by tens out loud.
text: Each rope holds 10 lanterns. Count by tens to 100.
key: Say: Count the lanterns by tens as each rope goes up. Check: says 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 with no help.
Keeps going: 60, 70, 80, 90, 100. Write the last number said in order.

title: More or Fewer
desc: comparing two groups of objects (more, fewer, the same)
dir: Look at the two groups. Answer out loud.
key: Card 1. Ask: Are there more lanterns or more stars? (stars. 8 is more than 6.)
Card 2. Ask: Which group has fewer, the houses or the trees? (the trees. 5 is fewer than 7.)

title: One for Each
desc: matching and counting to tell which group has more, fewer, or the same
dir: Look at the boxes. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the top box. Is there a star for every lantern?
In the top box, which has more: the lanterns or the stars?
key: Yes. There are 5 lanterns and 7 stars, so 2 stars are left over.
The stars (7 is more than 5)

title: Lanterns on the Bridge
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 10, with drawings
dir: Listen to each story. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer out loud.
text: You can draw a circle for each lantern on your paper, then count or cross out.
key: Say: 4 lanterns hang on the bridge rail. 3 more go up beside them. How many lanterns are on the rail now? (7. 4 + 3 = 7)
Say: 8 stars were out. Then 2 of them went behind a cloud. How many stars can you still see? (6. 8 - 2 = 6)

title: Two Windows
desc: breaking numbers up to 10 into two parts in more than one way
dir: Look at the lanterns. Put some in each window. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the first picture. There are 5 lanterns and 2 windows. Say one way to put them in the two windows. Say it like this: ____ and ____ makes 5.
Now tell me a different way to make 5.
key: Any true pair for 5: 4 and 1, 3 and 2, 2 and 3, 1 and 4, 5 and 0. The student has to say both parts.
A different true pair for 5 than the first one. Saying the same pair backwards (3 and 2, then 2 and 3) counts as different only if the student points to which window each part goes in.

title: Split It
desc: breaking a number up to 10 into two parts in more than one way and recording each way
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Here are 8.
key: Say: Show me one way to split these 8 into two groups. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 3 + 5 = 8. (a drawing with two groups, or an equation, that makes 8)
Say: Now show me a different way. (a second pair of parts that make 8. The same two numbers in the other order do not count as different.)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: showing a number from 11 to 19 as a ten and some more and recording it
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Look at the full ten frame and the extra ones.
key: Say: Show 15 as a ten and some more. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 15 = 10 + 5. (a drawing of a ten and 5 more, or the equation)
Ask: How many ones are left after the ten? (5)

title: Tall and Long
desc: comparing two objects to tell which has more or less of an attribute and describing the difference
dir: Look at the two poles and the two ropes. Answer out loud.
text: Both poles stand on the same street, and both ropes start at the same dotted line, so you can see which one is bigger.
key: Ask: Which lantern pole is taller? (Pole 2)
Ask: Which lantern pole is shorter? (Pole 1)

title: Heavy or Light
desc: comparing two objects by weight to say which is heavier and which is lighter
dir: Look at the scales. Answer out loud.
text: A B
key: Ask: Look at scale A. Which one is heavier? (the cake. It is on the side that goes down.)
Ask: Which one is lighter? (the partyHat)

title: Count and Tell
desc: counting a group and telling how many, and counting on by one
dir: Count the lanterns out loud. Then answer out loud.
qs: Point to each lantern and count out loud. How many lanterns are on the rope?
I will ask it again. How many lanterns are on the rope?
key: 7. One number word for each lantern, left to right, with no skips and no double counts.
7, said straight back without counting again. The last number you say when you count tells how many there are. Having to start the count over is worth a note.

title: Ten and Some More
desc: seeing a teen number as ten ones and some more ones
dir: Look at the full rope and the extra lanterns. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the first picture. The box holds one full rope. How many lanterns are in the box, and how many extra ones are beside it?
So how many lanterns are there in all? Say it this way: ten and ____ more.
key: 10 in the box and 4 extra. The box always holds exactly 10.
14. Ten and 4 more. Writing 14 = 10 + 4 is a bonus, not a requirement.

title: Count On
desc: counting on from a given number and telling the number that is one more
dir: Listen to your teacher. Count out loud.
text: Count with your teacher.
key: Say: Start at 4 and keep counting up. Stop at 9. (5, 6, 7, 8, 9. The student does not go back to 1.)
Say: Start at 13 and count up to 17. (14 to 17)

title: Sort the Night Tray
desc: sorting a mixed group into three given categories, counting each one, and ordering the categories by count
dir: Look at the tray. Answer out loud.
qs: The tray holds three kinds of things: lanterns, stars and pine trees. How many lanterns are on the tray?
How many stars?
key: 5 lanterns
3 stars

title: Name It and Place It
desc: naming the shapes of things in a scene and telling where they are with position words
dir: Look at the house at night. Answer out loud.
qs: What shape is the purple roof?
What shape is the blue window?
key: A triangle
A square

title: Flat or Solid
desc: telling two-dimensional (flat) shapes from three-dimensional (solid) ones
dir: Look at the four cards. Answer out loud.
qs: Which two cards show a flat shape, one that is drawn flat on the card?
Which two cards show a solid shape, one you could pick up and hold?
key: Cards 1 and 3, the yellow circle and the green triangle.
Cards 2 and 4, the blue box and the orange can.

title: What Living Things Need
desc: telling what an animal and a plant need to stay alive
dir: Look at both pictures. Answer out loud.
text: Wren is starting a bean seed in a cup on the windowsill. An owl lives in the big pine across the street.
qs: A bean seed in a cup starts to grow when it gets two of these. Which two? Water, light, or a sticker?
The owl in the pine stays alive by getting two of these. Which two? Mice to eat, water to drink, or a bell?
key: water and light. A sticker is not something a plant needs.
mice to eat and water to drink. A bell is not something an owl needs.

title: Weather in Town
desc: describing a weather pattern across four weeks of recorded observations
dir: Look at the four weeks. Count out loud.
text: All month the town kept a count of the rainy days, one week at a time. Week 1 Week 2 Week 3 Week 4
qs: Which week had the most rainy days? How many?
Which week had the fewest rainy days? How many?
key: Week 2, with 5 rainy days
Week 3, with 1 rainy day

title: Weather in Town
desc: telling how a living thing changes its surroundings
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A big pine grows right beside the brick path to the bridge.
qs: The roots of the pine have pushed the bricks of the path up into a bump. Did the tree change the path, or did the path change the tree?
Tell me one way a person changes the ground when they want to start a garden.
key: The tree changed the path. Its roots grew and lifted the bricks, and the bricks were flat before.
Any sensible answer: digs it up, pulls out the weeds, rakes it smooth, makes rows, adds soil, builds a box to hold the soil.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: matching animals to the places that give them what they need
dir: Match each animal to the place it lives. Answer out loud.
text: Three animals live near the bridge. Each one lives in one place. It gets what it needs. Here are the places. A hole in the ground. It is under the woodpile. A h
qs: Where does the mouse live?
Where does the owl live?
key: a hole in the ground under the woodpile. Accept a burrow or a nest in the ground.
a hollow high up in a tree

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: telling what a weather forecast is for and how people use one to get ready
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The town reads the forecast for tonight before it gets dark.
qs: The forecast says the air will drop below freezing tonight and the bridge will go icy. Should the town spread sand on the bridge before dark, or wait until somebody slips in the morning?
Who would really want to hear a forecast: somebody who left young plants outside, or somebody picking a favorite number?
key: spread the sand before dark. A forecast is useful because it comes before the weather does.
somebody who left young plants outside. Follow up out loud: what would that person do after hearing it? Covering the plants or bringing them in both count.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Land
desc: telling one way people can take better care of the land and water
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The creek runs under the bridge and out past the houses.
qs: Two neighbors rake their leaves. One sweeps the whole pile down the storm drain that runs to the creek. One piles the leaves in a corner of the yard to rot down into soil. Which choice is better for the creek?
Tell me one way your family could make less trash this year.
key: piling the leaves in the yard. What goes down the drain ends up in the creek.

Any sensible answer: carry a lunch box instead of bags, reuse a bag, fix something instead of throwing it out, pass clothes on to somebody smaller, put cans and paper in recycling, take a cup from hom

title: Pushes and Pulls in the Park
desc: telling a push from a pull, and comparing a strong push with a gentle one
dir: Answer out loud. Do not say push or pull for the student.
text: A push moves something away from you. A pull brings it toward you.
qs: Theo sits on the park swing. Wren stands behind him and sends him away from her. Is that a push or a pull?
Wren opens the shed door by taking the handle and bringing it toward her. Is that a push or a pull?
key: a push
a pull

title: Pushes and Pulls in the Park
desc: deciding from test results whether a push changed how far a thing moved, and whether something changed its direction
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Wren set up six blocks in a row and rolled the same ball at them twice. She counted the blocks that fell. Roll Blocks that fell a gentle roll 1 a strong roll 6
qs: Which roll knocked down more blocks, and how many?
Another ball is rolling straight down the sidewalk. Theo holds a board out on one side of it. The ball hits the board and goes off a new way. Did the board change where the ball was going?
key: the strong roll, 6 blocks. The gentle roll only knocked down 1.
Yes. It changed the direction the ball was going. Accept it turned it, it sent it sideways, it bounced it.

title: Sun and Shade on the Street
desc: telling what sunlight does to a surface it shines on
dir: Answer out loud. If you can, feel a sunny spot and a shady spot together first.
text: Here are two cups of water. The water is cold. Both were set out. They sit on the porch. Both went out together. The time was the same. One sits in the open sun
qs: By the middle of the day one cup has warm water in it. Which one, the cup in the sunlight or the cup in the shadow?
The bench on the sunny side of the street has no frost left on it. The bench in the shadow still has frost. The two benches are exactly the same. What made the difference?
key: the cup in the open sunlight
the sunlight. One bench got sunlight on it and the other did not, so the sunlight is what warmed the first bench and melted its frost.

title: Sun and Shade on the Street
desc: designing and drawing a cover that keeps a spot out of the sunlight
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Wren's cups hold new sprouts. They sit on the windowsill. The afternoon sunlight pours straight in. The little sprouts go limp. Draw something that keeps the af
qs: Draw your shade for the cups of sprouts.
Point to where the sunlight comes in and tell me how your shade keeps the cups cooler.
key: Any cover drawn BETWEEN the window and the cups, or above them. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one still counts. A cover drawn behind the cups is partial: ask which way the sunlig
Something like: it blocks the sun, the sun cannot get to them, it puts them in a shadow.

title: Solving a Problem in Town
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking a question about it
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem? The rain soaks the notices, or the board is made of wood?
Ask me one question about the board that would help you fix this.
key: The rain soaks the notices and nobody can read them.

Any real question: how big is the board, which way does the rain come in, how many notices go up, is there a roof anywhere nearby, could the paper be covered. A statement is not a question, so ask onc

title: Solving a Problem in Town
desc: drawing something whose shape would solve the problem
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would keep the notices dry, like a little slanted roof over the board, a clear flap that lifts, or a box with a lid on the front.
qs: Draw your fix.
Tell me what you drew and how its shape keeps the rain off the paper.
key: Anything that would turn rain away from the paper: a roof or ledge above it, a slanted top, a clear sheet over the front, a lid, a case. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one earns c
Naming it is what shows intent. Something like: the roof sends the rain off the side, the flap covers the paper, the lid shuts the rain out.

title: Solving a Problem in Town
desc: comparing test results from two fixes for the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The town put up 10 notices, tried two fixes, and counted how many were still dry after the rain. Fix Notices still dry a slanted roof over the whole board 8 a s
qs: Which fix worked better?
How do you know?
key: the slanted roof over the whole board
Because 8 notices stayed dry under the roof and only 3 stayed dry with the tape. The reason has to come from the chart, not from liking roofs.

title: Rules and Doing Right
desc: following rules, knowing what happens when they are broken, and naming an honest choice
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What did Theo choose to do? Put the chalk back and say so, or leave it in his pocket and say nothing?
One rule at the park is wait your turn at the ladder. What might go wrong if nobody waited their turn?
key: He put the chalk back and said so.
Somebody gets bumped or pushed, it stops being safe, children argue, somebody never gets a turn. Any real consequence counts.

title: Maps and Places
desc: reading map symbols, telling land from water, and naming places in a town
dir: Look at the map. Answer out loud.
text: Here is a map. It shows the town. The blue line is the creek. It runs down the middle. The gray lines are roads. The school is on one side. The creek runs betwe
qs: On this map, which part is the water and which parts are the roads?
The bridge crosses the creek. Is the bridge over the water or under the water?
key: The blue line is the water, which is the creek. The gray lines are the roads.
over the water

title: Left and Right
desc: telling where things are with left and right, near and far, and in front and behind
dir: Look at each picture. Point or answer out loud.
text: A B C
key: Ask: Look at picture A. Point to the one on the left. (the lantern)
Ask: Point to the one on the right. (the star)

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: recognizing national symbols of the country
dir: Look at both pictures. Answer out loud.
qs: One of these is our country's flag. Which one is it?
The other one is a bald eagle, and that is a symbol of our country too. Name one place where you have seen our flag.
key: the one with the stars and stripes. Accept pointing. Accept the flag of our country or the American flag.
Any real place: a school, a post office, a park, outside a building, on a coin, at a game.

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: telling how life long ago was different from life today, and what a commemorative holiday is for
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Long ago there were no electric lights in a house.
qs: Long ago, what did a family use to see after dark, an oil lantern they had to fill and light, or a lamp you switch on?
How does a light come on in your house today?
key: an oil lantern they had to fill and light
Any real answer: a switch on the wall, a button, a cord you pull, a lamp you plug in, asking a speaker to turn it on. Naming today's way is the then-and-now half of this standard.

title: Night Sound Check
desc: blending, segmenting, and isolating sounds, counting syllables, and telling long from short vowels in spoken words
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the sounds and words out loud.
text: Listen. Then say it.
key: Blend these sounds: /l/ /a/ /m/ /p/ (lamp)
Blend these sounds: /s/ /t/ /ar/ (star)

title: First Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the initial sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the first sound.
qs: What is the first sound in sun?
What is the first sound in map?
key: The sound /s/. Say the sound, not the letter name.
The sound /m/. Say the sound, not the letter name.

title: Middle Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the medial vowel sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the middle sound.
qs: What is the middle sound in cat?
What is the middle sound in pig?
key: The short vowel sound /a/.
The short vowel sound /i/.

title: Night Words
desc: reading words with digraphs, blends, final e, vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, endings, and two syllables
dir: Read each word out loud. The last one is a silly word. Just sound it out.
key: Count each word read correctly. zide is a silly word: listen for the long i that the final e makes.

Watch for: ch digraph (chin), nk ending (bank), blend plus a vowel team (glow), double letters (bell), final e (home), igh (night), three-letter blend plus a vowel team (street), r-controlled ar (star

title: How Many Parts?
desc: using the rule that every syllable has a vowel sound to find the number of syllables in a printed word
dir: Read the word to yourself. Tell how many syllables, or parts, it has. Clap it if that helps.
text: sunset cat rabbit bed
key: Point to “sunset”. How many syllables? (2)
Point to “cat”. How many syllables? (1)

title: Our Town Tonight
desc: a 75-word night-town story read aloud
dir: Look at the three pictures. Then read the story out loud in your best reading voice.
text: a paper lantern the main street the bridge over the river Our Town Tonight Tonight our town looks like a big bowl. The bowl is full of light. Long ropes hang ov
key: 75 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Point to the three pictures first so lantern, street, and bridge are clear before the student reads.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: a paper lantern the main street the bridge over the river Our Town Tonight Tonight our town looks like a big bowl. The bowl is full of light. Long ropes hang ov
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the story about? What happened first?” (a summary or answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Noor's Lantern
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about a story the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: Noor's Lantern Noor made a lantern. She used red paper and thin sticks. She carried it down to the river. She wanted to hang it up. It would go with the rest. B
qs: What did Noor make?
What was it made of?
key: A lantern
Red paper and thin sticks

title: Sentence Spotter
desc: finding sentences by their first word, capital letter, and end mark
dir: Look at the sentences. Answer out loud.
text: The lanterns glow. Can you see the river?
qs: How many sentences do you see? How can you tell?
Read the first word of the second sentence. What kind of letter does it start with?
key: 2 sentences. Each one starts with a capital letter and ends with an end mark
The word is Can. It starts with a capital, or uppercase, C

title: Town Fix It
desc: spoken grammar items (past tense, plural nouns, subject and verb match, joining two sentences, describing words, place words)
dir: Listen to your teacher read each one. Say your answer out loud.
qs: Today we walk to the bridge. Last night we ____.
One lantern, two ____.
key: walked
lanterns

title: Which Word Fits?
desc: using indefinite pronouns such as everyone, anyone, someone, something, and nothing
dir: Listen to the sentence. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? ___ in our class likes to sing. (Everyone / Nothing)
Which word fits? I looked in the box, but there was ___ in it. (anyone / nothing)
key: Everyone. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)
nothing. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)

title: Whose Is It?
desc: using possessive nouns to show who owns something
dir: Listen. Say the answer. For the last one, you can point to the right one on paper.
qs: Maya has a hat. Whose hat is it? Say it with an apostrophe s.
The dog has a bone. Whose bone is it? Say it with an apostrophe s.
key: Maya’s hat. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)
the dog’s bone. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)

title: Commands and Big Feelings
desc: producing imperative (command) and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts
dir: Listen. Say your answer out loud in a full sentence.
qs: Tell a friend to wash their hands. Say it as a command.
You get a surprise present! Say one sentence that shows a big feeling.
key: A command such as “Wash your hands.”
An exclamation, for example “Wow, I love it!”

title: Print the Alphabet
desc: printing all upper- and lowercase letters
dir: On your paper, print each big letter and its small letter. Print them in order. Hold up your paper when you finish.
text: A a B b C c D d E e F f G g H h I i J j K k L l M m N n O o P p Q q R r S s T t U u V v W w X x Y y Z z
key: Look at the paper. Mark each letter pair where both the capital and the small letter are formed correctly and sit on the line. Letters may be uneven. Count a pair when each letter can be told from the
Check the tall letters (b, d, f, h, k, l, t), the letters that drop below the line (g, j, p, q, y), and the look-alikes (b and d, p and q).

title: Listen Up
desc: asking and answering questions about a text read aloud
dir: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about a job from long ago. Then answer out loud.
text: Listen.
key: Ask: What was a lamplighter's job? (to light the oil lamps on the street corners, and to put them out again)
Ask: What did the lamplighter carry? (a long pole with a small flame on the end)

title: Tell Me About It
desc: describing a thing with relevant details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about something you can see out a window at night. What is it? What does it look like? How do you feel when you see it?
key: Names the thing and gives 2 or more details about it (SL.1.4)
Gives 2 or more details about what it looks like, and they stay on this one thing (SL.1.4)

title: Two-Step Directions
desc: giving, restating, and following simple two-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear, say it back, and give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do what your teacher says. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once, without repeating: “Touch your nose, then clap two times.” (does both steps, in the right order)
Say once, without repeating: “Stand up, then turn around.” (does both steps, in the right order)

title: Person, Place, Thing, Event
desc: describing a person, a place, a thing, and an event with relevant details, and saying ideas and feelings clearly
dir: Listen to your teacher. Tell about each one. Use lots of details.
text: Tell about a person, a place, a thing, and something that happened.
key: Say: “Tell me about someone in your family or a friend.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the person, such as who they are, what they look like, or what they do)
Say: “Tell me about a place you like to go.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the place, such as what is there or what you do there)

title: Pack the Night Walk
desc: using a provided chart to answer a question in writing
dir: Look at the chart. Write 1 sentence on your paper and hold it up.
text: The crew wants to write down every star they can see from the bridge. What will they take? Use the chart.
key: Finds the answer in the chart. Your help is fine: read the two columns out loud and point to the row headings
Writes a sentence drawn from the chart, such as: They will take the small notebook

title: Remember and Tell
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question
dir: Think about what happened to you. Tell your teacher your answer out loud. You can draw it, too.
qs: Think about getting ready for bed. Tell me two things you do.
Think about breakfast. What did you eat today or yesterday? Tell me about it.
key: Gives two real things the student does at bedtime. Any true answer counts.
Names a real food or meal from experience. (They may draw first, then tell. Write down what they say if you want a record.)

title: Night Journal
desc: an opinion piece about where to watch the night sky
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Would you rather watch the night sky from the bridge over the river, or from your own window? Write what you think and tell why. the bridge over the river your
key: Names the topic: watching the night sky from the bridge or from a window (W.1.1)
States an opinion, which one the student would pick (W.1.1)

title: Night Journal
desc: a narrative about a night the student remembers, told in order
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about a night you remember. Tell two things that happened, in order. Use the words first and then. End by telling how it felt. a night you remember what y
key: Tells about two or more things that happened, in an order that makes sense (W.1.3)
Includes some detail about what happened, not just a list (W.1.3)

title: Why Stars Look Small
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the six lines. Then answer out loud.
text: Stars are very big. Stars are very hot. But stars look small to us. That is because they are far away. Our sun is a star too. The sun looks big. That is because
qs: Why do stars look small to us?
The text says our sun is a what?
key: Because they are far away. Line 4 says it.
A star. Line 5 says our sun is a star too.

title: One True Thing
desc: a short informative piece that names a topic, gives a fact, and closes
dir: Write on your paper. Then hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Pick one: the moon, a paper lantern, or an owl. Write its name. Then write one or two true things about it. Finish with one sentence that ends it. the moon a pa
key: Names the topic, the one thing the writing is about (W.1.2)
Supplies at least one true fact about it, such as: The moon is in the night sky. A lantern is made of paper. An owl is awake at night (W.1.2)

title: Lantern Hops
desc: counting on and counting back or up to add and subtract
dir: Count out loud like you are hopping from lantern to lantern. Say each answer.
text: Each lantern on the rope is one hop.
qs: Start at 7. Count on 6. Where do you land? What adding sentence is that?
Start at 15. Count back 3. Where do you land? What take away sentence is that?
key: Counts 14, 13, 12. Lands on 12. 15 - 3 = 12

title: Count the Lanterns
desc: counting, reading, and writing numerals to 120 and counting objects
dir: Count and read out loud. Write your numbers on your paper and hold it up.
text: The town counts every lantern before it goes up on the rope.
qs: Count out loud from 88 to 104.
Read these numbers out loud: 67, 101, 115.
key: Sixty-seven, one hundred one, one hundred fifteen

title: Lantern Problems
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 20, with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen to each story problem. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer.
text: The town hangs its lanterns on long ropes across the street.
qs: One rope holds 9 lanterns and the other rope holds 8. How many lanterns in all?
There were 14 lanterns lit. The wind blew out 6 of them. How many are still lit?
key: 17 lanterns (9 + 8 = 17)
8 lanterns (14 - 6 = 8)

title: Smart Adding
desc: using turn-around facts and making ten as strategies to add
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
qs: 6 + 9 = 15. So what is 9 + 6?
Dev says 7 + 4 is easier if he turns it around and thinks 4 + 7. Is that OK? What is the total?
key: 15. Knows it without counting because the two numbers just switch places
Yes, that is fine. The order does not change the total. Both make 11

title: Ropes of Ten
desc: place value in two-digit numbers (bundles of ten and leftover ones)
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud.
text: A full rope holds 10 lanterns. A long block stands for one full rope of ten, and a small cube stands for one loose lantern.
qs: Look at the picture. How many full ropes of ten do you see, and how many loose lanterns? What number is that?
In the number 17, what does the 1 stand for? What does the 7 stand for?
key: 3 ropes of ten and 4 loose. That is 34
The 1 stands for one ten, which is ten lanterns. The 7 stands for seven ones

title: Add Up the Street
desc: adding within 100 (a two-digit number plus a one-digit number and plus a multiple of ten)
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Say your answer and tell how you got it.
text: The crew counts the lanterns street by street.
qs: River Street has 23 lanterns. The crew adds 5 more. How many now?
Pine Street has 47 lanterns. The crew adds 30 more. How many now?
key: 28 (23 + 5 = 28. Only the ones change)
77 (47 + 30 = 77. Adding tens to tens: 4 tens and 3 tens is 7 tens)

title: Explain Your Adding
desc: adding within 100 with a drawing, relating it to a written equation, and explaining the reasoning with tens and ones
dir: Solve on your paper. Draw tens and ones. Write the equation. Then tell how you added.
qs: Add 36 + 7. Draw tens and ones, write the equation, and tell how you added.
Why did you add the tens with the tens and the ones with the ones?
key: 36 + 7 = 43. The drawing shows tens and ones, the equation matches, and the explanation says tens were added to tens and ones to ones (and that ten ones were made into a new ten when needed).
Because tens are worth ten and ones are worth one. They are different amounts, so like parts go together.

title: Take Away Tens
desc: subtracting multiples of ten from multiples of ten within 100
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, tell how you know.
text: Every rope that comes down takes ten lanterns off the street.
qs: There are 70 lanterns up. Three ropes of ten come down. 70 - 30 is what?
key: 40 (7 tens take away 3 tens is 4 tens)

title: Measure the Rope
desc: measuring length as a whole number of same-size units laid end to end
dir: Look at the blocks under the rope and the scarf. Answer out loud.
qs: How many blocks long is the rope?
How many blocks long is the scarf?
key: 6 blocks
4 blocks

title: Lantern Tally
desc: reading a graph with three categories and answering how many more and how many in all
dir: Look at the graph. Answer out loud.
text: The crew counted the lanterns on three streets and made this graph.
qs: How many lanterns are on Pine Street?
Which street has the fewest lanterns?
key: Bridge Street, with 4

title: Make a Graph
desc: organizing and representing data with up to three categories, and answering questions about the total and about how many more or less
dir: Look at the list. Make a tally chart or a picture graph on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: Ten kids told us their favorite fruits. apple banana apple grape apple banana apple grape banana apple
key: A chart or graph with apple 5, banana 3, grape 2. Each item is counted once. Tally marks, pictures, or squares all work. Labels are on each group.
10 (the total of all three groups)

title: Lantern Clock
desc: telling and writing time to the hour and the half hour
dir: Look at each clock. Say the time out loud. Write the last one on your paper.
text: The clock on the bridge tells the crew when to light the ropes.
qs: What time is Clock A?
What time is Clock B?
key: 6:00, said as six o'clock. The minute hand is on the 12.
8:30, said as eight thirty or half past eight. Watch for a student who says nine thirty because the hour hand has moved halfway to the 9.

title: Fair Shares
desc: halves and fourths of circles and rectangles, and knowing that equal shares must be the same size
dir: Look at the three shapes. Answer out loud.
qs: Shape A is cut into 2 equal parts. What do we call one of those parts?
Shape B is cut into 4 equal parts. What do we call one of those parts, and how many of them make the whole rectangle?
key: A half, or one half. Two halves make the whole circle.
A fourth, or a quarter. 4 of them make the whole rectangle.

title: Copy an Owl Feather
desc: naming the job an animal body part does, then designing a tool that copies it to solve a human problem
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer the first out loud. Draw the second on your paper and hold it up.
text: An owl flies almost without a sound. Each wing feather has a front edge. It is not smooth. It is split into a soft fringe. The fringe breaks up the rushing air.
qs: How does a soft fringe on the edge of a feather make an owl's flight quiet?
Draw something for the door that copies the owl's soft fringed feather edge.
key: It breaks up the rushing air instead of letting it slap against a hard edge, so there is much less noise. Any answer about softening or breaking up the air or the sound counts.

Any soft edging: a strip of felt or cloth along the door frame, a soft pad where the door meets the frame, a brush along the bottom. A hard block is partial, so ask what the owl's feather edge is like

title: Owl Parents
desc: finding a pattern in what a parent animal does and what the young do in answer, and saying how it helps the young
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What does the parent owl do every single time it lands on the branch?
What do the young owls do when they hear the low hoot?
key: It gives one low hoot. Every time is what makes it a pattern.
They answer with a thin hiss, which tells the parent where they are.

title: Owl Parents
desc: making observations that young plants and animals are like their parents but not exactly like them
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
text: A new shoot coming up from a bulb. The grown plant it will become. A young owl and the owl that is its parent.
qs: Name one way the new shoot is like the grown plant.
Name one way the new shoot is not exactly like the grown plant.
key: Both are green, both come up out of the same bulb, both have a stem. Any likeness counts.
The shoot is much shorter, it has no flower, its leaves are not open yet. Any difference counts.

title: Stars That Come Back
desc: finding a pattern in sky observations made across a year and using it to predict what comes next
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The lamplighter writes down which group of bright stars is overhead at nine at night. Time of year Which star group was overhead last winter the hunter last sum
qs: Which star group was overhead last winter?
Which star group was overhead last summer?
key: the hunter
the swan

title: Stars That Come Back
desc: relating the number of hours of daylight to the time of year from observations made across a year
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The lamplighter wrote down how many hours the street lamps had to be lit. Month Hours of daylight Hours the lamps burned January 10 14 July 15 9
qs: Which month had more hours of daylight?
In which month did the lamps have to burn longer?
key: July, 15 hours
January, 14 hours of lamp light

title: Sound in the Hall
desc: planning an investigation showing that a shaking material makes sound and that a sound can make a material shake
dir: If you have a glass of water and a spoon, try the first part. Either way, answer out loud.
text: Fill a glass halfway with water. Tap the side of the glass with a spoon and watch the top of the water. Now stretch a balloon over the open mouth of a jar and t
qs: When you tap the glass and hear the ring, what happens to the top of the water?
Hold the side of the glass with your hand while it is ringing. What happens to the sound, and why?
key: Little ripples run across it. The glass is shaking, and the shaking passes into the water.
The ring stops, because your hand stops the glass shaking. No shaking, no sound.

title: The Dark Hallway
desc: accounting for why an object in darkness can be seen only when light shines on it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The hallway of the meeting house has no window. Late at night, with the lamp out, it is completely dark.
qs: A silver key is hanging on a hook in that hallway. Can you see it in the dark? Say why or why not.
What has to happen before you can see it?
key: No. No light reaches the key, and a thing can only be seen when light shines on it and comes back to your eyes.
Light has to reach it: a lamp lit, a flashlight, or a door opened to let light in.

title: The Dark Hallway
desc: using test results to tell what happens when different materials are put in the path of a beam of light
dir: Look at the test results. Answer out loud.
text: One lamp beam was pointed at four things in the hallway and what it did was written down. What was put in the beam What the beam did a clean window pane went st
qs: Which thing let the light through without changing it?
Which thing let the light through but spread it out and softened it?
key: the clean window pane
the paper lantern shade

title: Across the Square
desc: designing a device that uses light or sound to send a message over a distance too far to shout
dir: Draw your answer on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: The town square is wide, and the houses on the far street cannot hear anyone calling from the middle of it.
qs: Draw a device in the square that tells the far street that the meeting is about to begin. It has to use light or sound.
What is your device called, and is it a light signal or a sound signal?
key: Any device that carries light or sound across the square: a bell in the tower, a horn, a drum, a bright lamp hoisted on a pole, a lamp flashed on and off.
Names it and says which one it uses.

title: Fix the Falling List
desc: naming a problem people want to change, asking a question about it, and saying what to observe first
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem the class wants to change?
What question would you ask first if you wanted to fix this?
key: The paper list curls up and falls off the wall, so the jobs on it cannot be read.
Any real question: what is sticking it up, how big is the sheet, is the wall rough or smooth, does the door make a draught, how heavy is the paper. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Fix the Falling List
desc: making a simple drawing of a fix and explaining how the shape of the object makes it work
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
text: Draw something that keeps the list flat on the wall all week.
qs: Draw your fix on the wall with the list.
Point to the part that holds the paper and tell me its shape.
key: Any real fix: clips along the top, a stiff board behind the paper, a frame round the edge, a rod across the bottom, pins at all four corners, a pocket the sheet slides into.
Names a shape: a long bar across the top, a square frame, a flat stiff board, a narrow slot.

title: Which Holder Worked
desc: comparing the data from tests of two objects built to solve the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two holders were tested on the same wall for ten days each. Holder Days the list fell down, out of 10 a clip bar across the top 0 tape at two corners 5
qs: Which of the two held the list better?
Tell me the numbers you used to decide.
key: the clip bar across the top
The list never fell with the clip bar, 0 days out of 10, and it fell on 5 days out of 10 with the tape. The numbers have to be in the answer.

title: Rules for a Fresh Start
desc: telling a right from a responsibility and explaining why a group writes rules together
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: Everyone got a turn to say an idea. Is getting a turn a right or a responsibility?
Looking after the books is something each person does. Is that a right or a responsibility?
key: a right
a responsibility

title: The Town Square Map
desc: giving an exact grid location, describing a relative location, and telling a physical feature from a built one
dir: Look at the map grid. Answer out loud.
text: A map of the town square, drawn on a grid. 1 2 3 A B C shops the clock tower the old elm the stone bridge the river
qs: Find the clock tower. Give its exact spot on the grid, the letter and the number.
Where is the old elm compared to the clock tower? Use words like above, below, left of, or right of.
key: A2. Both parts are needed.
Below the clock tower, in the same column.

title: The Town Square Map
desc: naming built features of a familiar place and recognizing that people in one place come from many different places
dir: Answer out loud.
text: This town has a first street. There are eleven houses on it. Families live in them. They came from eight different places. Four different languages are spoken t
qs: Do the people on one street all come from the same place? Say how you know from the story.
Think of your own street or block. Name three things on it that people built.
key: No. Eleven families came from eight different places and four languages are spoken there.
Any three built things: houses, a sidewalk, a mailbox, a fence, a lamp post, a road, a shop.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: recognizing national symbols in everyday places and naming a building that stands for the country's government
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Look at a coin or a one dollar bill and you will find an eagle on it. The eagle is a symbol. It stands for the United States. So is the White House. The preside
qs: Where in your own pocket or purse could you find a symbol of the United States?
What is the White House, and why is a building put on stamps and coins instead of just being a place where somebody lives?
key: On a coin or on a dollar bill. Accept naming the eagle on a coin.
It is where the president lives and works. It is on stamps and coins because it stands for the country's government, not just for one person's house.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: comparing everyday life long ago with life today and telling what changed from what stayed the same
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Washing the clothes. Long ago Today how they were washed rubbed by hand on a ridged board turned by a machine how they were dried hung on a line outdoors a mach
qs: Long ago, how did people get the clothes clean?
How are clothes washed today?
key: Rubbed by hand on a ridged board.
Turned by a machine.

title: Lantern Word Flip
desc: reading words with silent e, vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, two syllables, a prefix, a suffix, and an irregular spelling
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are made-up words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word in order. spleet and blorn are made-up words: listen for the ee team sound and the or sound.

Watch for: the -ed ending said as /d/ (glowed), igh (bright), r-controlled or plus ch (porch), a three-letter blend with ea (stream), the ou diphthong (shout), silent k with ew (knew), a compound word

title: Two-Part Long Vowel Words
desc: decoding regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels
dir: Read each word out loud. Each word has two parts.
key: Mark each word read correctly. Each word has two syllables and at least one long vowel sound, such as pa-per, mu-sic, o-pen.
If the student breaks the word into syllables and then says it smoothly, count it correct.

title: Read the Story
desc: a 105-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Juno woke before anyone else in the house. She pulled on two sweaters. Then she carried the last paper lantern down to the river. All week the crew had strung r
key: 105 words. Mark each missed word and each self-correction on the passage in the record sheet.
Note pace and expression in your notes.

title: Story Questions
desc: asking and answering who, what, why, and how questions about key details in a story
dir: Look back at the story if you need to. Then answer each question out loud.
text: The Last Lantern (click to open or close the story) Juno woke before anyone else in the house. She pulled on two sweaters. Then she carried the last paper lante
qs: Who carried the last lantern down to the river?
What did she put on before she went out?
key: Juno
Two sweaters

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Juno woke before anyone else in the house. She pulled on two sweaters. Then she carried the last paper lantern down to the river. All week the crew had strung r
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the text about? Tell me two things you remember.” (an answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Why Stars Twinkle
desc: asking and answering what, where, why, and who questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about stars. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Why Stars Twinkle A star does not blink. Far out in space it shines with a steady light. The twinkle happens much closer to you, in the air above your head. Air
qs: What makes a star seem to twinkle?
Where does the twinkle happen?
key: Moving air bends the thin beam of starlight this way and that
In the air above your head, not out at the star

title: Say It Right
desc: spoken grammar items (irregular past tense, irregular plural, reflexive pronoun, adverb, word order, joining two sentences)
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: Tonight the lanterns shine. Last night they ____.
One child, two ____.
key: shone (shined is also used, but shone is the one to listen for)
children

title: Write It Right
desc: written conventions (capital letters in place names, an apostrophe for a possessive and a contraction, a comma in a letter greeting, spelling two patterns)
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Fix this sentence: we walked along pine street to the bear river
The ladder belongs to the crew. Write the missing word: the ____ ladder
key: We walked along Pine Street to the Bear River. (capital W to start, capital P and capital S in the street name, capital B and capital R in the river name, and a period)
crew’s (apostrophe before the s)

title: Capital Letters
desc: capitalizing holidays, product names, and geographic names
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each sentence. Write it again with the right capital letters. Hold up your paper when you finish.
qs: Fix the capital letters: we eat turkey on thanksgiving.
Fix the capital letters: my family went to california in july.
key: We eat turkey on Thanksgiving.
My family went to California in July. (California; July may be accepted as a month name)

title: Use a Dictionary
desc: using a beginning dictionary and ABC order to check and correct spellings
dir: Listen. Answer out loud. If you have a beginning dictionary, you may use it.
qs: Put these words in ABC order the way a dictionary does: tiger, apple, mouse.
The guide words at the top of a dictionary page are cat and dog. Would the word cow be on this page? Tell why.
key: apple, mouse, tiger
Yes. cow comes after cat and before dog in ABC order.

title: Group Words
desc: using collective nouns
dir: Listen. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? A group of fish swimming together is called a ___. (school / pile)
Which word fits? A group of birds flying together is called a ___. (flock / bunch of rocks)
key: school. (A collective noun names a group.)
flock. (A collective noun names a group.)

title: A New Year Story
desc: a short narrative with events in order, details about actions and feelings, time words, and an ending
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: You are on the lantern crew. You are about to hang the last lantern of the night, and the rope slips out of your hand. Write a story about what happens next. Te
key: Tells about one event or a short set of events in order
Includes details about actions, thoughts, or feelings

title: Listen Up
desc: recounting and describing key ideas and details from a text read aloud
dir: Listen first. Then answer your teacher's questions out loud.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read a report from the lantern workshop.
key: Ask: What is a paper lantern made of? (a thin paper shell stretched over a frame of split bamboo, with a small light inside on a metal cup)
Ask: Describe why the whole lantern glows instead of one bright point. (the paper spreads the light out)

title: Tell Me About It
desc: telling about an experience in order, with facts and details, in clear complete sentences
dir: Tell about it out loud. Say what happened first, next, and last.
text: Tell me about a time you stayed up later than usual, or a time you were outside after dark. Where were you? What did you do? What did you see or hear? First Nex
key: Tells what happened in an order that makes sense
Gives facts that fit (where, when, who, or what)

title: Longer Directions
desc: following three- and four-step oral directions, requesting clarification when something is not understood, and giving multi-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear. Ask a question if you are not sure what to do. Then give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do the steps in order. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once: “Stand up, push in your chair, and touch the door.” (does all three steps in order)
Say once: “Draw a square, color it blue, write your name inside it, and draw a dot above it.” (does all four steps in order)

title: Plan and Tell a Story
desc: planning and delivering a short narrative presentation that recounts an event with details, a logical sequence, and a conclusion
dir: Pick one idea. Plan what you will say: the start, the middle, and the end. Then tell your story out loud.
text: Pick one: a day you will always remember, the time you tried something new, or a trip or a day away from home. Beginning Middle End
key: Plans first: says or draws what will happen at the start, the middle, and the end before telling (give about one minute to plan)
Tells one event with enough detail (who, where, and what happened)

title: The Crew Log
desc: gathering information from a provided log and recalling information from experience to answer questions
dir: Use the log to answer. Say the first two answers out loud. Write number 3 on your paper and hold it up. Then say number 4.
text: The lantern crew writes down how many lanterns went up each night, and what the weather was like.
qs: Use the log. Which night did the crew hang the most lanterns?
Which nights were clear?
key: Tuesday, with 31 lanterns
Monday and Thursday

title: Read the Signs
desc: applying grade-level phonics and word-analysis skills to decode words in text
dir: Read each line out loud. Sound out any word that is tricky.
text: The bright lanterns glowed above the crowded street. We unpacked eight boxes and relit every flame. The river carried the moonlight downstream.
key: Line 1: listen for igh in bright, the -ed ending said as /d/ in glowed, the ow diphthong in crowded, and the two syllables in lanterns.
Line 2: listen for the prefix un in unpacked, the -ed ending said as /t/ in unpacked, the irregular eigh in eight, and the prefix re in relit.

title: The Two Lanterns
desc: retelling a short fable in order and naming its lesson
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the short story. Then answer out loud.
text: The Two Lanterns A brand new lantern hung beside an old one on the rope. My paper is bright red, said the new lantern. Everyone will look at me, not at you. Tha
qs: Retell this story in your own words. Tell what happened first, next, and last.
What is the lesson of this story?
key: The retelling has the three parts in order: the new lantern boasted about its bright red paper, the wind came hard that night, and the new lantern slipped crooked while the old one held up straight an
Careful work lasts, or doing a job well matters more than looking new and bright, or do not boast. Any lesson the student can tie back to the knots or to the boasting counts. Retelling the plot again

title: What Do You Think
desc: a short opinion piece with a topic, an opinion, a reason joined by a linking word, and a closing sentence
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: You are on the lantern crew. Which job would you rather have? You could be tying the knots. The knots go on the rope. You could carry the ladder down the street
key: Introduces the topic: which crew job the writing is about (W.2.1)
States an opinion, which job the student would rather have (W.2.1)

title: Tell a Reader
desc: a short informative piece with a topic, facts or a definition, and a closing sentence
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Pick one: a paper lantern, the moon, or the river at night. Write 2 or 3 sentences that tell a reader about it. Use facts, or tell what the thing is.
key: Introduces the topic, so a reader knows what the writing is about (W.2.2)
Uses facts or a definition to develop the point, such as: A paper lantern is a thin paper shell on a bamboo frame. The paper spreads the light out (W.2.2)

title: Hang the Lanterns
desc: one-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100 with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each problem. Solve it on your paper. You can draw or write a number sentence. Say your answer.
text: The lantern crew hangs paper lanterns on ropes across the main street.
qs: A rope holds 45 lanterns. So far 28 of them are lit. How many are not lit yet?
River Street got 34 lanterns and Pine Street got 29. How many lanterns is that in all?
key: 17 lanterns (28 + a box = 45, or 45 - 28 = 17)
63 lanterns (34 + 29 = 63)

title: Boxes, Ropes, and Ones
desc: three-digit place value, including a hundred as ten tens
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud.
text: The crew packs lanterns like this. A flat is a box of 100. A long block is a rope of 10. A small cube is one loose lantern.
qs: Look at the picture. How many hundreds, tens, and ones are there? What number is that?
A box holds 100 lanterns. How many ropes of ten does it take to fill one box?
key: 2 hundreds, 4 tens, and 3 ones. That is 243
10 ropes. A hundred is the same as ten tens

title: Count Along the River
desc: counting within 1000 and skip-counting by 5s, 10s, and 100s
dir: Count out loud.
text: The crew hangs a lamp every 5 steps along the river path, so the counting goes 5, 10, 15, and on.
qs: Skip count by 5s from 65 to 105.
Skip count by 10s from 360 to 430.

title: Count by 2s
desc: skip-counting by 2s within 1000
dir: Count out loud by 2s.
qs: Count by 2s from 24 to 40. Say all the numbers.
Count by 2s from 36. Say the next five numbers.

title: Three Ways to Write It
desc: reading and writing numbers to 1000 as numerals, number names, and expanded form
dir: Say the first two answers out loud. Write the rest on your paper and hold it up.
text: The crew writes the lantern count three different ways in the logbook.
qs: Read this number out loud: 519.
What number is 600 + 30 + 8?
key: five hundred nineteen

title: Logbook Math
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with a place value strategy and relating it to a written method
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Show your work and hold it up. Say your answer.
text: Every year the crew writes down how many lanterns went up in the whole town.
qs: Last year 327 lanterns went up on the east side and 248 on the west side. How many in all? Show how you added.
The town wants 600 lanterns up this year. So far 254 are up. How many more are needed?
key: 575 lanterns (327 + 248 = 575). Listen for hundreds with hundreds, tens with tens, ones with ones, and for making a new ten.
346 more (600 - 254 = 346). This one needs two decomposes, so watch the work.

title: Why Regroup?
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with place value, and explaining why a ten or hundred is composed or decomposed
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work. Then tell why you had to regroup.
qs: Solve 53 + 29 with a drawing or a written method. Then tell why you had to make a new ten.
Solve 71 - 38. Tell why you had to take a ten apart.
key: 82. The ones made 12 (3 + 9), which is more than 9, so 10 ones were regrouped as 1 ten.
33. There were not enough ones (1 is less than 8), so 1 ten was broken into 10 ones.

title: Read the Clock
desc: telling time on an analog clock to the nearest five minutes
dir: Look at each clock. Say the time out loud.
text: The clock on the town hall tower keeps the crew on time.
key: Clock A: 7:05, said as seven oh five or five past seven. The minute hand is on the 1, and one number mark is five minutes.
Clock B: 8:30, said as eight thirty or half past eight. Watch for a student who says nine thirty because the hour hand has moved halfway to the 9.

title: Write the Time
desc: writing times to the nearest five minutes and using a.m. and p.m.
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Look at the digital clock. Write that time.
The lanterns go up at that time in the evening. Write the time again and add a.m. or p.m.
key: 6:15 p.m. (evening is after noon, so it is p.m.)

title: Time Facts
desc: knowing relationships of time such as minutes in an hour, days in a month, and weeks in a year
dir: Listen. Answer out loud.
qs: How many minutes are in one hour?
About how many days are in one month?
key: 60 minutes
Between 28 and 31 days. 30 or 31 is the usual answer.

title: Two Ropes at Once
desc: two-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100
dir: Each problem has two steps. Solve it on your paper and say your answer.
text: The crew works two ropes at a time, so most nights take two steps to count.
qs: The crew had 52 lanterns. They hung 19 on the first rope and 14 on the second rope. How many lanterns are left?
One cart carries 8 crates of lanterns. A second cart carries 9 crates. The crew unloads 6 crates at the bridge. How many crates are still on the carts?

title: Pairs and Leftovers
desc: telling odd from even by pairing, and writing an even number as a sum of two equal addends
dir: Look at the two groups. Answer out loud.
qs: Group A has 14 lanterns. Is 14 even or odd? How can you tell from the picture?
Group B has 9 lanterns. Is 9 even or odd? How can you tell?
key: Even. Every lantern in the top row has a partner below it, so they pair up with none left over.
Odd. The top row has 5 and the bottom row has 4, so one lantern in the top row has no partner.

title: Rows on the Cart
desc: finding the total in a rectangular array and writing it as a sum of equal addends
dir: Look at the cart. Answer out loud.
qs: How many rows of lanterns are on the cart, and how many lanterns are in each row?
Write an addition sentence that gives the total.
key: 3 rows, with 5 lanterns in each row.
5 + 5 + 5 = 15. One addend per row. 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15 also counts, as long as the student says it is one addend for each column.

title: Pick the Tool
desc: measuring a length with a ruler, choosing a sensible measuring tool, and measuring a real object with a ruler
dir: Look at the ruler. Answer out loud. For the last one, get a real ruler and measure.
qs: How long is the lantern hook?
How do you know where to line the hook up on the ruler?
key: 4 inches. The hook starts at 0 and ends at the 4.
The end of the hook goes on the 0, not on the edge of the ruler. Starting at 1 by mistake gives 3 or 5 instead of 4.

title: Count the Coins
desc: solving word problems with coins, using the cent symbol
dir: Look at the coins. Answer out loud.
qs: How much money is this in all? Say it in cents.
A sheet of lantern paper costs 45 cents. You pay with 2 quarters. How much change do you get back?
key: 28 cents, written 28¢. Two dimes make 20¢, the nickel makes 25¢, and the three pennies make 28¢.
5 cents, written 5¢. Two quarters is 50¢, and 50 - 45 = 5.

title: Color Graph
desc: reading a single-unit picture graph, comparing two rows, and drawing a row of a graph
dir: Look at the picture graph. Answer out loud. Then draw on your paper.
qs: How many gold lanterns are on this rope?
How many more gold lanterns are there than violet ones?
key: 7 gold lanterns.

title: Count the Sides
desc: naming flat shapes by their number of sides and angles, and drawing a shape with given attributes
