dir: Look at the four shapes. Answer out loud. Then draw on your paper.
qs: How many sides does Shape C have, and what is that shape called?
Which shape is a hexagon? How do you know?
key: 5 sides, so it is a pentagon. It has 5 angles too.
Shape D. A hexagon has 6 sides, and Shape D is the one with 6.

title: Draw a Picture Graph
desc: drawing a picture graph from a data set with four categories and solving put-together, take-apart, and compare problems
dir: Look at the table. Draw a picture graph on your paper. Use one picture for each 1. Then answer out loud.
text: Favorite fruits: number of kids Choice Number of kids Apple 6 Banana 4 Grape 3 Pear 2
qs: Draw a picture graph of the table. Give it a title and label each row.
How many kids chose Apple and Banana together?
key: A picture graph with 6 symbols for Apple, 4 symbols for Banana, 3 symbols for Grape, 2 symbols for Pear. Each symbol stands for 1, the symbols are the same size and lined up, and the rows are labeled.

title: Draw a Bar Graph
desc: drawing a bar graph with a single-unit scale from a data set and solving put-together, take-apart, and compare problems
dir: Look at the table. Draw a bar graph on your paper. Count by ones up the side. Then answer out loud.
text: Ways to get to school: number of kids Choice Number of kids Walk 3 Bus 7 Car 5 Bike 2
qs: Draw a bar graph of the table. Give it a title, label each bar, and number the side by ones.
How many kids chose Car and Bike together?
key: A bar graph with bars of height 3 for Walk, 7 for Bus, 5 for Car, 2 for Bike, a title, labels, and a side scale counting by ones that starts at 0.

title: Three Bulbs in the Workshop Window
desc: reading the results of a plant test and planning a fair test of one thing a plant needs
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Then answer out loud.
text: Three flower bulbs were put in jars in the workshop at the start of the year and checked three weeks later. Jar What it got After three weeks 1 water touching t
qs: Which jar did best, and what did it get?
Jar 3 was watered and still grew 9 centimeters. Why is it almost white and why has it no bud?
key: Jar 1, a 14 centimeter green shoot with a bud. It got both water and light.

It was in a dark cupboard with no light. The bulb had food stored inside it, which is why it got tall, but without light it cannot make more food, so it stays white and has nothing spare for a flower.

title: Three Bulbs in the Workshop Window
desc: making a simple model that does the job an animal does when it moves seeds
dir: Draw your model on your paper. Then tell your teacher about it.
text: Down by the river, seeds have tiny hooks. They catch in a dog's thick coat. The dog is passing by. They are carried along the path. Then they work loose and dro
qs: Draw your model. Label the part the seed hooks onto and show how it comes loose again.
Which animal job does your model copy, and why does the seed need to come loose at some point?
key: Any model with a rough or looped carrying surface and a way for the seed to work free: rough cloth on a tube, a loop of fabric with a shake, a brush that can be tapped. The two labelled parts are what
It copies an animal carrying seeds in its coat to a new place. The seed has to come loose or it would never reach the ground, and a seed that never reaches soil cannot grow.

title: The Riverbank and the Stone Wall
desc: comparing the kinds of living things found in two different habitats
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both lists. Answer out loud.
text: Two children looked for living things in two places, twenty minutes in each, and wrote down what they found. The wet riverbank The dry top of the old stone wall
qs: How many kinds of living things are on the riverbank list?
Which place has more different kinds of living things?
key: 10. Three reeds and rushes, two snails, one frog, one heron, one water beetle and two willows.
the wet riverbank

title: One Night, or a Canyon
desc: using two sources as evidence that some Earth events happen quickly and some happen slowly
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both notes. Answer out loud.
text: Two notes about this river, from two different places. Where it came from What it says the town water office record On one night of high water the bank below th
qs: Which note tells about a change that happened in one night?
Which note tells about a change that has taken many thousands of years?
key: The water office record, the bank falling in and three paces of path lost in one night.
The display board at the gorge, the river cutting down through rock for many thousands of years.

title: One Night, or a Canyon
desc: telling where water is found on Earth and whether it is solid or liquid
dir: Answer out loud.
text: There is water all through this town, and not all of it is in the river.
qs: Name three places in or near this town where you would find water.
Most of the water on Earth is in the ocean and it is salty. Is the water in this river salty or fresh, and how would you know?
key: Any three: the river, the canal, a well, the rain barrel, clouds, frost or ice, under the ground, the town pipes.
Fresh. You can tell because people and animals drink it and crops are watered with it, and salty water would kill the plants. Accept tasting it or boiling it away and finding no salt.

title: Holding the Bank, and a Map of the Town
desc: comparing two things built to stop water from washing the land away
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The river keeps eating into the bank beside the footpath. The town tried two ways to hold it and measured how much bank was lost in a year. What was put along t
qs: Which one held the bank best in that first year?
How do you know, using the numbers in the chart?
key: the facing of heavy stones, with only 5 centimeters lost
Only 5 centimeters of bank was lost behind the stones, 10 centimeters behind the willows, and 60 centimeters where there was nothing. The reason must come from the numbers.

title: Holding the Bank, and a Map of the Town
desc: making a model of an area that shows the shapes of the land and the bodies of water in it
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Make your own model map of the town. Put in the hill with the clock tower on it, the flat market square, the river, and the lake the river runs into. Add a key
qs: Draw your model map with the hill, the flat square, the river and the lake on it.
Show me your key. Which parts are land and which parts are water?
key: All four on the page and told apart by shape or colour: the hill as a bump or as rings, the square left flat, the river as a line, the lake as a closed shape the river reaches.
Points to each part and reads the key. The key is what makes this a model and not just a picture.

title: Sorting the Lantern Workshop
desc: describing materials by properties you can see or feel and sorting them into groups
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Four things from the workshop bench, and what was noticed about each one. Item Material What was noticed a lantern shade paper thin, bends easily, light shines
qs: Sort the four items into a hard group and a group that bends easily.
Two of them let light through. Which two, and which one of those two would you use for a shade?
key: Hard: the wire hoop and the glass bead. Bends easily: the paper shade and the wool string.
The paper shade and the glass bead. The paper, because it is thin and bends so it can be shaped round a frame, and because light spreads through it instead of going straight through like glass.

title: Sorting the Lantern Workshop
desc: using test data to choose the material that suits a job
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The workshop needs a shade material for lanterns that hang outside along the river path. Three materials were tested on the same lamp, outside, through one damp
qs: Which material should the outdoor shades be made of?
Which two pieces of the chart make you sure?
key: the waxed paper
The glow was bright through it and it had no damage after a damp evening. Both columns have to be used, not just one.

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: telling how a thing built from a few pieces can be taken apart and built into something new
dir: Answer out loud. You may draw if it helps.
text: A lantern frame is made of wire. It has 12 short pieces. It has 8 ties. One of the makers undid every tie. He laid the wire out straight. It lay on the bench.
qs: The frame is gone. Are the wire pieces gone too? What is on the bench now?
Build something new in your head out of those 12 wire pieces and 8 ties. What is it, and how do the pieces go together?
key: No. All 12 wire pieces and all 8 ties are still there. They are the same pieces, just not tied together as a lantern frame any more.
Any real thing from 12 wire pieces and 8 ties: a star, a basket, a bird feeder hook, a spinner for the wind, a frame for a paper fish, a plant support. Listen for how the pieces join, because that is

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: arguing with evidence that some heating and cooling changes can be undone and some cannot
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two things happened in the workshop on the same evening. What happened A block of candle wax was warmed in a tin and ran into a smooth pool. A sheet of paper wa
qs: Take the tin of melted wax off the heat and let it stand overnight. What happens to it?
Take the brown brittle paper away from the lamp and let it stand overnight. Does it go back to white paper?
key: It goes hard again and is a block of wax, the shape of the tin.
No. It stays brown and brittle. Cooling does nothing for it.

title: The Lanterns That Tangle
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking a question about it
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the note. Answer out loud.
text: The paper lanterns hang from a long line. The line is above the river path. Each one hangs on a short piece of string. The wind comes up the river. The lanterns
qs: What is the problem the makers want to fix? Say it in one sentence.
Ask one question that would help you fix it.
key: The lanterns spin in the wind and their strings twist together into a knot. Naming the spinning and twisting, not the untangling, is the problem.

Any real question: how long are the strings, how far apart are the lanterns, how heavy is a lantern, which way does the wind come, how high is the line. A statement is not a question, so ask once more

title: The Lanterns That Tangle
desc: drawing a design and telling how its shape does the job
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.

No lanterns tangled and none were damaged with the rods, while 3 tangled and 2 were damaged with the weights. Both columns have to be used, not just the tangling.

Lines 1 and 3, finishing the lanterns yesterday and winding the clock this morning.

the people we vote for in Congress. A town council makes rules only for its own town.

title: Someone Who Made a Difference

curious. Any reason taken from the text: he asked questions nobody could answer, he kept thinking in his spare time even when his job was checking papers.

What does the ending mean in careful? What does careful mean?

-ful means full of. careful means full of care.

Proxima Centauri. Reads “The closest star after our sun is called Proxima Centauri.” (RI.3.1)

title: The Goal Card
desc: asking and answering story questions using the exact words in the text

Reads “His goal was to swim the whole length of the pool without stopping.” (RL.3.1)

Nonliteral. It means everyone on the hill went completely quiet and still. The story says “nobody said a word” right before it. (RL.3.4, nonliteral language)

Last night we sang a song by the water. (L.3.1, irregular past tense verb)

The town will light the lanterns and will sing by the river. Both verbs need to change, so accept “will light the lanterns and sing by the river” too. (L.3.1, simple future tense)

key: each other
one another or each other

What does the word small do in the sentence? What kind of word is it?
key: Dog is a noun. It names the animal the sentence is about.
Small is an adjective. It tells about the dog (what kind).

Short notes in the student’s own words, not copied sentences.

Each text measures the distance a different way. How does Old Light do it. How does Counting the Years do it?

Adds relevant descriptive details that help the listener picture it, such as what it looked like, sounded like, or felt like. Details that wander off the topic do not count. (SL.3.4, relevant descript

title: The Lantern Line
desc: naming a fraction as a number on a number line and placing fractions on a number line
dir: Look at the ropes. Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: Each rope runs from one bank of the river to the other. The 0 is the near bank. The 1 is the far bank. The dot is one lantern on the rope.
qs: Rope A is cut into 4 equal parts. What fraction of the way across is the lantern?
Rope B is cut into 6 equal parts. Name the fraction where the lantern hangs. What is one part of this rope called?
key: 3/4. The rope from 0 to 1 is cut into 4 equal parts and the lantern sits at the end of the third part. Partial: 3/4 right with no account of the equal parts is approaching. (3.NF.A.2)
1/6. One part of this rope is 1/6, because the whole from 0 to 1 is cut into 6 equal parts. Partial: the fraction right with no name for one part is approaching. (3.NF.A.2)

title: Which Lantern Holds More?
desc: explaining equivalent fractions and comparing fractions by reasoning about their size
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know. You can draw on your paper to show your thinking.

qs: Which is more oil in the same lantern, 2/3 or 2/6? How do you know?
Which is more, 5/8 of a lantern or 3/8 of the same lantern? How do you know?
key: 2/3. The top numbers are the same, so compare the piece sizes: thirds are bigger pieces than sixths, so 2 thirds is more than 2 sixths. Partial: naming 2/3 with no reason about the size of the pieces
5/8. The pieces are the same size, so the one with more pieces is more. Partial: naming 5/8 with no reason is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with the same numerator or denominator, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can draw a model.
qs: Which is greater, 3/8 or 5/8? Write the comparison with >, = or <. Tell how you know.
Compare 1/4 and 1/6 with a symbol. Tell how you know. Draw a model if it helps.
key: 5/8 > 3/8 (or 3/8 < 5/8). Same denominator, so the one with more parts of the same size is greater.
1/4 > 1/6. Same numerator, so the one with fewer, bigger parts (fourths) is greater.

title: Tile the Square
desc: relating the area of a rectangle to multiplication and addition
dir: Answer out loud. For numbers 4 and 6, write your work on your paper. Then hold it up.
text: The town is laying square tiles in the square by the bridge so the night walk has a dry path. Every tile is 1 square meter.
qs: Look at the tiled corner. How many tiles cover it? Write the multiplication equation that matches the picture.
A banner is 3 meters tall and 8 meters long. What is its area? Say the unit.
key: 24 tiles. 4 × 6 = 24, or 6 × 4 = 24. The picture shows 4 rows of 6 tiles. Partial: the count right with no multiplication equation written is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)
24 square meters. 3 × 8 = 24. The unit has to be square meters, not meters. Partial: 24 with no square unit named is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)

title: Cut the Paper Panels
desc: cutting shapes into parts with equal areas and naming one part as a unit fraction of the whole
dir: Look at the panels. Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: A paper lantern is built from flat panels. The crew cuts each panel into parts. Every helper gets the same amount of paper to fold.
qs: Panel A is cut into 4 parts with equal areas. What fraction of the whole panel is one part?
Panel B is cut into equal strips. What fraction of the whole panel is one strip?
key: 1/4. The panel is cut into 4 parts with the same area, so one part is 1 of 4 equal parts of the whole. Partial: 4 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.G.A.2)
1/6. There are 6 equal strips, so one strip is 1/6 of the panel. Partial: 6 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.G.A.2)

title: Crates and Shares

Describe a different thing at the night walk that 5 × 7 could stand for.

title: Tell a Story for a Product

Tell a story where 3 × 5 tells the total.

3 equal groups of 5, such as 3 plates with 5 cookies each. The total is 15.

Tell a story where 24 ÷ 6 means the number of shares.
key: 24 things shared equally among 6 people; each share has 4.

title: Round It
desc: rounding whole numbers to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred

Round 847 to the nearest hundred.
key: 130 to the nearest ten, because 8 ones rounds up. 100 to the nearest hundred, because 28 is less than 50. Partial: one of the two roundings right is approaching. (3.NBT.A.1)
800. 47 is less than 50, so the hundreds digit stays. Partial: 900 rounds up when the tens digit is 4 and does not count. (3.NBT.A.1)

title: One Part of the Banner

qs: Banner A is cut into 6 equal parts and 1 part is shaded. What fraction of the whole banner is shaded?

key: 1/6. The whole is cut into 6 equal parts and 1 of them is shaded. Partial: 6 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.NF.A.1)
The 6 tells how many equal parts the whole banner is cut into. The 5 tells how many of those parts you have. Partial: one of the two numbers explained is approaching. (3.NF.A.1)

Variation. They are all still her kittens: inherited traits vary from one offspring to the next, so a group of similar organisms is not identical. (3-LS3-1)

An ocean, or at least salt water. A shark tooth and clams belong in the sea, and the sand ripples show moving water. Naming them is the evidence. (3-LS4-1)

dir: Read the table. Answer out loud.
text: The town straightened a bend out of the creek to make room for a new road. The water now runs fast and shallow with no pools. A class surveyed the creek before
qs: Which living thing survived well after the creek was straightened? Give the evidence.
Which one vanished from the creek completely. Which one hung on but did worse?
key: The water moss. It went from a thin film to thick cover on every rock, so the fast shallow water suited it. (3-LS4-3)
The freshwater mussels could not survive there at all, from 31 down to none. The trout survived less well, from 24 down to 5. (3-LS4-3)

title: A Season of Weather
desc: reading and making a graphical display of typical weather for one season
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your graph on your paper and hold it up.
text: A class kept a weather board for the first four weeks of the year and counted the kind of day each week brought. Week Rainy days Foggy days Clear days 1 4 2 1 2
qs: Across all four weeks, which kind of day happened most often? Work it out from the table.
What would you tell a visitor to expect in a typical week of this season?
key: rainy days, 14 in all against 10 foggy and 4 clear (3-ESS2-1)
Mostly wet and grey: about two to five rainy days, a few foggy days, and about one clear day a week. Any description that uses the table and gives a typical week rather than one week. (3-ESS2-1)

title: Two Parts of the World
desc: combining information to describe the climates of two different regions of the world
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: The same month, the first month of the year, in two regions on opposite halves of the globe. Region Average temperature that month Season there Rain that month
qs: In the same month, one region is in winter and the other is in summer. What does the table say about their temperatures?
How can two regions be in different seasons at the same time?
key: The northern region averages 7 C and the southern region 24 C, a difference of 17 degrees in the very same month. (3-ESS2-2)

Because the two halves of the globe tilt toward the sun at different times of the year, so when one half is having its winter the other is having its summer. Accept the idea of the tilt in the student

title: Ready for the Flood
desc: making a claim about the merit of a design that reduces the impact of a weather hazard
dir: Answer out loud.
text: When a long rain falls, water runs off the hard parking lot. It floods the street at the bottom of the hill. The town digs a shallow dish of ground beside the l
qs: Which weather hazard is this design built to reduce?
Make a claim. Does the planted dish have merit? Give your reason.
key: street flooding when a long rain runs off hard ground (3-ESS3-1)
Yes, with a reason attached: the water gathers in the dish and soaks into the gravel and soil instead of running down the street. A yes with no reason is not yet a claim. (3-ESS3-1)

title: Balanced or Not
desc: planning an investigation of balanced and unbalanced forces acting on an object
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two people are moving a long, heavy table across the hall floor. One pushes from the west end and one pushes back from the east end. The table does not budge.
qs: Are the forces on the table balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
The person at the east end steps away. What happens, and what changed about the forces?
key: Balanced. Two equal pushes in opposite directions add up to no change in motion, and the table staying still is the evidence. (3-PS2-1)
The table slides east. Nothing balances the push from the west end now, so the forces are unbalanced. (3-PS2-1)

title: Predict the Next Mark
desc: using a pattern in motion data to predict where an object will be later
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: A class rolls a toy car down a long ramp and across the hall floor. Tape marks sit every 50 cm along the floor, and a timer calls out each second. Seconds on th
qs: Is the car covering the same distance in every second, or less each time? Use the numbers.
Look at how much is added each second: 80, then 60, then 40. What would you predict for the fifth second. What do you think happens after that?
key: Less each time. The gaps shrink: 100, then 80 more, then 60 more, then 40 more. The car is slowing down. (3-PS2-2)
About 20 cm more, so around 300 cm, and then the car stops, because the next step in the pattern would be nothing added. Accept any answer the student reaches by continuing the pattern and explaining

title: Ask About the Pull
desc: asking questions about cause and effect in electric or magnetic interactions between objects not touching
dir: Answer out loud. Your two questions have to be questions, not statements.
text: A wool sweater is pulled off over someone’s head. The hall is dry. Afterwards a comb is rubbed on that sweater. The comb is held above a pile of torn paper bits
qs: The comb never touches the paper bits, yet they jump. What does that tell you about this force?
Name two questions about it you could settle by trying something.
key: The force acts across a distance, with no contact between the objects. (3-PS2-3)

Any two real investigable questions: how long does the comb have to be rubbed, how high can it be held and still lift a bit, do bigger pieces of paper jump, does a plastic ruler work instead, does rub

title: A Problem for a Magnet
desc: defining a design problem that magnets can solve, with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Answer out loud. For the third one you may write your two sentences on your paper.
text: The hall has a recycling table. Steel cans and aluminum cans go in different bins. Sorting them by hand takes two people all morning.
qs: Say the problem in one sentence that begins: The problem is.
Why is a magnet a sensible idea here? A magnet pulls steel but not aluminum. How does that help you sort?
key: A problem statement about sorting steel cans from aluminum cans faster or with fewer people. The problem has to be about the sorting, not about recycling in general. (3-PS2-4)
Pass all the cans by a magnet. The steel ones are pulled aside and the aluminum ones are not, so the two kinds separate themselves without anyone reading a label. (3-PS2-4)

title: Three Ways to Do It
desc: comparing several possible solutions against stated criteria and constraints
dir: Look at the table and the three rules. Answer out loud.
text: The hall garden club needs trays to start seeds in. Three designs are tried, twenty seeds in each. Design Seeds that sprouted Cost for one tray Reusable next ye
qs: Which design sprouted the most seeds?
Which tray meets all three rules? Explain using the table.
key: the plastic tray, 18 of 20 (3-5-ETS1-2)
The wooden box lined with cloth. 17 sprouted, it costs 2 dollars, and it can be used again. Another choice counts only if the student argues it against all three rules using the table. (3-5-ETS1-2)

title: Make the Test Fair
desc: judging whether a test is fair, naming controlled variables, and identifying a failure point
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two watering amounts were tested to see which grows better seedlings. Tray Water Where it sat Seeds planted tray 1 50 ml a day sunny window 20 tray 2 150 ml a d
qs: Is that a fair way to compare them? Explain.
Name two things that should have been kept the same.
key: No. Three things were different at once, the water, the light and the number of seeds, so better growth cannot be pinned on the watering. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two controlled variables: the same light, the same number of seeds, the same soil, the same tray, the same temperature, the same seed kind. (3-5-ETS1-3)

title: Maps and Places
desc: using a map grid and a table to describe physical and human features and where they sit
dir: Use the map grid and the table. Answer out loud.
text: A map grid of the neighborhood around the community hall. North is the top row. west middle east north low hill park library middle creek community hall bakery
qs: What lies directly south of the community hall?
Which two directions do you walk to get from the hall to the library?
key: the bus stop (HSS-3.1)
north and east, in either order. The library sits in the north row and the east column. Partial: one of the two directions is approaching. (HSS-3.1)

title: The First Nations Here
desc: describing how the languages of California’s American Indian nations are part of the land itself, and how a nation is part of the state today
dir: Answer out loud. Use what is on the screen and what you have learned.
text: Many California place names come from other languages. Those are the languages of the nations. These are their homelands. Rivers, mountains, valleys and towns c
qs: The screen says the words were in use long before the names were written on a map. Name two kinds of places in California that carry words from those languages. Then say whose languages those words come from.
A place can have its own name in a language. That language comes from the nation that lived there. What does that tell you about the place?
key: Any two of rivers, mountains, valleys, and towns. The words come from the languages of the American Indian nations whose homelands those places are. Partial: two kinds of places named with nothing sai

That people were living there, naming the land and knowing it, long before anyone drew it on a map, and that their language is still part of the place today. Partial: saying people lived there with no

title: A Town Over Time
desc: sequencing local historical events and describing the mark each period left on the land
dir: Look at the timeline. Answer out loud.
text: A timeline for the town of Bell Crossing. Year What happened 1848 a wagon road crosses the creek at the shallow ford 1872 a brickworks digs clay from the creek
qs: Put these three in order, earliest first: the streetcar line, the wagon road, the brickworks.
Which event changed the creek bank. What did it do to it?
key: wagon road, brickworks, streetcar line. Partial: two of the three in the right order is approaching. (HSS-3.3)
the brickworks in 1872, which dug a clay pit out of the bank. Partial: naming the brickworks with no account of what it did to the bank is approaching. (HSS-3.3)

title: Rules, Laws and Government
desc: telling rules from laws and naming the basic parts and levels of United States government
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A town council meets in the hall. They talk about a new speed limit. It is for the street outside the park.
qs: A speed limit set by the town council is a law. How is that different from a rule the hall posts on its own door?
How do the people of a town get a say in the laws the council makes?
key: A law is made by a government, applies to everyone on that street, and the government decides what happens when it is broken. A posted rule is set by whoever runs the hall and applies only inside. Par

They vote for the council members, and they can speak at a council meeting or write to them. Accept voting, speaking up, or contacting a representative. Partial: naming voting with nothing else a resi

title: Choices and the Local Economy
desc: basic economic reasoning about producers, consumers, specializing and goods and services
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: A new bakery opens next door to the hall. The baker buys flour from a mill in the next county and sells bread to people in town. She also teaches a bread class
qs: Who in this table is the consumer, and who are the producers?
The baker does not grow her own wheat or grind her own flour. Why is it better for each of them to do just one job?
key: The family in town is the consumer. The farmer, the mill and the baker are all producers. Partial: the consumer named with one producer missed is approaching. (HSS-3.5)

Each one gets good at one job and has the right land, machines or skill for it, so the work is faster and better than if everyone did all of it. Accept specializing explained in the student’s own word

title: Read the Rope Crew
desc: a 173-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: The Rope Crew The rope crew works in the hour before dark, when the light goes flat and gray. There are nine of them this year, and every one has a job. Lucia w
key: 173 words, not counting the title. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy. Let the student finish the passage.
Winter grade 4 benchmark: about 120 words correct per minute (Hasbrouck and Tindal 2017, winter 50th percentile). 25th percentile is about 95.

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice. Let the rhythm and the rhymes show.
text: Thunder Walk The storm is rolling over the hill, With a rumble that rattles the window sill. The lightning flashes, a silver thread, And the thunder booms above
key: 43 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm, pauses at the end of lines or punctuation, and a voice that fits the mood of the poem.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: The Rope Crew The rope crew works in the hour before dark, when the light goes flat and gray. There are nine of them this year, and every one has a job. Lucia w
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: The Canvas Bag
desc: story questions answered with details and examples from the text
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud and point to the details that prove your answer.
text: The Long Way Round Hana had asked for the rope job three years running, and three years running her mother had said she was too young. This year her mother did
qs: How many years had Hana asked for the rope job before this one? Use a detail from the story.
How do you know the bag was heavy? Give two details from the story.
key: Three. The story says she had asked three years running and her mother said she was too young each time. (RL.4.1, explicit)
Any two: “The bag was heavier than it looked,” she set it down twice on the way across the bridge, and her palms had two red lines where the bag handle had been. (RL.4.1, details)

title: Reading the Night Sky
desc: informational text questions answered with details and examples from the text
dir: Read the text to yourself. Then answer out loud using details from the text.
text: Reading the Night Sky If you go outside at the same hour every month and look south, the stars will not be in the same place. They shift a little each night. Ov
qs: Why do the stars seem to cross the sky each night? Use a detail from the text.
Why do we face a slightly different part of space each month? Use the text.
key: Because Earth spins once a day. The text names that as the reason. (RI.4.1, explicit)
Because Earth travels all the way around the sun once a year, so from the ground we face a slightly different part of space each month. (RI.4.1, explicit)

title: Give It Some Slack
desc: the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a story
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud. Tell which words in the story helped you.
text: Give It Some Slack The wind came up just after the crew hoisted the last lantern, and the whole rope began to sway. “Give it some slack,” called Dmitri from the
qs: What does hoisted mean in the first sentence? What in the story helped you know?
What does slack mean when Dmitri says “Give it some slack”? Use the story.
key: Lifted or raised into place. The crew was putting lanterns up on the rope, and the rope started to sway right after, so hoisted has to mean they raised the last one up. (RL.4.4)
Looseness in the rope, the opposite of pulled tight. Dmitri says “A rope pulled tight is a rope that snaps,” and Lucia answers by letting out an arm's length of line. (RL.4.4)

title: Words from Myths
desc: determining the meaning of words and phrases that allude to significant characters found in mythology
dir: Read each sentence. Tell what the underlined words mean and where the idea comes from.
text: The mover said, “Carrying this piano up the stairs is a Herculean task.” What does Herculean mean here? Mia said, “My brother has the Midas touch. Everything he
qs: The mover said, “Carrying this piano up the stairs is a Herculean task.” What does Herculean mean here? Who is Hercules?
Mia said, “My brother has the Midas touch. Everything he sells turns to money.” What does the Midas touch mean?
key: Herculean means very hard and needing great strength. Hercules was a strong hero in Greek mythology who did twelve very hard jobs.
King Midas in a Greek myth turned everything he touched into gold. The Midas touch means being able to make money from everything.

title: Two Kinds of Bright
desc: putting together information from two texts on the same topic
dir: Read both texts to yourself. Then answer out loud. Use a fact from each text in every answer.
text: Both texts below are about the same question: why does a light look as bright as it does? Text 1: A Lantern on the Bridge from Light and Distance , a book by Im
qs: Use both texts. A star looks faint from Earth. Explain why that does not have to mean it is a small star.
Use both texts. A paper lantern on the bridge can look brighter than a star. That star gives off far more light. Explain why it looks brighter to you.
key: From Text 1: light spreads out as it travels, so the farther away a light is, the less of it reaches your eyes, and it does not mean the light got weaker. From Text 2: distance changes how bright a st
From Text 1: close up, a lot of a lantern's light lands on you, while far away the same light has to cover a much wider circle. From Text 2: how bright a star looks depends on both the light it gives

title: Star Notes
desc: taking notes in their own words, sorting the notes, and listing the sources
dir: Read the two sources. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: You are gathering facts for a report on why some lights look brighter than others. Text 1: A Lantern on the Bridge from Light and Distance , a book by Imani Bar
qs: Write three notes. Use both sources. Keep them short and use your own words, not the sentences from the page.
Sort your notes. Write a heading above each one: How Distance Changes Light, or What Makes a Star Bright.
key: Three short notes drawn from both sources, in the student's own words and not copied sentences. Examples: light spreads out as it goes; twice as far means about a quarter the light; a star can look br

Each note sits under the heading that fits. Spreading out, the wider circle, and the one quarter rule go under How Distance Changes Light. True brightness, how bright it looks from Earth, and faint hu

title: Fix the Crew Log
desc: spoken grammar items (relative pronouns, progressive tense, modal words, order of adjectives, run-ons, confused words)
dir: Say each line out loud the correct way.
qs: The neighbor ____ ties the knots has done the job for ten years. (who or which)
Right now the crew ____ the rope across the bridge. (pull) Start with is.
key: who. A relative pronoun for a person. (L.4.1)
is pulling. (L.4.1, progressive verb tense)

title: Cursive Writing
desc: writing fluidly and legibly in cursive or joined italics
dir: Write this sentence on your paper in cursive or joined writing. Write smoothly and keep it neat.
text: Write this sentence: The little brown rabbit hopped across the meadow.
key: Letters are joined within words (cursive or joined italics)
Writing is legible: another reader can read each word

title: Bridge Writer
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: How does the rope crew get a hundred lanterns onto the bridge safely? Write to explain it. Use facts from the chart. Write 5 to 7 sentences. Introduce your topi
key: Introduces the topic clearly (W.4.2)

Develops the topic with facts and details from the chart, such as walking the rope first and taping frayed spots, hanging from the middle outward, never passing a hook, lighting last and slowly, leavi

title: Bridge Writer
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Every lantern is lit and the crowd has gone home. You are the last person still on the bridge, and you have one job left to finish before you go. Write the stor
key: Sets up the situation and introduces the narrator or characters (W.4.3)
Events unfold in a clear order, helped by time words such as first, after that, by then, finally (W.4.3)

title: Long Words on the Log
desc: decoding multisyllable words using prefixes, suffixes, roots, and letter-sound patterns
dir: Read each word out loud. Look for a word part you already know.
key: Read each word in order: relighting, unbearable, astronomer, signature, cautiously, misjudge, foreigner, community.

Watch for: the prefixes re-, un-, mis- (relighting, unbearable, misjudge), the suffixes -ing, -able, -ly (relighting, unbearable, cautiously), the root astro in astronomer, the gn spelling in signatur

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and word parts
dir: Read each sentence out loud. Take your time with the long words.
text: The explorers discovered an enormous cavern beneath the mountain. Her curiosity led her to examine the unfamiliar footprints.
key: Listen for these six words read correctly in the sentences: explorers, discovered, enormous, cavern, curiosity, unfamiliar. Mark each one.
A word that is self-corrected on a second try counts as correct. Note words the student breaks into syllables to decode.

title: Say It Your Way
desc: paraphrasing a text read aloud and information shown in a graph
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then look at the graph. Answer out loud in your own words.
text: Your teacher will read a short report about what happens to the lanterns after the walk. Then look at the graph of how long each crew job takes.
qs: Put what I read about storing the lanterns into your own words.
Say in your own words what the graph shows.
key: A paraphrase, not a repeat: the lanterns come down the next morning, get folded flat, and fit in a small storage room, and torn ones are patched over the winter. Reciting the sentences word for word i

The graph shows how many minutes each of the four crew jobs takes on one evening. Hanging takes the longest and lighting takes the shortest. (SL.4.2, information presented visually and quantitatively)

title: Report on It
desc: reporting on a topic in an organized way with facts and descriptive details, at an understandable pace
dir: Talk for about a minute. Speak clearly and take your time.
text: Pick one job on the rope crew and report on it: what the job is, how it is done, and why it matters. Or report on something you know how to do well. Say what yo
key: Organized: names the topic first, then gives the steps or facts in an order a listener can follow. (SL.4.4, organized manner)
Uses appropriate facts and relevant descriptive details that support the main point. Details that wander off the topic do not count. (SL.4.4)

title: When Should the Walk Start
desc: an opinion piece with a stated point of view, grouped reasons, linking words, and a conclusion
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: The town has to pick a start time for the night walk. At dusk the sky is still pale, the path is easy to see, and younger children can come. An hour after dark
key: Introduces the topic and states a clear opinion about the start time (W.4.1)
Supplies reasons that support the point of view, drawn from the information given or from the student's own knowledge (W.4.1)

title: Times As Many
desc: reading a multiplication equation as a comparison and writing comparisons as equations
dir: Answer out loud. For numbers 1, 3, and 4, write the equation on your paper and hold it up.
text: The town hangs lanterns on two bridges. The small bridge is short. The long bridge crosses the whole river.
qs: The small bridge has 8 lanterns and the long bridge has 48. The long bridge has how many times as many lanterns? Write the multiplication equation.
Read 56 = 7 × 8 as a comparison. Say it two different ways.
key: 6 times as many. 48 = 6 × 8. Partial: 40 more is a difference and not a multiplicative comparison, so it does not count. (4.OA.A.1)
56 is 7 times as many as 8, and 56 is 8 times as many as 7. Partial: one of the two ways given is approaching. (4.OA.A.1)

title: Pack the Measures
desc: relative sizes of measurement units and changing a larger unit into a smaller one
dir: Say each answer out loud. For number 6, read the three missing numbers from the table.
text: Everything the crew carries up to the bridge gets written down in the smaller unit, so the numbers are whole.
qs: A rope is 4 meters long. How many centimeters is that?
A crate holds 3 kilograms of candles. How many grams is that?
key: 400 centimeters. 1 meter is 100 centimeters, so 4 × 100 = 400. Partial: 40 uses tens instead of hundreds and does not count. (4.MD.A.1)
3,000 grams. 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams, so 3 × 1,000 = 3,000. Partial: 300 uses hundreds instead of thousands and does not count. (4.MD.A.1)

title: Pounds and Ounces
desc: knowing the relative sizes of pounds and ounces, converting a larger unit to a smaller unit, and recording equivalents in a table
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work.
qs: A box of cereal weighs 24 ounces. How many pounds and ounces is that?
How many ounces are in 4 pounds?
key: 1 pound 8 ounces (24 = 16 + 8)
64 ounces

title: Around the Square
desc: area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real problems
dir: Solve each one on your paper and hold it up. Say the unit with every answer.
text: The town square by the bridge is a rectangle. The crew measures it before the walk so they know how much rail and how many tiles to order.
qs: The square is 24 meters long and 15 meters wide. What is its area?
What is the perimeter of the square?
key: 360 square meters. 24 × 15 = 360. Partial: 360 with no square unit named is approaching. (4.MD.A.3)
78 meters. 2 × (24 + 15) = 2 × 39 = 78. Or: 24 + 15 + 24 + 15 = 78. Partial: 39 adds only one of each side and does not count. (4.MD.A.3)

title: Sort the Panels
desc: classifying two-dimensional figures by parallel sides, perpendicular sides, and angle size
dir: Look at the five flat panels. Answer out loud. Point to the sides or the corners you mean.
text: A paper lantern is built from flat panels cut in different shapes. Parallel sides run the same direction and never meet. Perpendicular sides meet at a square co
qs: Which panels have at least one pair of parallel sides? Name them.
Which panels have perpendicular sides? Name them.
key: A, C, and D. Panel A is a square, so both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. Panel C is a parallelogram with two pairs. Panel D has one pair, the top side and the bottom side. Panels B and E are tr

A and B. Panel A has four square corners, so every pair of sides that meet is perpendicular. Panel B has one square corner, at its lower left. C, D, and E have no square corners. Partial: one of the t

title: Triangles by Their Sides
desc: classifying triangles as equilateral, isosceles, or scalene by their side lengths
dir: Answer out loud. For the drawing questions, draw on your paper.
qs: A triangle has sides of 5 cm, 5 cm, and 5 cm. What kind of triangle is it?
A triangle has sides of 6 cm, 6 cm, and 4 cm. What kind of triangle is it?
key: Equilateral (all three sides equal)
Isosceles (two sides equal)

title: Ten Times As Much
desc: a digit in one place is worth ten times the same digit in the place to its right
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: The county keeps one written count of every lantern hung in every town. 7,700
qs: Look at 7,700. The 7 in the thousands place has a value. The 7 in the hundreds place has a value. How do they compare?
The county count one year was 3,330. Say the value of each 3.
key: It is ten times as much. The first 7 is worth 7,000 and the second is worth 700, and 7,000 is ten times 700. Partial: naming the two values with no comparison is approaching. (4.NBT.A.1)
3,000, then 300, then 30. Each 3 is worth ten times the 3 to its right. Partial: two of the three values given is approaching. (4.NBT.A.1)

title: Round the Count
desc: rounding multi-digit whole numbers to any place
dir: Answer out loud. Tell which digit you looked at.
qs: Round 6,482 to the nearest hundred.
Round 6,482 to the nearest thousand.
key: 6,500. Look at the tens digit, 8. It is 5 or more, so the hundreds digit goes up. Partial: 6,400 rounds down when the tens digit is 8 and does not count. (4.NBT.A.3)
6,000. Look at the hundreds digit, 4. It is less than 5, so the thousands digit stays. Partial: 7,000 rounds up when the hundreds digit is 4 and does not count. (4.NBT.A.3)

title: Cut Every Piece
desc: explaining why two fractions are equivalent with a visual model, and generating equivalent fractions
dir: Look at the two banners. Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: Banner A and Banner B are exactly the same size.
qs: Is the same amount of banner shaded on both? Use the picture to explain.
Write 3/4 as an equivalent fraction with 12 as the bottom number.
key: Yes. Every fourth on Banner A was cut in half to make Banner B, so there are twice as many parts and each part is half as big. The shaded length is the same. 3/4 = 6/8. Partial: saying yes with nothin
9/12. Multiply the top and the bottom by 3, because each fourth is cut into 3 equal pieces. Partial: 9/12 right with no reason is approaching. (4.NF.A.1)

title: Which Is Greater
desc: comparing fractions with unlike numerators and denominators, and knowing a comparison needs the same whole
dir: Answer out loud. Record each answer with a symbol. Tell how you know.
qs: Which is greater, 5/6 or 7/12? Record it with a symbol.
Which is greater, 5/9 or 2/5? Use 1/2 as a benchmark.
key: 5/6 > 7/12. In twelfths, 5/6 is 10/12, and 10/12 is more than 7/12. Partial: the right choice with the sign the wrong way round is approaching. (4.NF.A.2)

5/9. Half of 9 is 4.5, so 5/9 is more than 1/2. Half of 5 is 2.5, so 2/5 is less than 1/2. Record it as 5/9 > 2/5. Partial: naming 5/9 with only one of the two benchmark checks is approaching. (4.NF.A

title: Write It as a Decimal
desc: writing fractions with denominators 10 and 100 in decimal notation and locating a decimal on a number line
dir: Look at the number line. Answer out loud. Write numbers 1 and 2 on your paper.
qs: Write 62/100 as a decimal.
Write 0.4 as a fraction with 10 as the bottom number. Again with 100 as the bottom number.
key: 0.62. Six tenths and two hundredths. Partial: 0.62 right with no place value words is approaching. (4.NF.C.6)
4/10 and 40/100. Both name the same amount. Partial: one of the two fractions given is approaching. (4.NF.C.6)

title: Which Cord Is Longer

dir: Read both texts to yourself. They are about the same night. Then answer out loud, using details from both.
text: body:not(.sup-big) .texts article p{font-size:1.06rem;line-height:1.5} Text A: “I Was Wrong About the Lamps,” a column by Marisol Ferrante. Hollowell Register,
qs: Name two facts that appear in both texts.
Name one thing Text B tells you that Text A leaves out. Then name one thing Text A tells you that Text B leaves out.
key: Any two of these shared facts: 420 street lamps were replaced, Text A “all four hundred and twenty street lamps” and Text B “420 lamps”; the new lamps put light on the pavement instead of into the air
Only in Text B: about 600 walkers, the state grant and the $96,000, the public works director’s name and statement, the sky reading about twice as dark, the two residents who objected, Priya Raghavan

title: Night Watch Log
desc: pronoun case, intensive pronouns, shifts in person, vague pronouns, and a variation from standard English
dir: Answer out loud. When you fix a sentence, say the whole sentence the correct way.
text: These sentences come from the lantern crew’s notebook. Some of them need fixing.
qs: Which one is correct, and why? “Mr. Nadeau gave the long pole to Priya and I.” Or “Mr. Nadeau gave the long pole to Priya and me.”
Fix this sentence: “Her and Theo carried the ladder down the street.”
key: “...to Priya and me.” The pronoun is the object of the preposition to, so it takes the objective case. Test it by dropping “Priya and”: you would say “gave the pole to me,” not “to I.” (L.6.1a, pronou
“She and Theo carried the ladder down the street.” The pronoun is part of the subject, so it takes the subjective case, she, not her. (L.6.1a, pronoun case)

title: Source Check

qs: Source 1 and Source 3 disagree about whether a capped lamp gives less light. Which source would you use in a report? Give two reasons that source is more credible.
Three students took notes from the Source 1 excerpt above. Which note is plagiarism? How could that student fix it?
key: Source 1. Two reasons, such as: it names an author who is a lighting engineer, it was published by a state research office, it is recent, and it reports measured trial results instead of a story. Sour

Note A. It copies the report’s sentence word for word with no quotation marks and no credit. Fix: put the copied words in quotation marks and name Ozturk, or rewrite it in new words and name Ozturk. N

key: States a clear claim: pay for the river road lamps, or pay for the parking lot lamps (SL.6.4)
Sequences ideas logically: claim, findings, closing (SL.6.4)

key: Left over carries the connotation of a remainder nobody wanted, something handed to you after the good part is gone, like leftover food. The rest of the street would be a neutral measurement. Left ove

Lean is figurative. It gives the flame weight and patience, so that lighting the wick becomes resting against it and waiting rather than a quick contact. Touch would be an instant. The whole stanza is

title: Lantern Oil
desc: dividing fractions, a visual model, a story context, a measurement problem, and finding an error
dir: Work on your paper. Hold it up or tell your teacher each answer. Show the division you used.
text: The lantern crew measures oil by the cup and paper by the meter. Nearly every job is a question about how many of one thing fit inside another.
qs: Each small lantern holds 1/8 of a cup of oil. How many can you fill from 3/4 of a cup? Write the division and the answer.
Divide: 5/6 ÷ 1/12. Then describe or draw a model that shows why your answer is right.
key: 6 lanterns. 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 3/4 × 8/1 = 24/4 = 6, because six 1/8-cup lanterns fit inside 3/4 of a cup. Or: common denominators, 6/8 ÷ 1/8 = 6 ÷ 1 = 6. (6.NS.A.1, quotient of fractions)

10. 5/6 ÷ 1/12 = 5/6 × 12/1 = 60/6 = 10. Model: 5/6 is the same as 10/12, so ten 1/12 pieces fit inside it. Or: common denominators, 10/12 ÷ 1/12 = 10 ÷ 1 = 10. Partial: the right answer with no model

title: Panel Shapes
desc: area of a triangle, a parallelogram, a trapezoid, and a composite figure, plus a missing height and an error
dir: Use the four panel drawings. Work on your paper and tell your teacher each answer. Include the units.
text: A paper lantern is built from flat panels. The crew has to know the area of each panel to order paper.
qs: Find the area of Panel A, the triangle.
Find the area of Panel B, the parallelogram.
key: 27 square inches. Area = 1/2 × 9 × 6 = 27. Or: 9 × 6 = 54, then halve. Partial: 54 square inches is the whole rectangle and does not count. (6.G.A.1, area of a triangle)

60 square inches. Area = base × height = 12 × 5 = 60. Watch for using the slanted side instead of the dashed height. Or: cut the triangle off one end and slide it to the other, which makes a 12 by 5 r

title: Crate Volume
desc: volume of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths, by packing with unit cubes and by formula
dir: Use the drawing for number 1. Work on your paper and tell your teacher each answer. Include the units.
text: Finished lanterns ship in crates. Every crate is a right rectangular prism, and the crew measures them in fractions of a foot.
qs: The crate in the drawing is 1 1/2 feet long, 3/4 of a foot wide, and 1/2 of a foot high. It is packed with cubes 1/4 of a foot on every edge. How many cubes fit along each edge? How many cubes in all? What is the volume of the crate?
A taller crate measures 2/3 of a meter by 3/5 of a meter by 1 1/4 meters. Find its volume.
key: 6 cubes along the length, 3 across the width, and 2 high, because 1 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 6, 3/4 ÷ 1/4 = 3, and 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 2. That is 6 × 3 × 2 = 36 cubes. Each cube is (1/4)(1/4)(1/4) = 1/64 of a cubic foot,
1/2 of a cubic meter. 2/3 × 3/5 × 5/4 = 30/60 = 1/2. Or: cancel before multiplying, since the 3s and the 5s cancel to leave 2/4 = 1/2. (6.G.A.2, V = lwh with fractional edge lengths)

title: Lantern Racks
desc: writing and evaluating numerical expressions with whole-number exponents
dir: Work on your paper. Then tell your teacher each answer.
qs: Write 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 using an exponent. Then find its value.
The picture shows one lantern rack. Write an expression with an exponent for the number of lanterns on the rack, then find its value.
key: 4<sup>5</sup> = 1,024. Step by step: 4, 16, 64, 256, 1,024. Or: group the factors, 16 × 64 = 1,024. Partial: the power written right with the value wrong is approaching. (6.EE.A.1, writing a power)
5<sup>3</sup> = 125 lanterns. The rack is 5 by 5 by 5, and 5 × 5 × 5 = 125. Partial: the expression right with the value wrong is approaching. (6.EE.A.1, writing an expression with an exponent)

title: Put In the Number
desc: evaluating expressions and real-world formulas at given values
dir: Work on your paper. Hold it up or tell your teacher each answer. Include units where they are asked for.
qs: Find the value of 7n − 12 when n = 8.
Find the value of 5x 2 when x = 3.
key: 44. 7 × 8 = 56, then 56 − 12 = 44. Partial: 56 leaves the subtraction out and is approaching. (6.EE.A.2c, substitution)
45. Do the exponent first: 3<sup>2</sup> = 9, then 5 × 9 = 45. Watch for squaring 5x and getting 225. (6.EE.A.2c, order of operations with an exponent)

title: Lamps per Month
desc: rate and percent reasoning in a real context
dir: Work on your paper and hold it up. Say each answer out loud.
text: The town replaced 420 street lamps over 24 months, at a steady rate.
qs: How many lamps did the crews replace per month?
At that same rate, how many lamps would be replaced in 8 months?
key: 17.5 lamps per month. 420 ÷ 24 = 17.5. A unit rate may come out as a decimal. Or: halve twice, 420 ÷ 24 is 210 ÷ 12 is 105 ÷ 6 = 17.5. (6.RP.A.3, unit rate)
140 lamps. 17.5 × 8 = 140, or 420 × 8/24 = 140. An equivalent-ratio table works too: 24 months to 420 lamps is 8 months to 140. (6.RP.A.3)

title: Ratio Reasoning
desc: using ratio and rate reasoning with tables, graphs on the coordinate plane, tape diagrams, unit conversion, and percent
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work. Use graph paper for the plot.
qs: A recipe uses 2 cups of rice for every 3 cups of water. Make a table of equivalent ratios for 1, 2, 3, and 4 batches. Plot the pairs (rice, water) on a coordinate plane.
The ratio of cats to dogs is 3 to 5. There are 24 animals in all. Draw a tape diagram and find how many cats and dogs.
key: Table: (2, 3), (4, 6), (6, 9), (8, 12). The four points are plotted correctly with rice on the x-axis and water on the y-axis, and they lie on a straight line.
8 equal parts (3 + 5). 24 ÷ 8 = 3 per part. 9 cats and 15 dogs.

title: Above and Below Zero
desc: using positive and negative numbers to describe opposite directions, explaining what zero means in a context, and locating rational numbers on a number line and in the coordinate plane
dir: Look at the number line and the grid. Answer out loud.
text: The thermometer on the bridge reads in degrees Celsius. The crew also measures heights from the bridge deck, where the deck itself counts as 0.
qs: At midnight the thermometer reads -6 degrees and at noon it reads +2 degrees. What does 0 mean on this thermometer? Is 0 the same as having no temperature?
The river surface is 3 meters below the bridge deck and the lantern rope hangs 4 meters above it. Write each height as a signed number, and say what the signs mean here.
key: 0 is the freezing point of water, the dividing line between the temperatures above it and the temperatures below it. It is not no temperature at all. Positive and negative here describe opposite direc

-3 meters for the river surface and +4 meters for the rope. The sign tells the direction from the deck: minus is below, plus is above. The deck is 0 because it is the point both are measured from. Par

title: Two Variables
desc: writing an equation for two quantities that change together, and reading the relationship in a table
dir: Work on your paper and hold it up. Say each answer out loud.
text: On the night of the walk the crew hangs lanterns at a steady 4 lanterns an hour. Hanging rate Hours worked, h Lanterns hung, L 1 ? 2 ? 3 ? 4 ?
qs: Write an equation that gives the number of lanterns L in terms of the hours worked h. Which one is the dependent variable, and why?
Fill in the table for h = 1, 2, 3, and 4.
key: L = 4h. L is the dependent variable, because the number of lanterns depends on how long the crew has been working. h is the independent variable. Or: L = h × 4 or 4h = L count equally. Partial: h = 4L
4, 8, 12, 16. Each extra hour adds 4 lanterns, which is the 4 in the equation. Partial: three of the four values right is approaching. (6.EE.C.9, relating the table to the equation)

text: The Night Sky Monitoring Project counted stars by eye from five places in and around Hollowell on the same clear night.
qs: How many observations are in this data set, and what attribute was measured? In what units?
Find the median and the mean. Which one better describes a typical place in town, and why?
key: 5 observations, one from each place. The attribute is how many stars a person can count by eye from that spot on a clear night, measured as a plain count of stars. (6.SP.B.5a and b). Partial: the coun

Median 52, at Alder Street. Mean 78, because 14 + 26 + 52 + 88 + 210 = 390 and 390 ÷ 5 = 78. The median describes a typical place better here, because the single value of 210 pulls the mean up above f

title: Describe the Data
desc: summarizing a numerical data set by reporting the number of observations, the attribute and units, measures of center and variability, and any pattern or striking deviation
dir: Solve on your paper. Use words and numbers to describe the data set.
qs: Ages of kids at a camp: 8, 9, 9, 10, 10, 10, 11, 12, 14. Report how many observations there are, what was measured and in what unit, the median, and the range.
Describe the overall pattern of the data, any striking deviation, and why you chose your measure of center.
key: 9 observations. Age in years. Median 10. Range 14 − 8 = 6. Most ages cluster from 9 to 11; 14 is a high value.
Names the overall pattern (where most values fall), identifies any value far from the rest, and links the choice of median or mean to the shape of the data.

title: Growing From One Cell
desc: explaining how cells build an organism and how body structures are organized
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A seed planted at the start of the year becomes a plant with roots, a stem and leaves. All of it comes from cells dividing, and the new cells are not all alike.
qs: A plant grows larger. Explain what is happening at the level of its cells.
Put these in order from smallest to largest: organ, cell, tissue, organism. Then give one example of each from a plant.
key: Cells divide to make more cells, and the new cells take in material and grow. Growth is an increase in the number and the size of cells, not the stretching of existing ones. Partial: saying the cells

Cell, tissue, organ, organism. For example a leaf cell, the tissue inside a leaf, the leaf itself as an organ, and the whole plant as the organism. Partial: the four in the right order with an example

title: Growing From One Cell
desc: interpreting data on what a growing plant needs and tracing matter into new tissue
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Four seedlings were started on the same day and measured after three weeks. Seedling Light Water Height Colour 1 full yes 19 cm deep green 2 none yes 23 cm pale
qs: Seedling 2 grew taller than seedling 1 and is pale yellow. Explain both results.
Seedling 2 was taller. Was it healthier? Explain how you decide.
key: Without light it stretched upward searching for light and it could not make the green pigment or run photosynthesis, so it is tall, weak and pale. It grew using the food stored in the seed, which will

No. Height alone does not show health: it had no light, could not make food, and will die once the seed’s store is used. Colour, strength and the ability to make food are better measures. Partial: ans

title: What Comes Next
desc: predicting and explaining the pattern of inherited traits across offspring
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: A gardener crossed two pea plants and recorded the flowers of their offspring. One parent had purple flowers, the other white. Cross Offspring flowers purple pa
qs: In the first cross every offspring was purple. What does that tell you about the two gene versions for flower colour?
White flowers came back in the second cross. Explain how a trait can disappear in one generation and return in the next.
key: One version is expressed over the other: with one of each, the plant shows purple, so purple is the version that is displayed and white is the one that is hidden. Partial: saying purple is stronger, w

The purple offspring each carried a hidden white version as well. When two of them were crossed, some offspring received the white version from both parents, so white was expressed again. Partial: say

title: What Comes Next
desc: locating genetic information and distinguishing inherited from acquired change
dir: Answer out loud.

Where is the information for an inherited trait kept, and how does a seed come to carry two sets of it?
key: The pale streak, because it reappeared in the seedlings, which means it is carried in the genes. Cutting back and staking changed only those individual plants during their lives. Partial: naming the p

In genes on chromosomes inside the nucleus of the cell. A seed forms when a cell from each parent joins, so it receives one set of chromosomes from each. Partial: naming genes or the nucleus with noth

title: A New Year of Weather
desc: interpreting weather data to explain air masses and the water cycle
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Readings were taken at one town over three days as a weather system passed. Day Temperature Pressure Sky Wind 1 12 °C falling high thin cloud light, from the so
qs: Describe what happened across these three days in terms of air masses meeting.
The pressure fell before the rain and rose after it. What use is that pattern to someone forecasting?
key: Warm moist air moved in from the south, then a cold air mass arrived from the north and pushed under it, lifting the warm air so its moisture condensed and fell as rain. After the front passed, colder

Falling pressure usually comes before a storm and rising pressure after it, so pressure gives warning of what is coming before the sky shows it. Patterns in measurements are what forecasts are built o

title: A New Year of Weather
desc: explaining how uneven heating drives air and water movement
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The sun heats the ground more strongly near the equator than near the poles, and it heats land faster than water.
qs: Explain how uneven heating sets air in motion, step by step.
A lake shore is breezy on a sunny afternoon, with the breeze blowing from the water toward the land. Explain why, using what you just said.
key: Warmed air expands and becomes less dense, so it rises. Cooler denser air moves in underneath to take its place, and that movement is wind. Uneven heating makes pressure differences, and air flows bet

The land warms faster than the water, so air above the land rises and cooler air from over the water flows in to replace it. That inflow is the breeze. Partial: saying the air over the land rises, wit

title: Setting a Target
desc: analyzing resource use data and deciding where a change would do the most good
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: A school recorded where its electricity went last year and set out to cut its use. Use Share of the total heating and cooling 44 percent lighting 26 percent com
qs: Where should the school look first for a large saving, and what in the data supports that?
A student suggests switching off the hallway lights, which are a small part of lighting. Why might that still be worth doing even though the saving is small?
key: Heating and cooling, because it is the largest share at 44 percent, so a given percentage cut there saves more than the same cut anywhere else. Partial: naming heating and cooling with the 44 percent

It costs nothing, it is easy to keep doing, and small savings add up across a year. It also changes habits, which can lead to larger changes. Data decides size, not whether something is worth doing. P

title: Setting a Target
desc: evaluating how a human change affects a local system and what evidence would test it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A town plans to pave a large gravel lot to make a car park. A neighbour says the creek below it will flood more often afterward.
qs: Explain the neighbour’s reasoning, using what happens to rain on gravel and on pavement.
Name one thing the town could build or plant to reduce the effect without giving up the car park.
key: Rain soaks into gravel, so much of it enters the ground slowly. Pavement sheds almost all of it, so the same storm sends far more water to the creek far faster, which raises the peak and can overflow

Any workable answer: permeable paving, a holding basin or rain garden that stores runoff and releases it slowly, planted strips along the edges, or a channel that spreads the water out. Partial: namin

title: Energy Changing Form

A wound up toy holds energy before it moves. What kind, and what does it turn into when released?
key: Electrical energy goes in, and light and thermal energy come out. A lamp always warms as well as lights, which is why some lamps are hot to touch. Partial: naming electrical in and light out with the

Stored energy in the wound spring, a kind of potential energy. When released it is transferred to kinetic energy of the moving parts, with some going to sound and thermal energy from friction. Partial
