Supporters argued that Chinese workers lowered wages and would not assimilate, and Western labor organizations pushed hardest for it. Its passage shows that economic anxiety and organized racism could

title: Find the Letter
desc: matching a spoken letter name to its printed form (12 cards, 6 uppercase and 6 lowercase)
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
key: Say: Here are twelve letter cards from the kindness jar. I will say a letter name. Point to the card with that letter.
Say: Point to the letter q. (top row, fourth card)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: First Sound Check
desc: saying the first sound of a pictured word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the first sound.
key: Model first: Heart. The first sound in heart is /h/. Now you try.
Point to the cat. Say: Cat. What is the first sound in cat? (/k/)

title: Rhyme Time
desc: making a rhyme for a given word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say a word that rhymes.
key: Model first: Share, care, bear. They rhyme. They sound the same at the end.
Point to the hand. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with hand. (band, land, sand, stand, fand)

title: Put It Together
desc: blending syllables and sounds into a word with picture support
dir: Listen to the slow, sleepy voice. Say the whole word.
key: Say: I am going to talk very slowly. Put the parts together and tell me the word. The pictures can help you, but they are mixed up.
Say with a pause between the parts: rab ... bit. (rabbit)

title: Nell's Kind Morning
desc: questions about the character, the order of three events, and what happens next in a story read aloud
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Nell's Kind Morning
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: This is a rabbit named Nell. Here is her burrow, and here she is hopping across the meadow. Then comes a garden, then a gate, the
Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Nell comes to the pond.

title: Find the Letter
desc: matching a spoken letter name to its printed lowercase form
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
key: Say: Every paper heart has a tag with a small letter on it. I will say a letter name. Point to the heart with that letter.
Say: Point to the letter d. (fifth heart from the left)

title: Write the First Letter
desc: writing the letter for a beginning sound (h, f, b, d)
dir: Listen for the sound. Write the letter on your paper and hold it up.
key: Point to the first picture. Say: This is a heart. Heart starts with /h/. Write the letter that makes the /h/ sound. Hold it up. (h or H)
Point to the flower. Say: Flower starts with /f/. Write the letter for /f/. (f or F)

title: Label Your Kind Thing
desc: writing a few recognizable letters to stand for a word or an idea
dir: Draw on your paper. Then write some letters next to your drawing.
key: Say: Here is a kindness jar with five hearts in it. Think of one kind thing somebody did for you, or one kind thing you did. Draw it on your paper.
Look for: draws something you can see is a thing or a person, not only a scribble.

title: The Kindness Call
desc: asking questions to get missing information and to confirm understanding
dir: Your teacher is calling you. Ask questions until you know what to do.
key: Say: You live by the meadow. I will call you on the phone, but part of my message will be missing. Ask me questions until you know what to do.

Message 1. Say in a phone voice: Hello! Please carry the basket over to my friend's house. Look for: asks a question about which basket or which house (there are three baskets by the door and two hous

title: Mystery Box
desc: asking questions and follow-up questions to find out information
dir: Something is in the box on the path. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
key: Your secret: a loaf of warm bread is in the box. Do not tell.
Say: Somebody packed one thing in this box to bring to a neighbor. Ask me questions to find out what it is. You can ask things like: Is it alive? What do you do with it?

title: Name the Meadow Things
desc: naming objects, actions, and describing words from pictures
dir: Look at each picture. Answer out loud.
key: Picture 1. Say: What is this? (a block. Block, brick, or toy block all count.)
Picture 2. Say: What is this? (a flower. Daisy counts too.)

title: Under the Sea or Breakfast
desc: sharing an opinion with a reason, a description, and an explanation
dir: Pick one. Tell your teacher why.
key: Say: Pretend you can go to one place today. You can go under the sea and meet the animals, or you can sit down at the breakfast table. Which one would you pick? Tell me why.
Look for: tells an opinion (picks one).

title: A Garden Everyone Shares
desc: making an inference, making a connection, and asking a question about an informational text read aloud
dir: Listen to your teacher read about a shared garden. Then answer out loud.
key: Say: These facts are about a garden that a whole neighborhood shares. If picture supports are on, point to the picture. Then read the facts out loud.

Ask: What if nobody watered the garden for a whole week? What do you think would happen? (The plants would get dry, droopy, or floppy, or they would stop growing. The facts never say this part, so the

title: Count the Hearts
desc: counting 10 or more real objects one by one where the teacher can see, then counting groups of 10, 13, 11, and 12 objects one by one on the screen
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
key: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one

Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down

title: More or Fewer?
desc: comparing two groups by counting (more, same, fewer)
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
key: Box 1. Say: Are there more hearts or more flowers? How do you know? (More hearts. 8 hearts and 5 flowers.)
Box 2. Say: Are there more bees, more butterflies, or the same number of each? (The same. 6 bees and 6 butterflies.)

title: Garden Shapes
desc: naming, describing, and drawing circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud. Then draw a shape on your paper.
key: Say: Look at the garden picture. Four things in it are shapes. What shape is the purple flag? (triangle)
Say: What shape is the blue gate? (square)

title: Sort It
desc: sorting and classifying objects by color, by size, by two attributes at once, and making a rule
dir: Look at the tray and the pile. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the tray. Say: Here are the paper hearts for the kindness jar. How many hearts are on the tray in all? (9)
Say: Sort them by color in your head. How many pink? How many purple? (5 pink and 4 purple)

title: Pattern Strings
desc: reading, extending, describing, and copying repeating patterns (AB, AABB, and ABC)
dir: Look at the three strings. Answer out loud.
key: Point to string A. Say: Name the things out loud, left to right. (heart, cat, heart, cat, heart, cat) Then ask: What comes next? (heart)
Say: What is the part that keeps repeating on string A? (heart, cat. Saying it or pointing to the first two things both count.)

title: The Kindness Chart
desc: reading a picture chart where one picture stands for one thing, and adding one of your own
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
key: Say: This class puts one animal sticker on the chart every time somebody does a kind thing. Point to the top row. How many dogs are in the row that says Helped at home? (6)
Say: Which row has the most stickers? (Helped a friend, with 7)

title: Heart Jar Numbers
desc: naming the numerals 1 to 10
dir: Say the name of each number.
key: Say: Every jar on the kindness shelf has a number on it. What number is this? Click Next after each one.
The order is 3, 6, 1, 9, 4, 10, 7, 2, 8, 5. Correct means the child says the number name. Write down the ones missed.

title: Gate Ribbons
desc: ordering five objects by length
dir: Look at the five ribbons. Answer out loud.
key: Say: These are the ribbons for tying paper hearts onto the gate. Which ribbon is the longest? (C)
Say: Which ribbon is the shortest? (B)

title: Where Is It?
desc: position words (on, under, over, in front of, between)
dir: Look at the picture. Answer out loud.
key: Say: This is the shelf by Nell's door. Where is the jar of hearts? (On the shelf. Look for a position word, not only pointing.)
Say: Which animal is under the jar? (the cat)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the most common sound for all 26 letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What sound does this letter make? Mark each correct sound.
For a, e, i, o and u the short sound is what is expected. The long sound is also correct.

title: Two Lines
desc: print concepts (where to start, where to go at the end of a line, counting words and letters)
dir: Look at the two lines. Answer out loud.
text: We work in the garden. My row is wet. The four pictures are a boot, a little sprout, the sun, and a duck.
key: Say: I want to read this. Ask: Where do I start, at the boot, the sprout, the sun, or the duck? (the boot. Reading starts at the top on the left.)
Say: I read the top line and I stop at the sprout. Ask: Where do I go next? (to the sun, the start of the next line)

title: Book Parts
desc: print concepts (finding the title, where to start, which way to read, and the first and last word of a line)
dir: Look at the page. Point or answer out loud.
text: The Kind Garden I can help a friend We can be kind
key: Say: This is a page from a book. Point to the title. (the big words in the banner at the top: The Kind Garden. If the student cannot point on the screen, they can tell you where it is.)
Ask: Where do I start reading? Point to it. (the first word of the top line, on the left: I)

title: Rhyme and Clap
desc: hearing rhymes, making a rhyme, and clapping syllables
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
text: A row is a long line of plants in a garden.
key: Ask: Do share and care rhyme? (yes)
Ask: Do kind and friend rhyme? (no)

title: Put It Together
desc: blending spoken sounds and saying the first, last, and all sounds in a word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Put these sounds together: /h/ /e/ /l/ /p/. (help)
Say: Put these sounds together: /s/ /ee/ /d/. (seed)

title: Mo and Pip
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in a story read aloud to the student
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: Mo has a pot of soup. Pip has no soup. Mo gives Pip a cup. Now they both eat. A pot holds the soup. You cook in a pot.
key: Read the four lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Ask: What does Mo have? (a pot of soup)
Ask: Who has no soup? (Pip)

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the sounds of letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: The student says the most common sound for each letter: b /b/, A as in apple, f /f/, r /r/, o as in ox, H /h/, k /k/, j /j/, v /v/, i as in it. The letter name is not needed here.
The long sound for A, o or i is also fine. Write down any sounds that were missed.

title: Kind Words
desc: reading high-frequency words and short vowel words
dir: Read each word out loud.
text: see my you and come bud hug jam fit
key: High-frequency words the student should know by sight: see, my, you, and, come
Sounds out or reads: bud, hug, jam, fit

title: Listen to the Garden Club
desc: answering questions about key details in a text read aloud and asking for help
dir: Put your eyes on your teacher and listen. Then answer out loud.
text: Listening time. Your teacher will read you a report about the garden everybody shares.
key: Ask: How many rows does each family look after? (one row)
Ask: When do you water the row next to yours? (when that neighbor is away)

title: Little Kind Book
desc: reading a short emergent-reader book with purpose and understanding
dir: Point to each word and read it out loud.
text: I see a pup. The pup is sad. I can help. Now the pup is glad. Now he can play. We run and run. The pup can jump. I like my pup. Glad means happy.
key: Count the words the student reads correctly, out of 32, and enter the number in the box. A word the student fixes without help counts. Write down the words that were missed.
Points or tracks under each word, left to right and top to bottom

title: Bees and Flowers
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in an informational text about bees and flowers
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: A bee can help a flower. The bee gets food. The flower gets help. Bees go from flower to flower. Then the flower can make seeds. The bee helps the flower. The f
key: Read the six lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Ask: Who can help a flower? (a bee. Line 1.)
Ask: What does the bee get? (food. Line 2.)

title: Garden Talk
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, question words, position words in complete sentences)
dir: Look at the picture. Listen to your teacher. Say your answer out loud.
key: Say: One heart, two ____. (hearts)
Say: One bush, two ____. (bushes)

title: Kindness Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write opinion piece about which job is the better way to help
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Somebody needs a hand today. Would you rather rake the leaves in the yard, or wash the dishes after dinner? Draw the one you pick. Write or tell what you think
key: Tells the reader what the choice is about: raking the leaves or washing the dishes (W.K.1)
States an opinion, which one the student would pick. Drawing, telling, or writing all count (W.K.1)

title: Kindness Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write informative piece about a bee, a dog, or a garden
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Pick one: a bee, a dog, or a garden. Draw it. Write its name. Then write or tell one true thing about it. A bee is an insect. It lands on flowers.
key: Names what the drawing and writing are about: a bee, a dog, or a garden. The student may say it, label the picture, or write a letter or word for it (W.K.2)
Gives at least one piece of true information about it, such as: A bee lands on flowers. A dog likes to run. A garden needs water (W.K.2)

title: Kindness Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write story about a time somebody helped, told in order with a reaction
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Think of a time somebody helped you, or a time you helped somebody. Draw what happened. Then tell what happened first and what happened next. Tell how you felt.
key: Tells about one real thing that happened, not a list of facts (W.K.3)
Tells two parts, a first and a next, in the order they happened (W.K.3)

title: The Helping Chart
desc: answering questions from a picture chart and from experience
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the chart. What do you use to carry a heavy box?
Look at the chart. What can you take to a sick friend?
key: Two hands. Uses the chart to answer.
Soup. Uses the chart to answer.

title: Tell Me More
desc: describing a familiar thing you do, with details
dir: Tell your teacher out loud. Use lots of details.
text: Tell me about one job you do to help at home.
key: Names the job and tells something about it
Adds a detail when you ask: Where do you do it?

title: Down the Row
desc: counting out loud by ones
dir: Count out loud. Start at 1. Go as high as you can.
text: The garden club hangs a paper heart on the string for every kind thing somebody does. Count out loud as the hearts go up.
key: Say: Start at 1 and count as high as you can. Check: counts 1 to 20 in order with no skips.
Keeps going from 20 to 40 and gets across each new ten (29 to 30, 39 to 40).

title: Ten to a String
desc: counting by tens
dir: Count by tens out loud.
text: Each string holds 10 paper hearts. Count by tens to 100.
key: Say: Count the hearts by tens as each string goes up. Check: says 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 with no help.
Keeps going: 60, 70, 80, 90, 100. Write the last number said in order.

title: Hearts in the Jar
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 10, with drawings
dir: Listen to each story. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer out loud.
text: You can draw a circle for each heart on your paper, then count or cross out.
key: Say: There are 3 paper hearts in the jar. Four more kind things happen, so 4 more hearts go in. How many hearts are in the jar now? (7. 3 + 4 = 7)
Say: 9 flowers were in the row. A friend picked 2 of them for her grandma. How many flowers are still in the row? (7. 9 - 2 = 7)

title: Two Baskets
desc: breaking numbers up to 10 into two parts in more than one way
dir: Look at the hearts. Put some in each basket. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the first picture. There are 6 hearts and 2 baskets. Say one way to put them in the two baskets. Say it like this: ____ and ____ makes 6.
Now tell me a different way to make 6.
key: Any true pair for 6: 5 and 1, 4 and 2, 3 and 3, 2 and 4, 1 and 5, 6 and 0. The student has to say both parts.
A different true pair for 6 than the first one. Saying the same pair backwards (4 and 2, then 2 and 4) counts as different only if the student points to which basket each part goes in.

title: Split It
desc: breaking a number up to 10 into two parts in more than one way and recording each way
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Here are 6.
key: Say: Show me one way to split these 6 into two groups. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 3 + 3 = 6. (a drawing with two groups, or an equation, that makes 6)
Say: Now show me a different way. (a second pair of parts that make 6. The same two numbers in the other order do not count as different.)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: showing a number from 11 to 19 as a ten and some more and recording it
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Look at the full ten frame and the extra ones.
key: Say: Show 18 as a ten and some more. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 18 = 10 + 8. (a drawing of a ten and 8 more, or the equation)
Ask: How many ones are left after the ten? (8)

title: Count and Tell
desc: counting objects one by one and saying how many there are in all
dir: Count the hearts. Then answer out loud.
key: Say: The club cut these paper hearts for the jar. Count them and tell me how many. (8. One number word for each heart, with no skips and no double counts.)
Say it again a different way: So how many hearts are in the tray? (8, said straight back. Having to count all over again is the thing to write down.)

title: Greater, Less, or Equal
desc: deciding whether one group is greater than, less than, or equal to another
dir: Look at the two boxes. Count, then answer out loud.
key: Box 1. Ask: Which group is greater, the hearts or the leaves? How do you know? (The hearts. 9 hearts and 6 leaves. The leaves are spread out, so the two rows look about the same length. Look for count
Box 1 again. Ask: So which group is less? (The leaves. 6 is less than 9.)

title: Count On
desc: counting on from a given number and telling the number that is one more
dir: Listen to your teacher. Count out loud.
text: Count with your teacher.
key: Say: Start at 5 and keep counting up. Stop at 10. (6, 7, 8, 9, 10. The student does not go back to 1.)
Say: Start at 14 and count up to 18. (15 to 18)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: seeing a teen number as ten ones and some more ones
dir: Look at the hearts. Answer out loud.
key: Say: The box holds one full set of hearts and the rest are loose. How many hearts are in the box? (10)
Say: Now count them all. How many hearts in all? (14. Starting at ten and counting on 11, 12, 13, 14 is the goal. Counting every heart from 1 still counts, but write that down.)

title: Longer, Shorter, Taller
desc: comparing two objects directly by length and by height, and describing the difference
dir: Look at the picture. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the two ribbons. Say: Both ribbons start at the same line. Which one is longer, A or B? (A)
Say: Now tell me about B. (B is shorter than A, or B is the short one. Look for a comparing word, not only pointing.)

title: Heavy or Light
desc: comparing two objects by weight to say which is heavier and which is lighter
dir: Look at the scales. Answer out loud.
text: A B
key: Ask: Look at scale A. Which one is heavier? (the watermelon. It is on the side that goes down.)
Ask: Which one is lighter? (the strawberry)

title: Sort the Garden Tray
desc: sorting objects into categories, counting each category, and ordering the categories by count
dir: Look at the tray. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Somebody tipped the garden tray out. Put these into groups by what they are. How many groups? (3: paper hearts, leaves, and sprouts.)
Say: Count each group. How many in each? (6 hearts, 4 leaves, 3 sprouts. 13 things in all.)

title: Shapes and Where They Are
desc: naming shapes of things in a picture and telling where they are with position words
dir: Look at the shed. Answer out loud.
key: Say: The shed is drawn as two shapes. What shape is the wall? What shape is the roof? (a square wall and a triangle roof)
Say: Is the roof above the wall or below the wall? (above)

title: Flat or Solid
desc: telling flat two-dimensional shapes apart from solid three-dimensional ones
dir: Look at the six things. Answer out loud.
key: Say first: Some shapes are flat, like a shape drawn on paper. Some are solid, like something you can pick up and hold. Then ask: Which numbers are flat? (1, 3, and 5)
Ask: Which numbers are solid? (2, 4, and 6)

title: What Living Things Need
desc: telling what a plant and an animal need to stay alive
dir: Look at both pictures. Answer out loud.
text: Esme looks after a row of sunflowers in the shared garden. A duck lives on the garden pond.
qs: Esme was away for a week and nobody watered her row. The sunflowers drooped right over. What were they missing?
The duck on the pond needs food too. Does a duck make its own food the way a plant does, or does it have to go and find food?
key: water
It has to go and find food. A plant makes its own food out in the light, and an animal cannot.

title: Weather for the Garden Club
desc: describing a weather pattern from a week of observations and using it
dir: Look at the week on the chart. Count out loud.
text: The garden club writes down the weather every morning. Here is one week. Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat
qs: Count the days it rained. How many?
Count the days it did not rain. How many?

title: Weather for the Garden Club
desc: telling how a living thing changes its surroundings
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Last fall a squirrel buried acorns in the empty corner of the garden.
qs: This spring a small oak is growing up in that corner. Did the squirrel change that corner of the garden, or did the corner change the squirrel?
Tell me one way you could change a corner of a yard to make it a kinder place for birds.
key: The squirrel changed the corner. It put acorns in the ground, and a tree grew where there was nothing before.
Any sensible answer about changing a space on purpose: set out a dish of water, hang a bird house, plant a flower, leave seeds out, pile up a few branches, keep away and stay quiet.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Pond
desc: matching animals to the places that give them what they need
dir: Match each animal to the place it lives. Answer out loud.
text: Three small animals live here. It is the shared garden. Each one lives in one place. It gets what it needs. Here are the places. A hive. Under a cool damp leaf.
qs: Where does the bee live?
Where does the snail stay in the heat of the day?
key: a hive. Accept a nest of bees.
under a cool damp leaf. Accept somewhere damp and shady.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Pond
desc: telling what a weather forecast is for and how people use one to get ready
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Tomorrow the club is giving away its extra seedlings at a table by the gate. Tonight they read the forecast.
qs: The forecast says heavy rain all day tomorrow. Should the club move the giveaway table in under the shed roof, or leave it standing out in the open?
A forecast tells what the weather will probably do next. Why is that helpful to somebody with a garden?
key: move the table in under the shed roof. Knowing beforehand is the whole use of a forecast.
Any sensible answer: they can cover the young plants, skip the watering, pick the beans before the rain, bring the tools in, pick a better day.

title: Homes, Forecasts and the Pond
desc: telling one way people can take better care of the land and water
dir: Answer out loud.
text: There is a small pond at the end of the garden with frogs and ducks in it.
qs: Two gardeners scrub out their dirty pots with soap. One tips the soapy water straight into the pond. One tips it out on the gravel path. Which choice is better for the pond and the animals living in it?
The club wants to use less water this summer. Tell me one way they could.
key: tipping it out on the gravel path. Soap in the pond would reach the frogs and the ducks.
Any sensible answer: catch rain in a barrel, water early in the morning so less dries away, water the roots and not the leaves, put straw or leaves on the soil to hold the water in, use a can instead

title: Pushes and Pulls in the Garden
desc: telling a push from a pull, and comparing a strong pull with a gentle one
dir: Answer out loud. Do not say push or pull for the student.
text: A push moves something away from you. A pull brings it along with you.
qs: Rafi leans on the garden gate and sends it away from him to open it. Is that a push or a pull?
Esme takes the handle of the cart full of pots and brings it along behind her. Is that a push or a pull?
key: a push
a pull

title: Pushes and Pulls in the Garden
desc: deciding from test results whether a change worked, and telling a change of direction from a change of speed
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Rafi set a hoop flat on the grass and tried to roll a ball into it. He tried each kind of roll 5 times and counted how often the ball got there. Kind of roll Ti
qs: Which kind of roll got the ball to the hoop more often, and how many times out of 5?
The next ball is rolling straight past the hoop. Rafi puts his foot out on the far side, and the ball turns and goes into the hoop. Did his foot change the ball's direction, its speed, or both?
key: the firm roll, 5 times out of 5. The soft tap only got there 1 time out of 5.
its direction. Accept both if the student explains that it also slowed the ball down. Direction on its own is the answer to listen for.

title: Sun and Shade in the Garden
desc: telling what sunlight does to a surface it shines on
dir: Answer out loud. If you can, feel a sunny spot and a shady spot together first.
text: Two full watering cans stood out all morning. One sat in the open sunlight by the rows. One sat inside the shed.
qs: Which can has warm water in it now, the one in the open sunlight or the one in the shed?
The stone bench out in the sun is warm to sit on. The stone bench under the oak is cool. The two benches are exactly the same. What made the difference?
key: the can that sat in the open sunlight
the sunlight. One bench had sunlight on it all morning and the other was in the shade of the tree.

title: Sun and Shade in the Garden
desc: designing and drawing a cover that keeps a spot out of the sunlight
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: The giveaway table is here. It is by the gate. It stands out in the open. The little seedlings sit on it. By the afternoon they are dry. They have dried right o
qs: Draw your sun cover over the giveaway table.
Point to where the sunlight is coming from and tell me how your cover keeps the seedlings cooler.
key: Any cover drawn ABOVE or OVER the table. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one still counts. A cover drawn only beside the table is partial: ask where the sunlight is coming from.
Something like: it blocks the sun, the sun cannot reach them, it puts the table in a shadow.

title: Solving a Problem at the Gate
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking a question about it
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem? The beans keep spilling out of the basket, or the beans are green?
Ask me one question about the basket that would help you fix this.
key: The beans keep spilling out of the basket and into the dirt.

Any real question: how heavy is the basket, how hard does the wind blow there, how high is the post, could it have a lid, how many beans go in, do the birds come every day. A statement is not a questi

title: Solving a Problem at the Gate
desc: drawing something whose shape would solve the problem
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would keep the beans in, like a box with a lid, a heavier tub set low on the ground, or a cover with a weight on top of it.
qs: Draw your fix.
Tell me what you drew and how its shape keeps the beans in.
key: Anything that would stop a tip or a spill: a lid, a heavy tub, a deep box, a low wide base, a cover held down with a stone, a strap. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one earns credi
Naming it is what shows intent. Something like: the lid shuts the birds out, the heavy tub does not tip, the deep box holds them in.

title: Solving a Problem at the Gate
desc: comparing test results from two fixes for the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The club put 20 beans out each day, tried two fixes, and counted the beans still in the container at the end of the day. Fix Beans still in it at the end of the
qs: Which fix worked better?
How do you know?
key: the heavy box with a lid
Because all 20 beans were still there in the box and only 12 were left under the cloth. The reason has to come from the chart, not from liking boxes.

title: Rules and Doing Right
desc: following rules, knowing what happens when they are broken, and naming an honest choice
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What did Rafi choose to do? Say that he lost the trowel, or say nothing and let everybody wonder?
One rule at the shed is a tool goes back clean. What might go wrong if nobody followed that rule?
key: He said that he had borrowed it and lost it.
The next person gets a dirty or a broken tool, the tools rust, dirt gets everywhere, somebody has to clean up after everybody else. Any real consequence counts.

title: Maps and Places
desc: reading map colors, telling land from water, using position words, and naming shared places
dir: Look at the map. Answer out loud.
text: Here is a map. It shows the shared garden. The blue circle is the pond. The brown strips are the rows. They are garden rows. The green is the grass. The shed is
qs: On this map, which part is the water?
On a map the colors stand for things. What does the green stand for here?
key: the blue circle, which is the pond
the grass, which is land you can walk on. Accept the lawn or the ground.

title: Left and Right
desc: telling where things are with left and right, near and far, and in front and behind
dir: Look at each picture. Point or answer out loud.
text: A B C
key: Ask: Look at picture A. Point to the one on the left. (the heart)
Ask: Point to the one on the right. (the bee)

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: recognizing the flag as a symbol of the country
dir: Look at the flag. Answer out loud.
qs: This is our country's flag. Are the little shapes up in the corner stars or hearts?
A flag is a symbol, and that means it stands for something bigger than itself. What does our flag stand for?
key: star
our country. Accept the United States, America, or all the people who live here. If the student only says a flag, ask once: what does it stand for?

title: Our Flag and Long Ago
desc: telling how life long ago was different from life today, and what a commemorative holiday is for
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Long ago there were no washing machines.
qs: Long ago, how did a family get the clothes clean, by hand in a tub of water, or in a machine?
How do the clothes get washed at your house today?
key: by hand in a tub of water
Any real answer: a washing machine, at a laundry place, somebody puts them in a machine, by hand sometimes. Naming today's way is the then-and-now half of this standard.

title: Garden Sound Check
desc: blending, segmenting, and isolating sounds, counting syllables, and telling long from short vowels in spoken words
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the sounds and words out loud.
text: Listen. Then say it.
key: Blend these sounds: /h/ /e/ /l/ /p/ (help)
Blend these sounds: /sh/ /e/ /d/ (shed)

title: First Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the initial sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the first sound.
qs: What is the first sound in bed?
What is the first sound in cup?
key: The sound /b/. Say the sound, not the letter name.
The sound /k/. Say the sound, not the letter name.

title: Middle Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the medial vowel sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the middle sound.
qs: What is the middle sound in hen?
What is the middle sound in dog?
key: The short vowel sound /e/.
The short vowel sound /o/.

title: Garden Words
desc: reading words with digraphs, blends, final e, vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, endings, and two or more syllables
dir: Read each word out loud. The last one is a silly word. Just sound it out.
key: Count each word read correctly. blean is a silly word: listen for the ea team saying long e.

Watch for: sh digraph (shed), th digraph plus nk (thank), blend plus a vowel team (grow), double letters (fuzz), final e (vine), igh (right), a three-letter blend plus the ou diphthong (sprout), r-con

title: How Many Parts?
desc: using the rule that every syllable has a vowel sound to find the number of syllables in a printed word
dir: Read the word to yourself. Tell how many syllables, or parts, it has. Clap it if that helps.
text: basket dog picnic fish
key: Point to “basket”. How many syllables? (2)
Point to “dog”. How many syllables? (1)

title: Our Garden Day
desc: an 82-word shared-garden story read aloud
dir: Look at the three pictures. Then read the story out loud in your best reading voice.
text: a bean sprout a garden boot the bees Our Garden Day Our street has a garden. It is at the end. Every family takes care of one row. My job is the row of beans. O
key: 82 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Point to the three pictures first so beans, boots, and bees are clear before the student reads.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: a bean sprout a garden boot the bees Our Garden Day Our street has a garden. It is at the end. Every family takes care of one row. My job is the row of beans. O
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the story about? What happened first?” (a summary or answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: The Top Shelf
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about a story the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: The Top Shelf Ines could not reach the top shelf. The shelf was in the tool shed. The trowel she wanted was up there. It was right at the top. It sat next to a
qs: What could Ines not reach?
What did she want from up there?
key: The top shelf in the tool shed
The trowel, which was next to a ball of string

title: Sentence Spotter
desc: finding sentences by their first word, capital letter, and end mark
dir: Look at the sentences. Answer out loud.
text: We water the rows. Can you hold this?
qs: How many sentences do you see? How can you tell?
Read the first word of the second sentence. What kind of letter does it start with?
key: 2 sentences. Each one starts with a capital letter and ends with an end mark
The word is Can. It starts with a capital, or uppercase, C

title: Garden Fix It
desc: spoken grammar items (past tense, plural nouns, subject and verb match, joining two sentences, describing words, place words)
dir: Listen to your teacher read each one. Say your answer out loud.
qs: Today we share the tools. Yesterday we ____.
One bench, two ____.
key: shared
benches

title: Which Word Fits?
desc: using indefinite pronouns such as everyone, anyone, someone, something, and nothing
dir: Listen to the sentence. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? ___ is knocking at the door. (Someone / Nothing)
Which word fits? ___ was wrong with the toy, so it did not work. (Something / Everyone)
key: Someone. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)
Something. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)

title: Whose Is It?
desc: using possessive nouns to show who owns something
dir: Listen. Say the answer. For the last one, you can point to the right one on paper.
qs: Sam has a bike. Whose bike is it? Say it with an apostrophe s.
The bird has a nest. Whose nest is it?
key: Sam’s bike. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)
the bird’s nest. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)

title: Commands and Big Feelings
desc: producing imperative (command) and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts
dir: Listen. Say your answer out loud in a full sentence.
qs: Tell me to open the door. Say it as a command.
You see a rainbow! Say one sentence that shows a big feeling.
key: A command such as “Open the door.” or “Please open the door.”
An exclamation such as “What a big rainbow!” or “Look how pretty it is!”

title: Print the Alphabet
desc: printing all upper- and lowercase letters
dir: On your paper, print each big letter and its small letter. Print them in order. Hold up your paper when you finish.
text: A a B b C c D d E e F f G g H h I i J j K k L l M m N n O o P p Q q R r S s T t U u V v W w X x Y y Z z
key: Look at the paper. Mark each letter pair where both the capital and the small letter are formed correctly and sit on the line. Letters may be uneven. Count a pair when each letter can be told from the
Check the tall letters (b, d, f, h, k, l, t), the letters that drop below the line (g, j, p, q, y), and the look-alikes (b and d, p and q).

title: Listen Up
desc: asking and answering questions about a text read aloud
dir: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about how neighbors helped each other long ago. Then answer out loud.
text: Listen.
key: Ask: What could one family not do alone? (build a barn)
Ask: What did the neighbors do with the long poles? (they lifted whole walls up on end, all together)

title: Tell Me About It
desc: describing an event with relevant details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about a time somebody gave you a hand with something. What were you trying to do? What did the person do? How did you feel after?
key: Names what they were trying to do and gives 2 or more details about it (SL.1.4)
Says what the other person did, with 1 or more details, all about this one time (SL.1.4)

title: Two-Step Directions
desc: giving, restating, and following simple two-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear, say it back, and give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do what your teacher says. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once, without repeating: “Pick up your pencil, then put it on your head.” (does both steps, in the right order)
Say once, without repeating: “Clap your hands, then touch your toes.” (does both steps, in the right order)

title: Person, Place, Thing, Event
desc: describing a person, a place, a thing, and an event with relevant details, and saying ideas and feelings clearly
dir: Listen to your teacher. Tell about each one. Use lots of details.
text: Tell about a person, a place, a thing, and something that happened.
key: Say: “Tell me about your best friend or a neighbor.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the person, such as who they are, what they look like, or what they do)
Say: “Tell me about your room or your backyard.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the place, such as what is there or what you do there)

title: Use the Shed List
desc: using a provided chart to answer a question in writing
dir: Look at the chart. Write 1 sentence on your paper and hold it up.
text: A neighbor on your row is home sick in bed. You want to bring her something from the shed. What will you take? Use the chart.
key: Finds the answer in the chart. Your help is fine: read the two columns out loud and point to the row headings
Writes a sentence drawn from the chart, such as: I will take the pot of soup

title: Remember and Tell
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question
dir: Think about what happened to you. Tell your teacher your answer out loud. You can draw it, too.
qs: Think about your favorite place to play. Tell me what you do there.
Think about a time you helped someone. Tell me what you did.
key: Names a place and at least one thing they do there.
Tells one real time and what they did. (They may draw first, then tell. Write down what they say if you want a record.)

title: Garden Journal
desc: an informative piece naming a helping job and giving facts about it
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Pick one job that helps other people: watering a neighbor's row, walking a dog, setting the table, or feeding a pet. Name the job. Then write some facts about i
key: Names the topic: the one job the student picked (W.1.2)
Supplies at least two facts about the job, such as what you do or what you need (W.1.2)

title: Garden Journal
desc: a narrative about a day the student helped or was helped, told in order
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about a day you helped somebody, or a day somebody helped you. Tell two things that happened, in order. Use the words first and then. End by telling how i
key: Tells about two or more things that happened, in an order that makes sense (W.1.3)
Includes some detail about what happened, not just a list (W.1.3)

title: The Book Box
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the facts. Then answer out loud.
text: The Book Box Our street has a little book box on a post. Anyone may open it. You take a book you want to read. You do not pay. When you are done, you bring it b
qs: What is inside the book box?
What do you do when you are done with a book?
key: Books
You bring it back, or you put in a book of your own. Either half counts

title: What I Think
desc: a short opinion piece naming the choice, stating an opinion, and giving a reason
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: A new family just moved in. They came onto your street. What is the better way? You want to make them feel welcome. You could take them some soup. Take a pot of
key: Names what the choice is about, the soup or the garden walk, so a reader who did not hear the question still knows (W.1.1)
States an opinion: which one the student would pick (W.1.1)

title: Count the Hearts
desc: counting, reading, and writing numerals to 120 and counting objects
dir: Count and read out loud. Write your numbers on your paper and hold it up.
text: The garden club counts every paper heart before it goes up on the string.
qs: Count out loud from 92 to 108.
Read these numbers out loud: 73, 100, 116.
key: Seventy-three, one hundred, one hundred sixteen

title: Kindness Problems
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 20, with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen to each story problem. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer.
text: The club hangs a paper heart on the string for every kind thing somebody does.
qs: On Monday 8 hearts went up and on Tuesday 7 more went up. How many hearts is that in all?
There were 16 hearts on the string. The wind blew 9 of them off. How many are still up?
key: 7 hearts (16 - 9 = 7)

title: Strings of Ten
desc: place value in two-digit numbers (bundles of ten and leftover ones)
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud.
text: A full string holds 10 paper hearts. A long block stands for one full string of ten. A small cube stands for one loose heart.
qs: Look at the picture. How many full strings of ten do you see, and how many loose hearts? What number is that?
In the number 28, what does the 2 stand for? What does the 8 stand for?
key: 4 strings of ten and 6 loose. That is 46
The 2 stands for two tens, which is twenty hearts. The 8 stands for eight ones

title: Add Up the Rows
desc: adding within 100 (a two-digit number plus a one-digit number and plus a multiple of ten)
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Say your answer and tell how you got it.
text: The club counts the seeds that go in each row.
qs: The bean row has 34 seeds in it. The club plants 5 more. How many now?
The corn row has 52 seeds in it. The club plants 30 more. How many now?
key: 39 (34 + 5 = 39. Only the ones change)
82 (52 + 30 = 82. Adding tens to tens: 5 tens and 3 tens is 8 tens)

title: Explain Your Adding
desc: adding within 100 with a drawing, relating it to a written equation, and explaining the reasoning with tens and ones
dir: Solve on your paper. Draw tens and ones. Write the equation. Then tell how you added.
qs: Add 28 + 5. Draw tens and ones, write the equation, and tell how you added.
Why did you add the tens with the tens and the ones with the ones?
key: 28 + 5 = 33. The drawing shows tens and ones, the equation matches, and the explanation says tens were added to tens and ones to ones (and that ten ones were made into a new ten when needed).
Because tens are worth ten and ones are worth one. They are different amounts, so like parts go together.

title: The Clock in the Shed
desc: telling and writing time to the hour and the half hour on an analog clock
dir: Look at each clock. Say the time out loud. Then write the last two answers on your paper.
text: The clock in the tool shed tells the club when to start and when to stop.
qs: What time does Clock A say?
What time does Clock B say?
key: 3:00, said as three o'clock. The long hand is on the 12 and the short hand is on the 3
7:30, said as seven thirty or half past seven. The long hand is on the 6. Watch for a student who says eight thirty, because the short hand has moved halfway toward the 8

title: Turn It Around
desc: using the order of addends and making a ten as strategies to add
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: The club hangs hearts on two strings.
qs: You know 8 + 5 = 13. So what is 5 + 8? How do you know?
Is 7 + 6 the same as 6 + 7? How do you know?
key: 13. The same two parts, just said in the other order, so the total does not change
Yes, both make 13. Same parts, other order. Look for the reason, not only the answer

title: Count On, Count Back
desc: counting on to add and counting back to subtract
dir: Answer out loud. You may count on your fingers.
qs: There are 9 hearts on the string. 3 more go up. Count on from 9 to find how many. Say the numbers you count.
There are 14 hearts on the string. 2 blow off. Count back to find how many are left.
key: 12. Says 10, 11, 12, starting from 9 and not from 1

title: Tens Off the String
desc: subtracting a multiple of ten from a multiple of ten using tens
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Say your answer and tell how you got it.
text: A full string holds 10 paper hearts.
qs: The picture shows the hearts on the gate. The club takes 3 whole strings down. How many hearts are left?
key: 40 hearts. 7 strings of ten take away 3 strings of ten leaves 4 strings of ten, which is 70 - 30 = 40
40. 9 tens take away 5 tens is 4 tens

title: How Many Hearts Long
desc: measuring length as a whole number of same-size units laid end to end
dir: Look at the picture. Answer out loud.
qs: The heart cards are all the same size. How many cards long is the ribbon?
How many cards long is the trowel handle?
key: 6 cards long
4 cards long

title: Read the Chart
desc: reading a graph with three categories: total, how many in each, and how many more
dir: Look at the graph. Answer out loud.
qs: How many kind things are on the whole graph?
Which kind thing happened the fewest times?
key: Carried, with 4

title: Share It Fair
desc: halves and fourths of circles and rectangles, and equal shares
dir: Look at the three pictures. Answer out loud.
qs: Which picture shows a loaf cut into halves, A or C?
Picture B is a garden bed cut into four equal parts. What do you call one of those parts?
key: A. One line down the middle, and the two pieces are the same size
A fourth, or a quarter. A fourth of the bed, or one quarter of the bed, both count

title: Make a Graph
desc: organizing and representing data with up to three categories, and answering questions about the total and about how many more or less
dir: Look at the list. Make a tally chart or a picture graph on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: Ten kids told us their pets at home. cat dog dog fish cat dog cat dog dog cat
key: A chart or graph with dog 5, cat 4, fish 1. Each item is counted once. Tally marks, pictures, or squares all work. Labels are on each group.
10 (the total of all three groups)

title: Copy a Butterfly
desc: naming the job an animal body part does, then designing a tool that copies it to solve a human problem
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer the first out loud. Draw the second on your paper and hold it up.
text: A butterfly has a long thin tongue. It rolls up like a spring. It does that when not in use. It unrolls it and reaches down. It goes all the way down. The throa
qs: How does a long thin tongue get a butterfly to food that a short wide mouth could never reach?
Draw a tool that copies the butterfly's long thin tongue and gets the plant food out of the tall jar.
key: It is thin enough to fit down a narrow opening and long enough to reach the bottom. Any answer about being long and thin counts.
Any long thin tool: a straw, a thin tube, a long narrow spoon, a stick with a cup on the end, a pipe that sucks up liquid. A wide scoop is partial, so ask what the butterfly's tongue is like.

title: Cat and Kittens
desc: finding a pattern in what a parent animal does and what the young do in answer, and saying how it helps the young
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What do the kittens do every single time the cat makes her soft chirruping sound?
What does the cat do before she lets them feed?
key: They turn toward it and crawl to her. Every time is what makes it a pattern.
She licks each one all over, and they stay still for it.

title: Cat and Kittens
desc: making observations that young plants and animals are like their parents but not exactly like them
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
text: Two tulips grown from seeds of the same parent plant. A kitten and the cat that is its parent.
qs: These two tulips came from the same parent plant, but one is red and one is purple. Does that mean one of them is not a tulip? Say why.
Name one way both tulips are like the plant they came from.
key: No. Both are tulips. Plants grown from the same parent are like it, but not exactly like it, and not exactly like each other either.
Both have a stem, green leaves, and a cup shaped flower on top. Any likeness counts.

title: The Moon Walks East
desc: finding a pattern in a log of sky observations and using it to predict what comes next
dir: Look at the log. Answer out loud.
text: At eight o'clock on four evenings a child in the garden wrote down where the moon was. Evening Where the moon was at eight first evening just over the garden ga
qs: Which way is the moon moving from one evening to the next?
On the fifth evening at eight o'clock, do you predict the moon will be over the big tree, or further to the left of it?
key: To the left, a little more each evening.
further to the left of the big tree

title: The Moon Walks East
desc: relating the number of hours of daylight to the time of year from observations made across a year
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: How long there was enough daylight to work in the garden. Month Hours of daylight February 11 May 14 August 14 November 10
qs: Which month on the chart had the shortest amount of daylight?
Two months on the chart had the same number of hours. Which two?
key: November, 10 hours
May and August, both 14 hours

title: The Twanging Ruler
desc: planning an investigation showing that a shaking material makes sound and that a sound can make a material shake
dir: If you have a ruler, try the first part. Either way, answer out loud.
text: Hold a ruler flat on a table with most of it sticking out over the edge. Press the end down and let it go. Now tear a tiny scrap of paper and lay it on an uptur
qs: What does the end of the ruler do, and what do you hear while it does it?
Catch the ruler in your hand. What happens to the sound, and why?
key: It shakes up and down very fast, and you hear a buzzing or twanging note while it moves.
The sound stops at once, because the ruler can no longer shake. No shaking, no sound.

title: The Dark Closet
desc: accounting for why an object in darkness can be seen only when light shines on it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The closet by the back door has no window, and the door fits tightly.
qs: A bright red paper heart is on a shelf inside the closed closet. Can you see it? Say why or why not.
What would you have to do before the paper heart could be seen?
key: No. No light gets into the closet, and a thing can only be seen when light shines on it and comes back to your eyes.
Light has to reach it: a flashlight, a lamp, or the door opened to let light in.

title: The Dark Closet
desc: using test results to tell what happens when different materials are put in the path of a beam of light
dir: Look at the test results. Answer out loud.
text: One flashlight beam was pointed at four things in the dark closet and what it did was written down. What was put in the beam What the beam did a clear glass vas
qs: Which thing stopped the beam and made a dark shadow?
Which thing let a soft glow through?
key: the cardboard box
the thin tissue paper

title: Window to Window
desc: designing a device that uses light or sound to send a message over a distance too far to shout
dir: Draw your answer on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: Two friends live in houses. The houses are facing each other. A wide courtyard is across the middle. At bedtime both windows are shut. Neither one can hear the
qs: Draw a device for one window that tells the other window good night. It has to use light or sound.
Tell me about your drawing. Does it send light, or does it send sound?
key: Any device that carries light or sound across the courtyard: a flashlight flashed at the window, a lamp switched on and off, a bell on a string, a card held up with a lamp behind it.
Names it and says which one it uses.

title: Fix the Mixed Up Cards
desc: naming a problem people want to change, asking a question about it, and saying what to observe first
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem the gardeners want to change?
Ask me something about the problem that would help you work out a fix.
key: The cards slide about and get mixed up in the open box, so the wrong seeds go into the wrong row.

Any real question: how many cards are there, how big is the box, how far is it carried, are the cards all the same size, does it happen on the way out or on the way back. A statement is not a question

title: Fix the Mixed Up Cards
desc: making a simple drawing of a fix and explaining how the shape of the object makes it work
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
text: Draw a better box or holder for the cards, one that keeps them in order while it is carried.
qs: Draw your new holder.
Point to the part that keeps each card in its place and tell me its shape.
key: Any real fix: a tray with a divider between each card, slots for each card, a ring through a hole in every card, pockets, a lid with a clip, cards taped to a board in order.
Names a shape: upright walls between the cards, narrow slots, a ring, a row of pockets.

title: Which Tray Worked
desc: comparing the data from tests of two objects built to solve the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two card holders were carried out to the beds and back, twelve cards in each, five trips each. Holder Cards out of order at the end, out of 12 a tray with divid
qs: Which one kept the cards in order better?
What do the two numbers in the chart tell you?
key: the tray with dividers
No cards were out of order in the tray, 0 out of 12, and 9 out of 12 were out of order in the bag. The numbers have to be in the answer.

title: Sharing the Garden Bench
desc: telling a right from a responsibility, and explaining why rules exist for places everybody shares
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: Anybody may sit on the bench. Is being allowed to sit there a right or a responsibility?
Taking the cups and tools back inside is a job. Is that a right or a responsibility?
key: a right
a responsibility

title: The Garden Map
desc: giving an exact grid location, describing a relative location, and telling a physical feature from a built one

qs: Find the kindness bench. Give its exact spot on the grid, the letter and the number.
Where is the garden shed compared to the kindness bench? Use north, south, east or west.
key: C2. Both parts are needed.
North of the bench and east of it. Both directions are needed for a full answer, and north east counts.

title: The Garden Map
desc: naming built features of a familiar place and recognizing that people in one place come from many different places
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Each family helps in this garden. Each one planted one thing. They grew up eating it. There are nine different plants. They are in the beds. No two families cho
qs: Nine families planted nine different things. What does that tell you about where those families came from?
Name three places in your own town that people built, and say which one you go to most often.
key: They came from different places and grew up with different food. Any answer about different backgrounds counts.
Any three built places, with one named as most visited: a school, a store, a park, a library, a playground, a bus stop.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: telling why a country makes lasting symbols and naming one the student has seen
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Four presidents have their faces carved. The faces are in a mountain side. It is in South Dakota. The carving is called Mount Rushmore. It took fourteen years t
qs: What is carved into the side of the mountain at Mount Rushmore?
It took fourteen years of work. Why would people spend that long carving faces into a mountain?
key: The faces of four presidents.
So the country would remember those people for a very long time. Stone lasts, and a symbol is meant to last. Any answer about remembering counts.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: comparing everyday life long ago with life today and telling what changed from what stayed the same
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Sending a kind note to someone far away. Long ago Today how the note travelled a rider on a horse carried the bag a message on a screen how long it took several
qs: Long ago, who carried a note to someone far away?
How does a note get there today?
key: A rider on a horse, carrying the bag of letters.
On a screen, as a message.

title: Garden Word Flip

key: Read each word in order. plean and drorn are made-up words: listen for the ea team saying long e, and for the or sound.

Watch for: the -ed ending said as /d/ on a final-e base (shared), the suffix -ly (kindly), th plus r-controlled or (thorn), a three-letter blend plus the ou diphthong (sprout), the ea team plus ch (re

title: Two-Part Long Vowel Words
desc: decoding regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels
dir: Read each word out loud. Each word has two parts.
key: Mark each word read correctly. Each word has two syllables and at least one long vowel sound, such as pa-per, mu-sic, o-pen.
If the student breaks the word into syllables and then says it smoothly, count it correct.

title: Read the Story
desc: a 104-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Tess was the only one still working when the light started to go. Every other row on the hill had been weeded and watered hours before. Hers was the long row at
key: 104 words. Mark each missed word and each self-correction on the passage in the record sheet.
Note pace and expression in your notes.

title: Story Questions
desc: asking and answering who, what, why, and how questions about key details in a story
dir: Look back at the story if you need to. Then answer each question out loud.
text: The Long Row (click to open or close the story) Tess was the only one still working when the light started to go. Every other row on the hill had been weeded an
qs: Who was still working when the light started to go?
Why did nobody want the row at the bottom of the hill?
key: Tess
The hose would not stretch that far, so every bucket of water had to be carried by hand.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Tess was the only one still working when the light started to go. Every other row on the hill had been weeded and watered hours before. Hers was the long row at
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the text about? Tell me two things you remember.” (an answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: The Crow and the Badger
desc: recounting a fable and determining its central message or lesson
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then answer each question out loud.
text: The Crow and the Badger A crow and a badger lived on two sides of the same hedge. All summer the crow found shiny bits of foil and wire. She dropped them over o
qs: Tell me what happened in this story, from the beginning to the end.
What did the crow give the badger, and what did the badger give the crow?
key: Retells it in order: all summer the crow passed shiny things over the hedge, the badger passed beetles back, neither of them kept track, and when winter came the badger had the warmest burrow and the
The crow gave shiny bits of foil and wire. The badger gave fat beetles.

title: The Tool Library
desc: asking and answering what, why, how long, and who questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about tool libraries. Then answer each question out loud.
text: The Tool Library A tool library works like a book library, except for one thing. The shelves hold drills and ladders and wheelbarrows. You join for a small fee.
qs: What kinds of things are on the shelves of a tool library?
How long may you keep something you borrow?
key: Drills, ladders and wheelbarrows
A week

title: Say It Right
desc: spoken grammar items (irregular past tense, irregular plural, reflexive pronoun, adverb, word order, joining two sentences)
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: Today we bring the tools back. Yesterday we ____.
One goose, two ____.
key: brought
geese

title: Write It Right
desc: written conventions (capital letters in place names, an apostrophe for a possessive and a contraction, a comma in a letter greeting, spelling two patterns)
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Fix this sentence: we walked along elm street to the green hill garden
The bucket belongs to the club. Write the missing word: the ____ bucket
key: We walked along Elm Street to the Green Hill Garden. (capital W to start, capital E and capital S in the street name, capital G, H and G in the garden name, and a period)
club’s (apostrophe before the s)

title: Capital Letters
desc: capitalizing holidays, product names, and geographic names
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each sentence. Write it again with the right capital letters. Hold up your paper when you finish.
qs: Fix the capital letters: we watch fireworks on the fourth of july.
Fix the capital letters: she lives near the pacific ocean.
key: We watch fireworks on the Fourth of July.
She lives near the Pacific Ocean.

title: Use a Dictionary
desc: using a beginning dictionary and ABC order to check and correct spellings
dir: Listen. Answer out loud. If you have a beginning dictionary, you may use it.
qs: Put these words in ABC order the way a dictionary does: pig, cow, hen.
The guide words are fish and goat. Would the word frog be on this page? Tell why.
key: cow, hen, pig
Yes. frog comes after fish and before goat.

title: Group Words
desc: using collective nouns
dir: Listen. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? A group of bees is called a ___. (swarm / stack)
Which word fits? A group of ships is called a ___. (fleet / team of pencils)
key: swarm. (A collective noun names a group.)
fleet. (A collective noun names a group.)

title: Guide Dog Report
desc: recounting and describing key ideas and details from a text read aloud
dir: Listen first. Then answer your teacher's questions out loud.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read a report about dogs that are trained to help people.
key: Ask: Who does a guide dog live with for its first year? (a volunteer family, not the person it will one day lead)
Ask: Describe what that family's job is. (to make the puppy calm and friendly everywhere, taking it on car rides, into crowds, into lifts and onto loud streets)

title: Longer Directions
desc: following three- and four-step oral directions, requesting clarification when something is not understood, and giving multi-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear. Ask a question if you are not sure what to do. Then give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do the steps in order. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once: “Get a pencil, write the number 8, and circle it.” (does all three steps in order)
Say once: “Clap two times, turn around, touch your toes, and sit back down.” (does all four steps in order)

title: The Bucket Log
desc: gathering information from a provided log and recalling information from experience to answer questions
dir: Use the log to answer. Say the first two answers out loud. Write number 3 on your paper and hold it up. Then say number 4.
text: The club writes down how many buckets of water got carried each day, and how many people came to help.
qs: Use the log. Which day did the club carry the most buckets?
Which days did more than 5 people come?
key: Tuesday, with 20 buckets
Tuesday and Thursday (7 people and 6 people)

title: Write It Down
desc: an opinion piece with reasons, linking words, and a concluding statement
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: The club has saved enough money for one thing. It can buy a wheelbarrow that everybody shares, or it can build a bench by the gate where people can sit and talk
key: Introduces the topic: what the club is choosing between
States a clear opinion, the wheelbarrow or the bench

title: Write It Down
desc: an informative piece with an introduced topic, facts, a definition, and a concluding statement
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about one way neighbors help each other, such as a shared garden, a tool library, or watching a pet while somebody is away. Introduce your topic in the fi
key: Introduces the topic in the first sentence, so the reader knows what the piece is about
Gives at least 2 facts about it

title: Read the Garden Signs
desc: applying grade-level phonics and word-analysis skills to decode words in text
dir: Read each line out loud. Sound out any word that is tricky.
text: We shared the heavy buckets and finished before dark. Tess unpacked eight trays and wrote down every row. The greenhouse was warm enough for the tiny sprouts.
key: Line 1: listen for the -ed ending said as /d/ in shared, the ea team saying short e in heavy, the ck plus -ed said as /t/ in buckets, and the r-controlled ar in dark.
Line 2: listen for the prefix un plus the -ed ending said as /t/ in unpacked, the irregular eigh in eight, and silent w plus final e in wrote.

title: Tell It Out Loud
desc: recounting an experience out loud with facts and descriptive details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly, in full sentences.
text: Tell me about somebody who taught you how to do something. What were you learning? What did that person say or do?
key: Recounts a real experience with facts: who it was, what was being learned
Adds descriptive details that fit, such as where it happened or what the person said

title: Plan and Tell a Story
desc: planning and delivering a short narrative presentation that recounts an event with details, a logical sequence, and a conclusion
dir: Pick one idea. Plan what you will say: the start, the middle, and the end. Then tell your story out loud.
text: Pick one: a time you helped someone, a game or a sport you played, or a time something surprised you. Beginning Middle End
key: Plans first: says or draws what will happen at the start, the middle, and the end before telling (give about one minute to plan)
Tells one event with enough detail (who, where, and what happened)

title: A Time I Gave a Hand
desc: a short narrative recounting one event in order, with details and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about one time you gave somebody a hand, or somebody gave you one. Tell what happened first and what happened next. End by telling how it turned out. Writ
key: Recounts one event, not a list, and tells two or more things that happened in an order that makes sense (W.2.3)
Includes details about what happened, what was said, or how it felt (W.2.3)

title: Trays in the Greenhouse
desc: finding the total in a rectangular array and writing it as a sum of equal addends
dir: Look at the three trays. Answer out loud. Write the addition sentences on your paper.
text: The club starts its seeds in trays. Every little pot holds one plant.
qs: Look at Tray 1. How many rows are there, and how many plants are in each row? How many plants in all?
Write an addition sentence for Tray 1 that shows one number for each row.
key: 4 rows with 3 plants in each row, 12 plants in all
3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. One addend for each of the 4 rows

title: Count Along the Path
desc: counting within 1000 and skip-counting by 5s, 10s, and 100s
dir: Count out loud.
text: The club sets a stepping stone every 5 paces along the garden path, so the counting goes 5, 10, 15, and on.
qs: Skip count by 5s from 75 to 115.
Skip count by 10s from 240 to 310.

title: Count by 2s
desc: skip-counting by 2s within 1000
dir: Count out loud by 2s.
qs: Count by 2s from 90. Say the next five numbers.
Count by 2s starting at 100. Say the next five numbers.

title: Club Logbook Math
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with a place value strategy and relating it to a written method
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Show your work and hold it up. Say your answer.
text: Every year the club writes down how many plants went into the ground across the whole hill.
qs: Last year 268 plants went in on the east side and 357 on the west side. How many in all? Show how you added.
The club wants 500 plants in the ground this year. So far 236 are in. How many more are needed?
key: 625 plants (268 + 357 = 625). Listen for hundreds with hundreds, tens with tens, ones with ones, and for making a new ten and a new hundred.
264 more (500 - 236 = 264). This one needs two decomposes, so watch the work.

title: Why Regroup?
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with place value, and explaining why a ten or hundred is composed or decomposed
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work. Then tell why you had to regroup.
qs: Solve 47 + 36. Tell why you had to make a new ten.
Solve 62 - 27. Tell why you had to take a ten apart.
key: 83. 7 + 6 = 13 ones, so 10 ones became 1 ten.
35. 2 ones is not enough to take away 7, so 1 ten was regrouped into 10 ones.

title: Read the Clock
desc: telling time on an analog clock to the nearest five minutes
dir: Look at each clock. Say the time out loud.
text: The clock by the garden gate keeps the club on time.
key: Clock A: 6:10, said as six ten or ten past six. The minute hand is on the 2, and one number mark is five minutes.

Clock B: 4:35, said as four thirty-five or twenty-five to five. The minute hand is on the 7. Watch for a student who says five thirty-five, because the hour hand has moved most of the way toward the 5

title: Write the Time
desc: writing times to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m., and knowing minutes in an hour
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Look at the digital clock. Write that time.
The club meets at that time in the evening. Write the time again and add a.m. or p.m.
key: 5:20 p.m. (evening is after noon, so it is p.m.)

title: Time Facts
desc: knowing relationships of time such as minutes in an hour, days in a month, and weeks in a year
dir: Listen. Answer out loud.
qs: How many days are in one week?
How many months are in one year?
key: 7 days
12 months

title: The Seed Sale
desc: solving word problems with dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies
dir: Look at the coins. Answer out loud. Write the money answers with a cents sign or a dollar sign.
text: The club sells seed packets by the gate and puts the money back into the garden.
qs: Count the coins in the picture. How much money is that?
Luz has 2 quarters and 3 dimes. How much money does she have?
key: 51¢ (a quarter is 25, two dimes are 20, a nickel is 5, a penny is 1: 25 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 = 51)
80¢ (2 quarters is 50 and 3 dimes is 30, so 50 + 30 = 80)

title: Shapes in the Beds
desc: identifying triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons and cubes by their angles and faces, and drawing a shape with given attributes
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud. Then draw the last one on your paper.
text: The club laid out its garden beds in different shapes, and keeps the seed boxes stacked by the gate.
qs: What is the name of Bed 1? How many sides and angles does it have?
What is the name of Bed 2? How many sides and angles does it have?
key: A triangle. 3 sides and 3 angles
A quadrilateral. 4 sides and 4 angles. Calling it a trapezoid as well is a plus, because every trapezoid is a quadrilateral

title: Pot and Bucket Problems
desc: one-step and two-step word problems within 100, with the unknown in different places
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Say your answer.
qs: There were 46 paper hearts on the string. Some blew off in the wind. Now there are 29. How many blew off?
The club filled 38 pots on Saturday and 26 more on Sunday. Then they gave 15 pots to the school. How many pots do they still have?
key: 49 pots. Two steps: 38 + 26 = 64, then 64 - 15 = 49

title: Two-Step Problems
desc: solving two-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100
dir: Listen to each problem. Solve it on your paper. Write an equation with a box or a letter for the number you do not know.
qs: A store had 45 apples. It sold 18 in the morning. Then it got 30 more. How many apples does the store have now? Show your work.
Eli had 62 stickers. He gave 15 to Max and 20 to Lia. How many stickers does Eli have left?

title: Odd or Even
desc: telling odd from even by pairing, and writing an even number as a sum of two equal addends
dir: Look at the two groups. Answer out loud. Write the last answer on your paper.
qs: Count Group A. Is that number odd or even? How do you know?
Count Group B. Is that number odd or even? How do you know?
key: 14, and it is even. Every heart has a partner underneath it, with none left over
9, and it is odd. The last heart on the top row has no partner underneath

title: What the Digits Mean
desc: place value in three-digit numbers, and knowing 100 as ten tens
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: The club wrote 462 in the logbook. What does the 4 stand for? What does the 6 stand for? What does the 2 stand for?
How many tens are in 100?
key: 4 hundreds, 6 tens, and 2 ones. Saying four hundred, sixty, and two is also correct
10 tens

title: Three Ways to Write It
desc: reading and writing numbers to 1000 in numerals, in words, and in expanded form
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Write 608 in words.
Write four hundred twenty using numerals.
key: six hundred eight. Watch for six hundred and eight, which is how it is said out loud, and for six hundred eighty
420. Watch for 4020

title: Measure It
desc: measuring length with a ruler and choosing the right tool for the job
dir: Look at the ruler. Answer out loud. Then measure one real thing.
qs: How long is the trowel on the ruler?
You want to measure how long the garden path is. Would you use this 12-inch ruler or a measuring tape? Why?
key: 5 inches. The trowel starts at 0 and ends at the 5 mark
A measuring tape, because the path is much longer than the ruler and a tape can reach all the way without being moved over and over

title: Read the Bar Graph
