desc: reading a bar graph with four categories and solving compare and put-together problems from it
dir: Look at the graph. Answer out loud.
text: The club turned the people column of the Bucket Log into a bar graph.
qs: How many more people came on Tuesday than on Wednesday?
How many people came in all across the four days?

title: Draw a Picture Graph
desc: drawing a picture graph from a data set with four categories and solving put-together, take-apart, and compare problems
dir: Look at the table. Draw a picture graph on your paper. Use one picture for each 1. Then answer out loud.
text: Pets at home: number of kids Choice Number of kids Dog 5 Cat 6 Fish 2 Bird 3
qs: Draw a picture graph of the table. Give it a title and label each row.
How many kids chose Dog and Cat together?
key: A picture graph with 5 symbols for Dog, 6 symbols for Cat, 2 symbols for Fish, 3 symbols for Bird. Each symbol stands for 1, the symbols are the same size and lined up, and the rows are labeled.

title: Draw a Bar Graph
desc: drawing a bar graph with a single-unit scale from a data set and solving put-together, take-apart, and compare problems
dir: Look at the table. Draw a bar graph on your paper. Count by ones up the side. Then answer out loud.
text: Favorite seasons: number of kids Choice Number of kids Winter 2 Spring 4 Summer 8 Fall 5
qs: Draw a bar graph of the table. Give it a title, label each bar, and number the side by ones.
How many kids chose Summer and Fall together?
key: A bar graph with bars of height 2 for Winter, 4 for Spring, 8 for Summer, 5 for Fall, a title, labels, and a side scale counting by ones that starts at 0.

title: Three Trays in the Club Greenhouse
desc: reading the results of a plant test and planning a fair test of one thing a plant needs
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Then answer out loud.
text: The garden club started three trays of lettuce on the same day so the members could see for themselves what a seedling needs. Tray What it got After two weeks A
qs: Which tray did best, and what did it get?
Tray C had 19 seedlings, nearly as many as tray A. Why would the club still say tray C failed?
key: Tray A, 24 strong dark green seedlings. It got both light and water.
Because they are tall, floppy and pale. Under the box they had no light, so they stretched looking for it and could not make food or go green. They would not survive being planted out.

title: Three Trays in the Club Greenhouse
desc: making a simple model that does the job an animal does when it pollinates plants
dir: Draw your model on your paper. Then tell your teacher about it.
text: Butterflies land on the club's flowers to drink. Pollen catches on their legs and comes off again on the next flower. That is how the flowers make seeds. Draw a
qs: Draw your model. Label the part that collects the pollen and show how it gets left behind.
Which animal job does your model copy, and why does your model have to leave some pollen behind instead of keeping all of it?
key: Any model with a fuzzy or sticky collecting part and a way for some to come off: pipe cleaner legs on a cork, a felt pad, a soft brush. The two labelled parts are what to look for.
It copies a butterfly moving pollen between flowers. If the model kept every grain, the second flower would get none, and a flower needs pollen from another flower to make seeds.

title: The Fern Corner and the Open Bed
desc: comparing the kinds of living things found in two different habitats
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both lists. Answer out loud.
text: Club members counted what was living in two corners of the same garden, half an hour in each. The shady damp fern corner The sunny open bed 3 kinds of fern 4 ki
qs: How many kinds of living things are on each list?
Name one living thing from the fern corner that would not do well in the sunny bed, and say why.
key: Both have 8. The fern corner has three ferns, two mosses, two slugs and snails and one woodlouse. The sunny bed has four flowers, two bees, one butterfly, one ladybug and one grasshopper.
Any sensible pick with a reason: a slug would dry out in the sun because its body has to stay damp, moss needs shade and damp or it shrivels, a fern burns in strong sun.

title: One Storm, or Many Winters
desc: using two sources as evidence that some Earth events happen quickly and some happen slowly
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both notes. Answer out loud.
text: Two notes about the club's land, from two different places. Where it came from What it says the club meeting notes One storm in March washed the gravel off the
qs: Which note tells about a change that happened in one afternoon?
Which note tells about a change that took many years?
key: The club meeting notes, the gravel washed off the top path in an afternoon.
The card on the big rock, the rock split after many winters of freezing water.

title: One Storm, or Many Winters
desc: telling where water is found on Earth and whether it is solid or liquid
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The club keeps track of every bit of water on its land, because it shares it.
qs: Name three places on this garden land where you would find water.
Most of the water on Earth is in the ocean and it is salty. Where does the club's water come from, and is it salty or fresh?
key: Any three: the rain barrel, the pond, the bird bath, the tap on the pipe, clouds, frost or ice, in the soil, inside the plants.
From rain caught in the barrel and from the town pipe. It is fresh, which is why plants can be watered with it. Salty water would kill them.

title: Holding the Beds, and a Map of the Garden
desc: comparing two things built to stop wind from blowing the soil away
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Dry wind lifts the loose soil out of the raised beds along the open side of the garden. Two screens were tried and the soil that had to be put back was weighed.
qs: Which screen held the soil best?
How do you know, using the numbers in the chart?
key: the row of low shrubs
Only 1 kilogram had to be put back behind the shrubs, 3 kilograms behind the willow fence, and 8 kilograms where there was nothing. The reason must come from the numbers.

title: Holding the Beds, and a Map of the Garden
desc: making a model of an area that shows the shapes of the land and the bodies of water in it
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Make your own model map of the club's land. Put in the mound of earth at the back, the flat bed area, the pond, and the ditch that carries rain away. Add a key
qs: Draw your model map with the mound, the flat beds, the pond and the ditch on it.
Show me your key. Which parts are land and which parts are water?
key: All four on the page and told apart by shape or colour: the mound as a bump or as rings, the beds left flat, the pond as a closed shape, the ditch as a line.
Points to each part and reads the key. The key is what makes this a model and not just a picture.

title: Sorting the Tool Library
desc: describing materials by properties you can see or feel and sorting them into groups
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The club lends out its tools to anyone who joins. Four things off the shelf, and what was noticed about each. Item Material What was noticed a trowel steel hard
qs: Sort the four items into a hard group and a group that bends.
Two of them soak water up. Which two, and which of those two would hold water in it for a plant?
key: Hard: the steel trowel and the clay pot. Bends: the rubber glove and the cotton apron.
The clay pot and the cotton apron. The clay pot, because it is a container that holds its shape, while the apron just gets wet.

title: Sorting the Tool Library
desc: using test data to choose the material that suits a job
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The tool library needs bags so members can carry borrowed tools home. Three materials were each loaded with a trowel, a fork and a watering can and carried a mi
qs: Which material should the lending bags be made of?
Which two pieces of the chart make you sure?
key: the coated canvas tote
It held the weight and the tools were dry at the end. Both columns have to be used, not just one.

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: telling how a thing built from a few pieces can be taken apart and built into something new
dir: Answer out loud. You may draw if it helps.
text: The bench is by the greenhouse. It is made of 3 long planks. It has 2 solid blocks. 8 bolts hold it together. The club unbolted it to move it.
qs: The bench is gone. Are the planks and blocks gone too? What is on the grass now?
Build something new in your head out of those 3 planks and 2 blocks. What is it, and how do the pieces go together?
key: No. All 3 planks, both blocks and all 8 bolts are still there. They are the same pieces, just not bolted together as a bench any more.

Any real thing from 3 planks and 2 blocks: a potting table, a frame for a raised bed, a step, a shelf, a ramp for a wheelbarrow, a sign. Listen for how the pieces join, because that is the evidence th

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: arguing with evidence that some heating and cooling changes can be undone and some cannot
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two things happened in the club kitchen on the same afternoon. What happened A lump of beeswax was warmed in a pot to make hand salve and became a clear liquid.
qs: Take the pot of melted beeswax off the heat and let it cool. What happens to it?
Let the toasted seeds cool right down. Do they go back to pale raw seeds?
key: It goes solid again and is a lump of wax, in the shape of whatever it cooled in.
No. They stay dark brown and nutty. Cooling does nothing for them.

title: The Tools That Go Missing
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking a question about it
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the note. Answer out loud.
text: The club keeps its small hand tools together. They go in one deep bucket. It sits by the shed door. Members dig through the bucket. They try to find what they w
qs: What is the problem the club wants to fix? Say it in one sentence.
Ask one question that would help you fix it.
key: The tools get lost at the bottom of one deep bucket and nobody can tell what has been borrowed. Naming the losing track of tools, not the digging, is the problem.
Any real question: how many tools are there, how many kinds, how long are they, how many members borrow at once, is there a wall to hang them on. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: The Tools That Go Missing
desc: drawing a design and telling how its shape does the job
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would hold the hand tools so anyone can see at a glance what is there and what is gone. Think hard about its shape.
qs: Draw your fix.
Tell me how the shape of what you drew shows at a glance that a tool is missing.
key: Any design that gives each tool its own place: a board with hooks, a rack with slots, a drawn outline for each tool, a row of open tubes, labelled boxes.

The shape is the part being checked. Something like: each tool has its own hook, so an empty hook shows one is gone; the outline shows the shape that belongs there; a slot with nothing in it is easy t

title: The Tools That Go Missing
desc: comparing test results from two designs built for the same problem
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The club tried both ideas for one month each. Fix Tools missing at the end of the month How long it took to find a trowel a board with a hook and an outline for
qs: Which fix worked better?
How do you know? Use both columns.
key: the board with a hook and an outline for each tool
No tools were missing and a trowel took only a few seconds to find, while the buckets lost 2 tools and took about half a minute. Both columns have to be used, not just the missing tools.

title: Sharing Then and Now
desc: telling things that happened long ago from things that happened in the last day or two
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the four lines. Answer out loud.
text: Four lines from the club's record book. Line What it says 1 This morning four members weeded the shared bed by the gate. 2 Long ago the families on this street
qs: Which two lines tell about things that happened long ago?
Which two tell about things that happened in the last day or two?
key: Lines 2 and 4, carrying water from one hand pump and swapping saved seeds.
Lines 1 and 3, weeding this morning and lending the tools yesterday.

title: Where Things Are in the Garden
desc: giving an exact place on a map with a letter and a number, and using north, south, east, west and between
dir: Look at the map. Answer out loud.
text: The club garden, drawn in nine squares. North is at the top. 1 2 3 A big hill bee hotel bird feeders B tool library shared beds herb rows C pond compost bins ra
qs: Give the exact square the shared beds are in, using their letter and number.
What is directly south of the shared beds?
key: B2
the compost bins, in square C2

title: Rules, Money and the Seed Sale
desc: telling who makes rules at each level here, and how another country chooses a leader differently
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The club has its own rules. They are written down. The members agreed them by a vote. The club also follows the rules of the city.
qs: The club votes on whether to open the garden on Saturday mornings. 11 members vote yes and 4 vote no. What happens, and why?
Who makes the laws for a whole city? A city council the people elect, or the oldest person in the city?
key: The garden opens on Saturday mornings. More members voted yes than no, and that is how a vote is decided.
a city council the people elect. Accept: the mayor and the city council.

title: Rules, Money and the Seed Sale
desc: telling goods from services, spending a set amount, and saying why people trade
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the price list. Answer out loud.
text: The club's spring seed sale, held to pay for new tools. What is on offer Price a packet of flower seeds 25 cents a seedling in a pot 40 cents a bag of compost 6
qs: Three things on this list are goods and one is a service. Which one is the service, and how do you know?
You have 65 cents. Name two things you could buy with it, and say what you give up.
key: A member coming to plant it for you. It is work someone does for you, not a thing you take home.
Any pair at 65 cents or less: seeds and a seedling is 65 cents, seeds and the planting is 60 cents, a seedling and the planting is 75 cents and is too much. The giving up is the part to listen for.

title: Someone Who Made a Difference
desc: telling what one person from the past did, naming a character strength, and saying how it helped others
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about him. Answer out loud.
text: Jackie Robinson was one of the best ballplayers. Anyone had seen that. But the big leagues would not sign him. He was a Black player. That went on for years. In
qs: What did Jackie Robinson do in 1947 that no Black player had been allowed to do before?
Which word fits him best from what you read: dignified, rude, or careless? Say why.
key: He played in the big leagues. He was the first Black player signed to a big league team.
dignified. Accept patient or strong with the same reasons. Any reason taken from the text: he kept his temper through a whole season, he let his playing answer for him instead of shouting back.

title: Gate Sign Words
desc: reading longer words with prefixes, suffixes, and more than one syllable
dir: Read each word out loud. Look for a part you already know at the start or the end of the word.
key: Read each word in order: kindness, teamwork, sunflower, replant, unpack, mislabel, thankful, spotless, helpful, invitation, neighbor, wheelbarrow.

Watch for: compound words (teamwork, sunflower, wheelbarrow), prefixes re-, un-, mis- (replant, unpack, mislabel), suffixes -ness, -ful, -less (kindness, thankful, helpful, spotless), the -tion ending

title: What Does the Ending Mean?
desc: identifying and knowing the meaning of common derivational suffixes and decoding words with Latin suffixes
dir: Read each word. Tell what the ending means and what the whole word means.
text: sadness helpful fearless quickly
qs: What does the ending mean in sadness? What does sadness mean?
What does the ending mean in helpful? What does helpful mean?
key: -ness means being or state of. sadness means being sad.
-ful means full of. helpful means full of help.

title: Read the Thursday Crew
desc: a 259-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: The Thursday Crew The Westmill garden sits behind the library, on a lot that used to be gravel. Twelve raised beds run in two long rows. A water barrel stands a
key: 259 words, not counting the title. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy. Let the student finish the passage.

Winter grade 3 benchmark: about 97 words correct per minute (Hasbrouck and Tindal 2017, winter 50th percentile). 25th percentile is about 79. The spring column rises to 112, so the bar moves at the ne

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice and let the rhymes show.
text: The Kite My kite goes up in the wind so blue. It dips and it dances, it swings and it flew. I hold on tight to the long white string. I feel like a bird on the
key: 36 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm and expression at the ends of lines: a pause at the end of each line or where the punctuation is.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: The Thursday Crew The Westmill garden sits behind the library, on a lot that used to be gravel. Twelve raised beds run in two long rows. A water barrel stands a
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: The Share Shelf
desc: questions about an informational text answered with the exact words in the text
dir: Read the text. Then answer out loud. Look back at the text to prove each answer.
text: The Share Shelf Behind the Westmill garden gate stands a wooden cabinet with four shelves. The town calls it the share shelf. The rule is painted on the door: t
qs: What is the rule painted on the door? Read the words from the text.
How many shelves does the cabinet have? Read the words that tell you.
key: Take what you need, leave the rest. Reads “The rule is painted on the door: take what you need, leave the rest.” (RI.3.1)
Four. Reads “a wooden cabinet with four shelves.” (RI.3.1)

title: The Row Nobody Planted
desc: asking and answering story questions using the exact words in the text
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud. Look back at the story to prove each answer.
text: The Row Nobody Planted Bed seven at the Westmill garden stayed empty all spring. It belonged to Mr. Okafor, who had broken his wrist in March and could not dig.
qs: Why did bed seven stay empty all spring? Read the words from the story.
Who noticed the empty bed first? Read the sentence that tells you.
key: Reads “It belonged to Mr. Okafor, who had broken his wrist in March and could not dig.” (RL.3.1)
Dalia. Reads “Dalia noticed it first.” (RL.3.1)

title: A Kitchen Like a Beehive
desc: word and phrase meanings in a story, telling literal from nonliteral language
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud. Use the story to explain each answer.
text: The Long Table Every August, Westmill carries its tables out to the garden path and sets them end to end. By noon the line of tables is longer than the garden i
qs: The story says Mina's kitchen was a beehive all morning. Was it really full of bees? What does it mean?
Mr. Haddad is called the kind of neighbor who would give you the shirt off his back. Does that mean he hands people his shirt? What does it really tell you about him?
key: Nonliteral. It means the kitchen was busy and full of people moving around, the way a beehive is. The story shows it: her uncle chopped, her cousin stirred, and somebody kept moving the salt. (RL.3.4,
Nonliteral. It means he is very generous and gives away whatever he has. The story shows it: he was already at the table with bread for everyone. (RL.3.4, nonliteral language)

title: One Mistake Each
desc: fixing spoken grammar mistakes (plurals, verb tense, agreement, comparing words, pronouns)
dir: Each line from the garden notice has one mistake. Say the whole line out loud the right way.
qs: The womans carried soup down to the long table.
Last week we bringed tomatoes to the share shelf.
key: The women carried soup down to the long table. (L.3.1, irregular plural noun)
Last week we brought tomatoes to the share shelf. (L.3.1, irregular past tense verb)

title: Build a Line
desc: spoken grammar items (joining sentences, future tense, adverbs, abstract nouns)
dir: Answer out loud. Say whole sentences.
qs: Join these two sentences into one. Use because: Theo brought an extra pair of gloves. His friend had cold hands.
Change this sentence so it tells about tomorrow: The crew waters the beds and pulls the weeds.
key: Theo brought an extra pair of gloves because his friend had cold hands. (L.3.1, subordinating conjunction that joins a cause to a result)
The crew will water the beds and will pull the weeds. Both verbs need to change, so accept “will water the beds and pull the weeds” too. (L.3.1, simple future tense)

title: Each Other
desc: using reciprocal pronouns such as each other and one another correctly
dir: Choose the word that fits. Say it or write it.
qs: The twins hugged ___ at the door. (each other / one another)
The students in the class helped ___ with spelling. (each other / one another)
key: each other (reciprocal pronoun for two)
one another (reciprocal pronoun for more than two). Each other is also accepted by many writers.

title: Write It in Cursive
desc: writing legibly in cursive or joined italics with margins and correct spacing between letters in a word and words in a sentence
dir: On your paper, write this sentence in cursive or joined writing. Leave a margin and keep space between your words.
text: Write this sentence: Every kind word helps a friend smile.
key: Letters are joined within each word (cursive or joined italics, not separate print letters)
Letters are formed so another person can read them

title: What Does the Word Do?
desc: explaining the function of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs in particular sentences
dir: Read the sentence. Then answer out loud. Tell what job each word does.
qs: Read: “She quickly ate the red apple.” What does the word She do? What kind of word is it?
What does the word quickly do? What kind of word is it?
key: She is a pronoun. It takes the place of a girl’s name.
Quickly is an adverb. It tells how she ate.

title: Listen to the Plan
desc: main ideas and supporting details from a text read aloud and from a graph
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud. For the last two, use the graph.
text: Your teacher will read you a short report about the Saturday work morning. Listen for the big idea and for the details that back it up. Then look at the graph.
qs: What is the main idea of the report your teacher read?
Give two details from the report that back up that main idea.
key: Main idea: the crew gets everything ready on Friday night and posts a job list, so on Saturday nobody has to wait around or ask what to do. (SL.3.2, main idea of a text read aloud)

Any two details: two people write the job list on Friday and hang it on the gate; one person fills the water barrels; one person counts the trowels because more people come than sign up; the tools are

title: Tell Me About It
desc: reporting on a topic with facts and descriptive details, speaking clearly
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly and not too fast.
text: Tell me about a time someone helped you, or a time you helped someone. Say what happened, and add details so I can picture it. What happened Facts Details
key: Gives facts that fit the topic, told in an order a listener can follow (SL.3.4)
Adds relevant, descriptive details, such as what it looked, sounded, or felt like (SL.3.4)

title: Shelf Notes
desc: taking brief notes from a text and sorting them into given categories
dir: Read the text. Write your notes on your paper and hold it up.
text: The Share Shelf Behind the Westmill garden gate stands a wooden cabinet with four shelves. The town calls it the share shelf. The rule is painted on the door: t
key: What it is box: two facts, such as a wooden cabinet with four shelves, behind the garden gate, rule says take what you need and leave the rest, open seven in the morning until dark, about 38 families

How it started box: two facts, such as a neighbor left a bag of seed packets in March, note said help yourself, three bags by the end of the week, five days of rain wrecked the bags, crew built the ca

title: Remember and Take Notes
desc: recalling information from experience and taking brief notes on a source, sorting the evidence into categories
dir: Write on your paper. First, remember a time from your own life and write about it. Then take notes on the text and sort them.
text: Read the text. Take brief notes. Sort your notes into two groups: Birds and Fish. A robin builds a nest of twigs and grass. A hawk hunts mice from the sky. A tr
qs: Think about a place you visit often. Write two or three sentences about what you do there.
Take brief notes on the text. Write short notes, not whole sentences. (for example: nest of twigs, hunts mice)
key: Names a real place and at least two details.
Short notes in the student’s own words, not copied sentences.

title: Garden Writer
desc: an opinion writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: The Westmill garden has saved enough for one new thing this year. It can build a second share shelf next to the school, or it can buy a rolling tool cart with e
key: Introduces the topic and states a clear opinion about the second shelf or the tool cart (W.3.1)
Gives reasons that support the opinion, such as food closer to families by the school, or nobody waiting for a trowel (W.3.1)

title: Garden Writer
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write to teach someone how the share shelf works and how it got started. Use facts from the text. Write 5 or 6 sentences. Start with a sentence that names your
key: Introduces the topic: what the share shelf is and how it works (W.3.2)

Develops the topic with facts from the text, such as the cabinet has four shelves, the rule is take what you need and leave the rest, it is open seven in the morning until dark, 212 pounds came in one

title: Two Share Shelves
desc: comparing and contrasting the most important points and key details in two texts on the same topic
dir: Read the second text. Then answer out loud about both texts.
text: The Bus Stop Pantry Two towns over from Westmill, a different shelf stands at a bus stop on Grove Road. It is a metal box with a glass door, bolted to a post. I
qs: Both texts are about a free shelf anyone can use. What is the most important point they both make?
Name one way the Westmill shelf and the Grove Road box are different.
key: Both say take what you need, and both are open to anyone with nothing to sign and nothing to pay. Either half counts

Any real difference: a wooden cabinet behind a garden gate against a metal box bolted to a post at a bus stop, fresh garden food against cans and rice, open until dark against a light inside so it wor

title: A Day at the Garden
desc: a short narrative with a situation, events in order, details, and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write a short story about a day at a garden like Westmill. It can be real or made up. Tell who is there, what happens, and how it ends. Write 4 or 5 sentences.
key: Sets up the situation and introduces at least one person or narrator (W.3.3)
Events happen in an order that makes sense, with a time word such as then, after that, or later (W.3.3)

title: Equal Rows
desc: understanding a unit fraction as one of b equal parts and a/b as a parts of that size
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: The crew splits beds into rows. They split snack trays into slices. That way everyone gets the same amount.
qs: Bed A is cut into 4 equal rows. What fraction of the whole bed is one row?
How much of Bed A is planted? Say the fraction. Then tell me what the top number counts.
key: 1/4. The whole bed is cut into 4 equal parts, so one part is 1 of those 4 equal parts. Partial: 4 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.NF.A.1)

3/4. The top number counts how many parts you have, and each part is 1/4, so 3/4 is 3 parts of size 1/4. Partial: the fraction right with no account of what the top number counts is approaching. (3.NF

title: The Watering Path
desc: naming a fraction as a number on a number line and placing fractions on a number line
dir: Look at the paths. Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: Each path runs from the gate to the far fence. The 0 is the gate. The 1 is the fence. The dot is where one watering can was set down.
qs: Path A is cut into 3 equal parts. What fraction of the way along is the can?
Path B is cut into 8 equal parts. Name the fraction where the can sits. What is one part of this path called?
key: 2/3. The space from 0 to 1 is cut into 3 equal parts and the can sits at the end of the second part. Partial: 2/3 right with no account of the equal parts is approaching. (3.NF.A.2)
1/8. One part of this path is 1/8, because the whole from 0 to 1 is cut into 8 equal parts. Partial: the fraction right with no name for one part is approaching. (3.NF.A.2)

title: Which Tray Holds More?
desc: explaining equivalent fractions and comparing fractions by reasoning about their size
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know. You can draw on your paper to show your thinking.
text: The crew writes down how full each snack tray is as a fraction. Bar A and Bar B below are the same size. So they stand for two trays that are the same size.
qs: Which is more food on the same tray, 3/4 or 3/8? How do you know?
Which is more, 5/6 of a tray or 2/6 of the same tray? How do you know?
key: 3/4. The top numbers are the same, so compare the piece sizes: fourths are bigger pieces than eighths, so 3 fourths is more than 3 eighths. Partial: naming 3/4 with no reason about the size of the pie
5/6. The pieces are the same size, so the one with more pieces is more. Partial: naming 5/6 with no reason is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with the same numerator or denominator, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can draw a model.
qs: Which is greater, 4/6 or 2/6? Write the comparison with >, = or <.
Compare 1/2 and 1/8 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
key: 4/6 > 2/6 (or 2/6 < 4/6). Same denominator, more parts.
1/2 > 1/8. Same numerator, and halves are bigger pieces than eighths.

title: Split the Plots
desc: cutting shapes into parts with equal areas and naming one part as a unit fraction of the whole
dir: Look at the plots. Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: A new plot gets split so that every helper has the same amount of ground to dig.
qs: Plot A is cut into 6 parts with equal areas. What fraction of the whole plot is one part?
Plot B is cut into equal strips. What fraction of the whole plot is one strip?
key: 1/6. The plot is cut into 6 parts with the same area, so one part is 1 of 6 equal parts of the whole. Partial: 6 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.G.A.2)
1/4. There are 4 equal strips, so one strip is 1/4 of the plot. Partial: 4 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.G.A.2)

title: Groups of Pots
desc: interpreting a product as a number of equal groups
dir: Answer out loud. Write the last answer on your paper.
qs: The crew sets out 6 trays with 7 pots in each tray. What does 6 x 7 mean here? How many pots in all?
In 8 x 5, if the 8 is the number of rows, what does the 5 count?
key: 6 groups of 7, that is 6 trays with 7 pots in each. 42 pots in all. Partial: 42 given with no account of what 6 x 7 means is approaching.
How many plants are in each row. Partial: naming the rows again instead of what is in each row does not count.

title: Equal Shares
desc: interpreting a quotient as the size of an equal share or the number of shares
dir: Answer out loud. Write the last answer on your paper.
qs: 56 carrots are shared equally into 8 bags. What does 56 divided by 8 mean here? How many carrots in each bag?
42 seedlings are packed into trays that hold 6 each. How many trays?
key: It means 56 split into 8 equal shares, so it asks how many are in one bag. 7 carrots in each bag. Partial: 7 given with no account of what the division means is approaching.
7 trays. Here the division asks how many groups of 6 fit in 42. Partial: 7 given with no account of what the division asks is approaching.

title: Tell a Story for a Product
desc: describing a context in which a total number of objects is expressed as a product
dir: Tell your teacher a story that fits the multiplication.
qs: Tell a short story where 5 × 7 tells the total number of things.
Tell a story where 2 × 9 tells the total.
key: 5 equal groups of 7, such as 5 boxes with 7 pencils each. The total is 35.
2 equal groups of 9. The total is 18.

title: Tell a Story for a Quotient
desc: interpreting a whole-number quotient as the number in each share and as the number of shares
dir: Tell your teacher a story that fits the division. Do it two ways.
qs: Tell a story where 20 ÷ 4 means the number of objects in each share.
Tell a story where 20 ÷ 4 means the number of shares.
key: 20 things shared equally among 4; each gets 5.
20 things put into groups of 4; there are 5 groups.

title: Two Steps at the Gate
desc: two-step word problems with an equation using a letter for the unknown, and checking for reasonableness
dir: Solve on your paper. Write an equation with a letter for the unknown. Say your answer.
qs: The crew picked 124 tomatoes. They left 38 on the share shelf and split the rest equally between 2 boxes. How many tomatoes went in each box? Write an equation with a letter.
A bag of seed packets costs 4 dollars. The crew buys 7 bags and pays with a 50 dollar bill. How much change do they get?
key: 43 tomatoes. Two steps: 124 - 38 = 86, then 86 divided by 2 = 43. The equation needs a letter, such as t = (124 - 38) / 2. Partial: 86 stops before the split between the two boxes and is approaching.
22 dollars. 7 x 4 = 28, then 50 - 28 = 22. Partial: 28 stops at the cost and leaves the change out, so it is approaching.

title: Round the Shelf Numbers
desc: rounding whole numbers to the nearest ten and the nearest hundred
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: The share shelf took in 212 pounds of food in one week. Round 212 to the nearest ten. Now round it to the nearest hundred.
About 38 families use the shelf. Round 38 to the nearest ten.
key: 210 to the nearest ten, because 212 is nearer to 210 than to 220. 200 to the nearest hundred, because 212 is nearer to 200 than to 300. Partial: one of the two roundings right is approaching.
40, because 38 is nearer to 40 than to 30. Partial: 30 rounds down when 38 is nearer 40 and does not count.

title: Area of a Bed
desc: relating area to multiplication and to addition over two side by side rectangles
dir: Look at the bed. Answer out loud.
text: A raised bed is marked off in square feet.
qs: How many rows does this bed have. How many squares are in each row? What is the area?
A second bed is 3 squares by 7 squares. What is its area?
key: 4 rows of 6, so the area is 4 x 6 = 24 square units. Counting all 24 squares is correct, but the multiplication is what to look for. Partial: counting all 24 squares counts here, and the multiplicatio
21 square units (3 x 7 = 21). Partial: 20 from adding the sides gives the perimeter and does not count.

title: Area Models and L-Shapes
desc: relating area to multiplication and addition, using the distributive property with area models, and finding areas of rectilinear figures by adding non-overlapping rectangles
dir: Draw on your paper. Show your work. Tell how you know.
qs: Tile a rectangle 3 rows by 8 columns, or draw it. What is the area? Show it as multiplication.
Break a 3 by 8 rectangle into a 3 by 5 part and a 3 by 3 part. Write the area as 3 × 5 + 3 × 3.
key: 24 square units, 3 × 8 = 24

title: Measure the Seedlings
desc: measuring to the half and quarter inch, generating measurements of real objects with a ruler, and reading a line plot of the measurements
dir: Look at the ruler and the line plot. Answer out loud. For the last one, get a ruler and measure.
qs: How tall is the seedling on the ruler? Use halves or quarters of an inch.
The crew measured 8 seedlings and made this line plot. How many were 3 and a quarter inches tall?
key: 3 and 1/4 inches. The seedling starts at 0 and ends one tick past the 3, and each small tick is a quarter inch. Partial: 3 inches rounds to a whole and is approaching.
3 seedlings. Partial: counting the dots above a different mark does not count.

title: Sense, Brain, Act
desc: using a model to show how an animal takes in information, processes it, and responds
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your model on your paper and hold it up.
text: A gentle old dog visits the library. Children can read to him there. He lies with his chin on the carpet. A child starts reading in a soft voice. His ears turn
qs: Which body part took in the information about the child’s voice?
He did not move toward the loud shelving cart. That cart was on the other side of the room. He moved toward her. What had to happen inside him before he chose?
key: His ears, which turned toward her voice. An ear is a sense organ for sound. (3-LS1-1)
His brain compared the sounds coming in and decided which one to move toward. The deciding happens in the brain, not in the ear. (3-LS1-1)

title: Taking Turns on Watch
desc: building an argument from data that forming a group helps animals survive
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Meerkats feed in the open. In a group, one animal stands up on watch while the rest dig. A team recorded how the feeding went. Meerkats Minutes spent digging, o
qs: Which meerkats got more digging done in half an hour?
Make an argument that living in a group helps a meerkat survive. Use a number from the table.
key: the group of nine, 26 minutes out of 30 against 11 (3-LS2-1)

The claim yes, with the numbers attached: a meerkat in the group dug for 26 minutes instead of 11 and nobody was caught, against four catches for the one alone, so it gets more food and is safer. A ye

title: Passed Down and Shaped
desc: reading trait data for parents and offspring, naming the variation, and telling when the surroundings shaped a trait
dir: Look at both tables. Answer out loud.
text: Table 1: a pair of rabbits with a white patch on the forehead, and their five kits. Rabbit Forehead Ear length in cm parent 1 white patch 11 parent 2 white patc
qs: Every kit has a white forehead patch, the same as both parents. Where did that trait come from?
The ear lengths are all a little different. What is that difference called. Does it mean one of them is not theirs?
key: It was inherited from the parents. A trait both parents have and every offspring has is passed down. (3-LS3-1)
Variation. They are all still their kits: inherited traits vary from one offspring to the next, so a group of similar organisms is not identical. (3-LS3-1)

title: Clues in the Creek Bank
desc: reading fossil data to say which organisms lived in a place and what the place was like
dir: Look at the table of rock layers. Answer out loud.
text: A high flood tore a new face into the creek bank behind the garden and exposed three layers. A class listed the fossils. The top layer is the youngest. Layer Fo
qs: Name two organisms that once lived where this creek bank now stands.
Was the bottom layer salt water or fresh water? Use the fossils as your evidence.
key: Any two the table names: a willow, a dragonfly, a fern, a salamander, a sea snail, a sea urchin. (3-LS4-1)
Salt water, the sea. Sea snails and sea urchins live in the ocean, and naming them is the evidence. An answer with no fossil named is not yet using the data. (3-LS4-1)

title: A Useful Difference
desc: explaining how a variation among individuals of one species gives an advantage
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: The garden is planted with deep tube-shaped flowers. A class measured bumblebee tongues and watched how many flowers each bee could feed from. Bees Tongue lengt
qs: Which bees fed from more flowers?
Explain why a long tongue is an advantage in a garden of deep tube-shaped flowers. Use the table.
key: the long-tongued bees, 19 flowers against 4 (3-LS4-2)

A long tongue reaches nectar at the bottom of a deep tube, so those bees can feed from flowers the short-tongued bees cannot, 19 against 4. The explanation has to lean on the data and has to tie the t

title: Who Survives, and What Would Help
desc: arguing from data who can survive in a changed habitat, then judging the merit of a solution
dir: Read the table. Answer out loud.
text: The rough meadow beside the garden used to be left tall. This year it was mowed short every two weeks all summer. A class counted before and after. Living thing
qs: Which living thing survived well after the mowing? Give the evidence.
Which one could not survive there at all? which one survived less well?
key: The short lawn grass. It went from patchy to thick across the whole meadow, so frequent mowing suited it. (3-LS4-3)
The meadow voles could not survive there at all, from 14 nests down to none. The butterflies survived less well, from 37 down to 6. (3-LS4-3)

title: A Season of Weather
desc: reading and making a graphical display of typical weather for one season
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your graph on your paper and hold it up.
text: The garden club measured the rain in its gauge every week of late winter. Week Rain in mm 1 22 2 8 3 35 4 19 5 26
qs: Which week was the wettest, and which was the driest?
Is this season steady from week to week, or does it jump around? What would you tell someone to expect in a typical week?
key: wettest week 3 with 35 mm, driest week 2 with 8 mm (3-ESS2-1)
It jumps around. A typical week brings about 20 to 25 mm, but any one week can be much wetter or much drier. The point is a typical value with the spread noticed. (3-ESS2-1)

title: Two Parts of the World
desc: combining information to describe the climates of two different regions of the world
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Two regions in the same country, one on the coast and one inland behind a mountain range. Region Summer average Winter average Rain in a year a coastal region 1
qs: Which region swings further between summer and winter, and by how much?
The inland region sits behind a mountain range. How could mountains help explain why it gets so little rain?
key: the inland desert, a swing of 31 degrees from 6 C to 37 C, against 8 degrees on the coast (3-ESS2-2)
Air blowing in off the ocean has to rise over the mountains, and it drops its rain on the way up, so the air that reaches the far side is dry. Accept the idea in the student’s own words. (3-ESS2-2)

title: Ready for the Water
desc: making a claim about the merit of a design that reduces the impact of a weather hazard
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Heavy winter rain floods the low path through the garden. The beds beside it turn to mud for a week. The club builds a raised wooden walkway on short posts. It
qs: Which weather hazard is the walkway meant to reduce?
Make a claim. Does the raised walkway have merit? Give your reason.
key: flooding of the path after heavy rain (3-ESS3-1)
Yes, with a reason attached: people walk above the water instead of through it, and the gravel lets the water drain away instead of standing. A yes with no reason is not yet a claim. (3-ESS3-1)

title: Balanced or Not
desc: planning an investigation of balanced and unbalanced forces acting on an object
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two people carry a heavy garden bench, one at each end. They lift together and hold it steady in the air. The bench stays level and still.
qs: The bench is heavy and gravity pulls it down, yet it stays still in the air. Are the forces on it balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
The person at one end lowers her hands a little. What happens to that end, and what changed about the forces?
key: Balanced. The two lifts together push up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down, and the bench holding still is the evidence. (3-PS2-1)
That end drops. The lift on that end is now less than the downward pull there, so the forces on that end are unbalanced. (3-PS2-1)

title: Predict the Next Mark
desc: using a pattern in motion data to predict where an object will be later
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: A ball is rolled along the smooth hall floor, past chalk marks spaced 2 m apart. A timer calls out each second. Seconds Mark the ball is passing 1 2 2 4 3 6
qs: What pattern do these numbers make?
Which mark will the ball pass at 6 seconds. How far from the start is that in meters?
key: Two marks every second, the same number each time. The ball is moving at a steady speed. (3-PS2-2)
mark 12, which is 24 m from the start, because 12 marks at 2 m each is 24 m. Both parts have to be there. (3-PS2-2)

title: Ask About the Pull
desc: asking questions about cause and effect in magnetic interactions between objects not touching
dir: Answer out loud. Your two questions have to be questions, not statements.
text: A paperclip is laid on a sheet of card. A magnet is moved underneath the card. The paperclip slides along on top, following it. A second magnet is brought near
qs: The magnet never touches the paperclip, yet the clip moves. What does that tell you about this force?
What two questions would you want to investigate here?
key: The force acts across a distance and straight through the card, with no contact between the objects. (3-PS2-3)

Any two real investigable questions: how many sheets of card can it work through, does a heavier clip still follow, does a copper wire follow, how fast can the magnet move before the clip is left behi

title: A Problem for a Magnet
desc: defining a design problem that magnets can solve, with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Answer out loud. For the third one you may write your two sentences on your paper.
text: Steel pins drop off the edge of the sewing table. That table is in the library. They scatter across the carpet. People sitting at the table find them. They use
qs: Name the problem in one sentence. Your sentence starts: The problem is.
Why is a magnet a sensible idea here? Would the same tool pick up a dropped plastic button?
key: A problem statement about picking dropped steel pins out of the carpet so nobody is stuck by one. The problem has to be about the pins in the carpet, not about the sewing. (3-PS2-4)
The pins are steel, and a magnet pulls steel without touching it, so it lifts pins out of the carpet without anyone feeling for them. A plastic button is not pulled by a magnet, so no. (3-PS2-4)

title: Three Ways to Do It
desc: comparing several possible solutions against stated criteria and constraints
dir: Look at the table and the three rules. Answer out loud.
text: The library door is heavy, and people carrying a stack of books cannot pull it open. Three designs are tried. Design Opens with no hands? Cost Keeps cold air ou
qs: Which design costs the least?
Which design meets all three rules? Explain using the table.
key: the permanently open doorway, which costs nothing (3-5-ETS1-2)

The long push bar at hip height. It opens with a hip or elbow, costs 25 dollars, and keeps the cold out. Another choice counts only if the student argues it against all three rules using the table. (3

title: Make the Test Fair
desc: judging whether a test is fair, naming controlled variables, and identifying a failure point
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two glues were tested to see which holds a paper card more strongly. Glue Amount used Drying time before the pull Card glue A one small dot 10 minutes thin pape
qs: Would this test tell you which glue is better? Why or why not?
Which two things would you hold steady to make this fair?
key: No. Three things were different at once, the amount, the drying time and the paper, so a stronger hold cannot be pinned on the glue. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two controlled variables: the same amount of glue, the same drying time, the same paper, the same pull, the same room conditions. (3-5-ETS1-3)

title: Maps and Places
desc: using a map grid and a table to describe physical and human features and where they sit
dir: Use the map grid and the table. Answer out loud.
text: A map grid of the town around the library. North is the top row. west middle east north oak woods library garden middle ridge town hall market south creek footb
qs: What lies directly north of the town hall?
Which two directions do you walk to get from the town hall to the creek?
key: the library (HSS-3.1)
south and west, in either order. The creek sits in the south row and the west column. Partial: one of the two directions is approaching. (HSS-3.1)

title: The First Nations Here
desc: describing how the American Indian nations of California taught their children and held places sacred, and how a nation is part of the state today
dir: Answer out loud. Use what is on the screen and what you have learned.
text: California nations taught their children by working beside them. They taught how to find the right plants. They taught when to gather and when to leave a patch
qs: The screen says children learned by working beside the grown-ups. Name the two things they were taught that way about the plants. Then say what the stories carried.
Children were taught which places their nation held sacred. Name one thing people did at such a place and one thing they did not do there. Then say what that shows about the nation’s beliefs.
key: How to find the right plants, and when to gather and when to leave a patch alone. The stories carried what the nation knew. Partial: the two plant lessons named with nothing said about the stories, or

Ceremonies were held there, and people did not go there to gather or to hunt. It shows that the nation’s religious beliefs were part of the land itself, so some places were set apart and treated diffe

title: A Town Over Time
desc: sequencing local historical events and describing the mark each period left on the land
dir: Look at the timeline. Answer out loud.
text: A timeline for the town of Willow Ford. Year What happened 1853 a store opens at the willow-lined ford across the creek 1877 a canal is dug to carry creek water
qs: Put these three in order, earliest first: the canal, the concrete lining, the first school.
Which event changed the dry flats. What did it do to them?
key: canal, first school, concrete lining. Partial: two of the three in the right order is approaching. (HSS-3.3)
the canal in 1877, which carried creek water out so the dry flats could be farmed. Partial: naming the canal with no account of what it did to the flats is approaching. (HSS-3.3)

title: Rules, Laws and Government
desc: telling rules from laws and naming the basic parts and levels of United States government
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A class writes its own agreement about how to treat each other. Everyone signs it. The town has a law that says a public building must have a ramp as well as st
qs: How is the class agreement different from the ramp law?
Why would a government make a law about ramps instead of leaving it to each building owner?
key: The class agreement is made by the class and applies in that class. The law is made by a government, applies to every public building in the town, and the government decides what happens when it is br
So that every person can get into a public building, not only the people whose building owner chose to help. Accept any answer about protecting people’s rights or treating everyone the same. Partial:

title: Choices and the Local Economy
desc: basic economic reasoning about cost, price, scarcity, and goods and services
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: A class holds a bake sale in the library lobby to buy books for the garden shelf. They spent money on supplies first. Item Amount flour, butter and sugar they b
qs: All twelve loaves sell. How much money comes in? How much is left after paying for the supplies?
Only six loaves are baked next time, and twenty people want one. What happens to the loaves. What do we call it when there is not enough to go around?
key: 48 dollars comes in, since 12 times 4 is 48, and 30 dollars is left after the 18 dollars of supplies. Partial: the 48 dollars right with no amount left over is approaching. (HSS-3.5)

The loaves run out, or the class could charge more for the few they have. That is scarcity: there is less than people want. Accept scarcity explained in the student’s own words. Partial: saying the lo

title: Shed Door Words
desc: reading multisyllable words using letter-sound, syllable, and word-part knowledge
dir: Read each word out loud. Break it into parts you already know, then put it back together.
key: Read each word in order: volunteer, community, neighborly, responsible, gratitude, uncomfortable, disagreement, generosity, interruption, reluctantly, arrangement, wheelbarrow.

Watch for: prefixes un- and dis- (uncomfortable, disagreement), the inter- prefix (interruption), suffixes -ible, -ity, -tion, -ly, -ment (responsible, generosity, interruption, neighborly, reluctantl

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and word parts
dir: Read each sentence out loud. Take your time with the long words.
text: The magnificent waterfall thundered over the ancient cliffs. The volunteers organized a celebration for the whole community.
key: Listen for these six words read correctly in the sentences: magnificent, waterfall, ancient, volunteers, organized, celebration. Mark each one.
A word that is self-corrected on a second try counts as correct. Note words the student breaks into syllables to decode.

title: Read Eight O'Clock
desc: a 164-word grade-level passage read aloud
dir: Read the passage out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Eight O'Clock The Westmill garden has two water barrels, one at each end of the beds, and the person on the rota fills them first. It takes about eleven minutes
key: 164 words, not counting the title. Time 1 minute, mark the last word read, and count errors and self-corrections on your own copy. Let the student finish the passage.
Winter grade 4 benchmark: about 120 words correct per minute (Hasbrouck and Tindal 2017, winter 50th percentile). 25th percentile is about 95, 10th percentile about 71.

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice. Let the rhythm and the rhymes show.
text: Autumn Wind The autumn wind is running free, It shakes the branch of every tree. The orange leaves go twirling down, Red and yellow, gold and brown. They dance
key: 38 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm, pauses at the end of lines or punctuation, and a voice that fits the mood of the poem.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Eight O'Clock The Westmill garden has two water barrels, one at each end of the beds, and the person on the rota fills them first. It takes about eleven minutes
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: What a Rota Does
desc: explaining what an informational text says and drawing inferences, using details and examples
dir: Read the article. Then answer out loud. Use details and examples from the article in every answer.
text: What a Rota Does A rota is a list of names and dates that says whose turn it is. Hospitals use them. Fire stations use them. So does the Westmill community gard
qs: What is a rota? Read me the words from the article.
How many Saturdays are in the garden's season? Read me the words that tell you.
key: A list of names and dates that says whose turn it is. Reads “A rota is a list of names and dates that says whose turn it is.” (RI.4.1, explicit)
28. Reads “The season runs from April to October, which is 28 Saturdays.” (RI.4.1, explicit)

title: Saturday Seven
desc: explaining what a story says and drawing inferences, using details and examples
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud. Use details and examples from the story in every answer.
text: Saturday Seven The Westmill garden runs on a paper rota taped inside the shed door. Seven names, seven Saturdays, and whoever is on the list opens the gate at e
qs: Why did Rosalind want to swap her Saturday? Give the details from the story.
Which Saturday did Rosalind end up working, and what was the weather? Read me the words.
key: Her cousin's band was playing at the library at nine on that same morning, and she “had been counting down to it for a month.” (RL.4.1, explicit with details)
The twelfth, and it rained. Reads “On the twelfth it rained from eight until noon.” (RL.4.1, explicit)

title: A Herculean Job
desc: the meaning of words and phrases as used in a story, including an allusion to a character from mythology
dir: Read the story again. Then answer out loud. Read me the words you are talking about.
text: Saturday Seven The Westmill garden runs on a paper rota taped inside the shed door. Seven names, seven Saturdays, and whoever is on the list opens the gate at e
qs: Mr. Ferreira calls the mulch “a Herculean job.” Hercules was a hero in Greek myths who was famous for his strength and for finishing twelve enormous tasks. What does Herculean mean here, and what in the story shows it?
Dev says “his whole May was a blank page.” What does that mean? Is there really a page?
key: Herculean means enormous, needing great strength or effort. The name comes from Hercules, so calling the mulch Herculean says it was a job that took the strength of a hero. The story shows it: “Nine w
No real page. It is a way of saying his May was empty, with nothing written on it and nothing planned, so one more Saturday cost him nothing. (RL.4.4, figurative language)

title: One Mistake Each
desc: fixing spoken grammar mistakes (relative pronouns, modal auxiliaries, adjective order, confused words, fragments)
dir: Each line from the garden handbook has one mistake. Say the whole line out loud the right way.
qs: Dev is the one which took the first Saturday.
We should of filled the barrels first.
key: Dev is the one who took the first Saturday. who is the relative pronoun for a person. (L.4.1a, relative pronouns)
We should have filled the barrels first. should of is not a correct form, so the modal auxiliary needs have. (L.4.1c, modal auxiliaries)

title: Say It Right
desc: spoken grammar items (progressive tense, relative adverbs, prepositional phrases, run-on sentences)
dir: Answer out loud. Say whole sentences.
qs: Change this sentence so it tells what was happening at nine o'clock yesterday: Dev waits under the eave.
Which word fits? The shed ____ the rota hangs is behind bed one. Is it where or which?
key: Dev was waiting under the eave. (L.4.1b, past progressive verb tense)
where. where is the relative adverb for a place. (L.4.1a, relative adverbs)

title: Cursive Writing
desc: writing fluidly and legibly in cursive or joined italics
dir: Write this sentence on your paper in cursive or joined writing. Write smoothly and keep it neat.
text: Write this sentence: A good book can take you anywhere you want to go.
key: Letters are joined within words (cursive or joined italics)
Writing is legible: another reader can read each word

title: Two Sources
desc: taking notes from two sources, sorting them into categories, and listing the sources
dir: Read both sources. Take your notes on your paper and hold them up.
text: Source 1: “What a Rota Does,” by Imogen Park. Westmill Register, March 2026. A rota is a list of names and dates that says whose turn it is. Hospitals use them.
key: What the rota is for box: two notes, such as says whose turn it is (Source 1), closes the gaps so no Saturday is missed (Source 1), spreads the work so seven share it instead of three (Source 1), the

What a person has to do box: two notes, such as be there at eight and open the gate (Source 1 or 2), fill both barrels first (Source 2), put the job list on the gate (Source 2), lock up at the end (So

title: Shed Desk
desc: an opinion writing piece built from a fact box
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: The garden has to decide what to do next season. Should it keep the rota, or go back to open Saturdays where anyone comes when they can? Write your opinion. Use
key: Introduces the topic and states a clear opinion about keeping the rota or going back (W.4.1a)
Reasons are grouped so that related ideas sit together (W.4.1a)

title: Shed Desk
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: A new family has joined the garden and nobody has explained the rota to them. Write to teach them what a rota is, how the garden's rota works, and what to do if
key: Introduces the topic clearly and groups related information together (W.4.2a)
Develops the topic with facts, definitions, and details from the article, such as what a rota is, seven names at a time, 28 Saturdays in the season, open the gate at eight (W.4.2b)

title: Shed Desk
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: You promised to be somewhere on a Saturday morning. The weather is terrible, and when you get there only one other person has come. Write the story of that morn
key: Orients the reader by setting up the situation and introducing the narrator and the other character (W.4.3a)
Events unfold naturally in an order that makes sense (W.4.3a)

title: Both Sources at Once
desc: pulling information from two texts on the same topic to speak about it knowledgeably
dir: Look at both sources. Answer out loud, and say which source each part comes from.
text: Source 1: “What a Rota Does,” by Imogen Park. Westmill Register, March 2026. A rota is a list of names and dates that says whose turn it is. Hospitals use them.
qs: Using both sources, tell me everything a person on the rota has to do on their Saturday.
Both sources talk about pencil. Put the two together: what is the pencil rule, and why does it matter?
key: Open the gate at eight, fill both barrels first, put the job list on the gate, and lock up when the last person leaves, all from Source 2, plus the one job named in Source 1, be there at eight and ope

Source 2 says write a swap on the sheet in pencil and never cross a name out in pen, because the sheet is the only record the garden keeps. Source 1 says the pencil matters because 9 swaps out of 28 S

title: Say It Back
desc: paraphrasing a text read aloud
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then say it back in your own words.
text: Your teacher will read about a seed swap. Listen, then put it in your own words.
key: Ask: What happens at the seed swap, and who may take seed? Paraphrase: people bring seed they saved and lay it out on tables, nothing is sold, and anyone may take seed even if they brought none. Count
Ask: Put the rule the organizers repeat into your own words. Paraphrase: seed does no good sitting unused in a drawer, so it should be passed on and planted

title: Report It
desc: reporting on a topic in an organized way with facts and descriptive details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly and at a pace your teacher can follow.
text: Tell me about something you and other people do together, such as a team, a class job, a club, or a chore everyone at home shares. How does it get organized. Wh
key: Organized: there is a beginning, a middle and an end, not a pile of facts in any order
Includes appropriate facts, such as how many people, how often, and who decides what

title: Ten Times the Seed
desc: recognizing that a digit in one place is worth ten times what the same digit is worth in the place to its right
dir: Look at the charts. Answer out loud and say what each digit is worth.
text: The garden counts seed in grams and keeps the totals on a place value chart.
qs: Chart A. What is the 4 in the hundreds place worth? What is the 4 in the tens place worth?
How do those two values compare? Say it as a sentence with ten times in it.
key: The 4 in the hundreds place is worth 400. The 4 in the tens place is worth 40. Partial: one of the two values given is approaching. (4.NBT.A.1)
400 is ten times 40. A digit is worth ten times what the same digit is worth one place to its right. Partial: naming ten times with no general rule given is approaching. (4.NBT.A.1)

title: Same Amount, New Pieces
desc: explaining and generating equivalent fractions using a visual model
dir: Use the bars for number 1. Answer the rest out loud and say how you know. You can write on your paper.
text: The crew splits the same long bed two different ways. The two bars below are the same length, so they stand for the same bed.
qs: Look at Bar A and Bar B. Is 2/3 equal to 4/6? Use the picture to explain what happened to each third.
Write a fraction equal to 3/4 that has 12 as the bottom number. Show the multiplying.
key: Yes, 2/3 = 4/6. Each third was cut into 2 equal pieces, so the 3 parts became 6 and the 2 shaded parts became 4. The bars are the same length and the shaded parts cover the same amount. As an equation
9/12. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number: 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 3 = 12. Partial: 9/12 right with no multiplying shown is approaching. (4.NF.A.1)

title: Which Row Is Further Along?
desc: comparing two fractions with different numerators and denominators, and knowing when a comparison is valid
dir: Answer out loud and say how you know. You can write on your paper.
text: Everyone reports how far along their row is as a fraction. The rows on this stop are all the same length unless a question says otherwise.
qs: Which is greater, 3/5 of a row or 5/8 of a row?
Write >, <, or = to make it true: 2/3 ____ 5/6
key: 5/8. In fortieths, 3/5 is 24/40 and 5/8 is 25/40, so 5/8 is greater by 1/40. Accept any correct common denominator or a clear benchmark argument. Partial: naming 5/8 with no common denominator and no
2/3 < 5/6. In sixths, 2/3 is 4/6, and 4/6 is less than 5/6. Partial: the right choice with the sign the wrong way round is approaching. (4.NF.A.2)

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators, recording the results with symbols, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know.
qs: Compare 3/5 and 1/2 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
Compare 5/8 and 3/4 with a symbol.

title: Write It as a Decimal
desc: writing fractions with denominator 10 or 100 in decimal notation
dir: Use the grid and the number line. Answer out loud, or write the answers on your paper and hold them up.
text: The crew measures stakes and rows with a meter stick. The big square below is one whole meter cut into 100 equal pieces.
qs: Write 7/10 as a decimal.
Look at the grid. Write the shaded part as a fraction with 100 on the bottom, then as a decimal.
key: 43/100 and 0.43. The grid shows 43 of the 100 equal parts shaded. Partial: one of the fraction and the decimal given is approaching. (4.NF.C.6)

title: Which Is More?
desc: comparing two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size
dir: Use the two grids. Answer out loud and say how you know.
text: Grid P and Grid Q are the same size. Each grid is one whole cut into 100 equal parts.
qs: Grid P shows 0.6 and Grid Q shows 0.56. Which is greater? Use the grids to explain.
Write >, <, or = to make it true: 0.3 ____ 0.30
key: 0.6 is greater. 0.6 is 6 tenths, which is 60 of the 100 small squares, and 0.56 is 56 of them. Grid P has 4 more squares shaded. Partial: naming 0.6 with no count from the grids is approaching. (4.NF.
0.3 = 0.30. Three tenths is the same as thirty hundredths. Partial: making one of them the greater counts digits instead of places and does not count. (4.NF.C.7)

title: Hose, Barrel, Bag
desc: knowing relative sizes of measurement units and converting from a larger unit to a smaller one
dir: Solve each one on your paper and tell your teacher the answer with its unit. For the last one, make the table on your paper.
text: Everything in the shed is labeled in the bigger unit. The jobs need the smaller one.
qs: The hose is 24 meters long. How many centimeters is that?
A watering can holds 8 liters. How many milliliters is that?
key: 2,400 centimeters. 1 meter is 100 centimeters, so 24 × 100 = 2,400. Partial: 240 uses tens instead of hundreds and does not count. (4.MD.A.1)
8,000 milliliters. 1 liter is 1,000 milliliters, so 8 × 1,000 = 8,000. Partial: 800 uses hundreds instead of thousands and does not count. (4.MD.A.1)

title: Pounds and Ounces
desc: knowing the relative sizes of pounds and ounces, converting a larger unit to a smaller unit, and recording equivalents in a table
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work.
qs: A baby weighs 8 pounds. How many ounces is that?
How many ounces are in 10 pounds?
key: 128 ounces (8 × 16)
160 ounces

title: Times as Many
desc: interpreting and writing multiplication as a comparison
dir: Answer out loud. Write the last answer on your paper.
qs: The crew moved 9 wheelbarrows of mulch and 3 wheelbarrows of compost. The number of mulch loads is how many times the number of compost loads?
What does the equation 35 = 5 x 7 say as a comparison?
key: 3 times as many. 9 = 3 x 3. Partial: 6 more is a difference and not a multiplicative comparison, so it does not count.
35 is 5 times as many as 7. Saying 35 is 7 times as many as 5 is also correct. Partial: 35 is 5 more than 7 reads it as an addition and does not count.

title: Round the Season
desc: rounding multi-digit whole numbers to a named place
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: The garden weighed 1,480 pounds of food last season. Round that to the nearest hundred. Now round it to the nearest thousand.
Round 4,728 to the nearest ten.
key: 1,500 to the nearest hundred, because 80 is past halfway to the next hundred. 1,000 to the nearest thousand, because 480 is less than halfway to 2,000. Partial: one of the two roundings right is appro
4,730. Partial: 4,720 rounds down when the ones digit is 8 and does not count.

title: Bed Size
desc: using the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real problems
dir: Solve on your paper. Say your answer with its unit.
qs: A raised bed is 12 feet long and 4 feet wide. What is its area? What is its perimeter?

text: Farmers grew more and earned less. Year Price of a bushel of wheat 1866 about $1.50 1880 about $0.95 1894 about $0.49 Meanwhile farmers borrowed to buy machiner
qs: Prices fell by two thirds while farmers produced more than ever. Explain how both happened at once.
Why would a farmer with a mortgage want more money in circulation?
key: Because more land, machinery, railroads and foreign competition put far more wheat on the market than demand was growing, and the railroads that let a farmer sell nationally also let every other farme

Because a mortgage is a fixed number of dollars. When there is little money in circulation and prices fall, those dollars are harder to earn, so the real burden of the debt rises every year even thoug

title: Find the Letter
desc: matching a spoken letter name to its printed form (12 cards, 6 uppercase and 6 lowercase)
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
key: Say: Here are twelve letter cards from the garden shed. I will say a letter name. Point to the card with that letter.
Say: Point to the letter i. (top row, fourth card)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: First Sound Check
desc: saying the first sound of a pictured word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the first sound.
key: Model first: Sun. The first sound in sun is /s/. Now you try.
Point to the rabbit. Say: Rabbit. What is the first sound in rabbit? (/r/)

title: Rhyme Time
desc: making a rhyme for a given word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say a word that rhymes.
key: Model first: Seed, weed, feed. They rhyme. They sound the same at the end.
Point to the bee. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with bee. (tree, see, key, me, zee)

title: Put It Together
desc: blending syllables and sounds into a word with picture support
dir: Listen to the slow, stretchy voice. Say the whole word.
key: Say: I am going to talk very slowly today. Put the parts together and tell me the word. The pictures are in the same order as my words, so they can help you.
Say with a pause between the parts: car ... rot. (carrot, the first picture)

title: Pip Plants a Row
desc: questions about the character, the order of three events, and what happens next in a story read aloud
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Pip Plants a Row
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: This is a garden the morning after the rain. The animal at the left is a young rabbit. A watering can is what you fill with water
Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Pip comes to the row of soil.

title: Find the Letter
desc: matching a spoken letter name to its printed lowercase form
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the packet on your screen.
key: Say: Every seed packet has a small letter on it. I will say a letter name. Point to the packet with that letter.
Say: Point to the letter d. (packet 2)

title: Write the Garden Sounds
desc: writing the letter for a beginning sound (r, f, d, t)
dir: Listen for the sound. Write the letter on your paper and hold it up.
key: Point to the first picture. Say: This is rain. Rain starts with /r/. Write the letter that makes the /r/ sound. Hold it up. (r or R)
Point to the frog. Say: Frog starts with /f/. Write the letter for /f/. (f or F)

title: The Garden Call
desc: asking questions to get missing information and to confirm understanding
dir: Your teacher is calling you. Ask questions until you know what to do.
key: Say: You are at home by the garden. I will call you on the phone, but part of my message will be missing. Ask me questions until you know what to do.

Message 1. Say in a phone voice: Hello! Please carry the watering can out to the garden bed. Look for: asks a question about which can or which bed (there are two watering cans and three garden beds).

title: Mystery Seed
desc: asking questions and follow-up questions to find out information
dir: One kind of seed is inside the packet. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
key: Your secret: a sunflower seed is in the packet. Do not tell.
Say: One kind of seed is sealed up in this packet. Ask me questions to find out what it is. You can ask things like: What does it look like? What will it grow into?

title: Name the Garden Things
desc: naming objects, actions, and describing words from pictures
dir: Look at each picture. Answer out loud.
key: Picture 1. Say: What is this? (a seed. Saying bean or pit counts too.)
Picture 2. Say: What is this? (an umbrella)

title: Plant or Puddles
desc: sharing an opinion with a reason, a description, and an explanation
dir: Pick one. Tell your teacher why.
key: Say: This morning you can kneel down and plant a whole row of seeds in the soft soil, or you can pull on your boots and splash in every puddle on the path. Which one would you pick? Tell me why.
Look for: tells an opinion (picks one).

title: Make a Garden Label
desc: writing a few recognizable letters to stand for a word or an idea
dir: Draw what you planted. Write letters to tell what it is. Hold it up.
key: Say: Gardeners push a little label into the soil so they remember what is planted in each row. Draw one thing you would plant, like a carrot, a bean or a sunflower. Then write some letters to tell wha
Look for: writing that is separate from the drawing (letters or marks that look like letters, not only a picture).

title: How a Seed Wakes Up
desc: making an inference, making a connection, and asking a question about an informational text read aloud
dir: Listen to your teacher read about seeds. Then answer out loud.
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture first. Say: This shows how a seed wakes up, step by step, in the order the facts come in. A seed, then water, then a root, then a shoot, then two leave

Ask: Someone leaves a seed in a dry pot on a cold shelf and never waters it. Do you think it will grow? Why? (No, or probably not. A seed needs water and warm air, and the dry cold pot has neither. Th

title: Count the Seed Trays
desc: counting 10 or more real objects one by one where the teacher can see, then counting groups of 11, 13, 15, and 12 objects one by one on the screen
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
key: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one

Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down

title: More Seeds or More Drops?
desc: comparing two groups by counting (more, same, fewer)
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
key: Box 1. Say: Are there more seeds or more raindrops? How do you know? (More seeds. 8 seeds and 5 drops.)
Box 2. Say: Are there more eggs, more sprouts, or the same number of each? (The same. 6 eggs and 6 sprouts.)

title: Garden Shapes
