desc: naming, describing, and drawing circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud. Then draw a shape on your paper.
key: Say: Here is the bird house in the garden. It is built out of shapes. What shape is the red roof? (triangle)
Say: What shape is the blue box under the roof? (square or rectangle. Accept either. The box is a little wider than it is tall.)

title: Tallest Stalk, Longest Hose
desc: ordering five objects by height and four objects by length
dir: Look at the sunflowers and the hoses. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the sunflowers. Say: The garden grew five sunflowers. Which one is the tallest? (D)
Say: Which one is the shortest? (A)

title: Seed Tray Numbers
desc: naming the written numerals 1 to 10
dir: Say the name of each number.
key: Say: Every seed tray in the garden shed has a number painted on it. What number is this? Click Next after each one.
The order is 3, 6, 2, 9, 5, 10, 1, 7, 4, 8. Correct means the child says the number name on sight. Write down the ones missed.

title: Sort the Garden Tiles
desc: sorting eight objects by kind, by size, and by two attributes at once
dir: Look at the eight tiles. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Eight picture tiles are laid out on the garden bench. Sort them by what they show. How many flowers? How many leaves? (4 flowers and 4 leaves)
Say: Now forget flowers and leaves. Sort them by size. How many big pictures? How many small ones? (4 big and 4 small)

title: Rows That Repeat
desc: extending two repeating patterns and naming the part that repeats
dir: Look at each row. Say what comes next.
key: Row 1. Say: Bee, bee, flower, flower, bee, bee, flower, flower. What comes next where the question mark is? (a bee. The row ends with the second flower, so the pattern starts over.)
Row 2. Say: Look at this row. What comes next? (an umbrella. The row ends with a boot.)

title: The Garden Notebook
desc: reading a picture chart with three groups, making one mark per data point, and adding to the chart
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud. Then make marks on your paper.
key: Say: One spring morning the garden notebook kept track of every visitor. Each picture in the chart stands for one visitor. How many butterflies came? (5)
Say: On your paper, make one mark for each ladybug in the chart. Hold it up. (3 marks. Tally marks, lines, dots or small drawings all count, as long as there are exactly 3.)

title: Where in the Garden?
desc: position words (in, next to or beside, over or above)
dir: Look at the garden. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Where is the bird? (In the tree, or up in the tree. Look for a position word, not only pointing at it.)
Say: Is the snail next to the watering can, or inside the watering can? (Next to it. Beside it or right by it counts too.)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the most common sound for all 26 letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What sound does this letter make? Mark each correct sound.
For a, e, i, o and u the short sound is what is expected. The long sound is also correct.

title: Two Lines
desc: print concepts (where to start, where to go at the end of a line, counting words and letters)
dir: Look at the two lines. Answer out loud.
text: We plant the small seeds. The rain is warm. The four pictures are a boot, a sprout, a rain cloud, and the sun.
key: Say: I want to read this. Ask: Where do I start, at the boot, the sprout, the cloud, or the sun? (the boot. Reading starts at the top on the left.)
Say: I read the top line and I stop at the sprout. Ask: Where do I go next? (to the cloud, the start of the next line)

title: Book Parts
desc: print concepts (finding the title, where to start, which way to read, and the first and last word of a line)
dir: Look at the page. Point or answer out loud.
text: The Spring Garden A seed is in the pot It will grow up
key: Say: This is a page from a book. Point to the title. (the big words in the banner at the top: The Spring Garden. If the student cannot point on the screen, they can tell you where it is.)
Ask: Where do I start reading? Point to it. (the first word of the top line, on the left: A)

title: Rhyme and Clap
desc: hearing rhymes, making a rhyme, and clapping syllables
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
text: A sprout is the first small green shoot that comes up out of a seed.
key: Ask: Do seed and weed rhyme? (yes)
Ask: Do rain and sun rhyme? (no)

title: Put It Together
desc: blending spoken sounds and saying the first, last, and all sounds in a word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Put these sounds together: /r/ /ai/ /n/. (rain)
Say: Put these sounds together: /s/ /ee/ /d/. (seed)

title: Bud and the Pot
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in a story read aloud to the student
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: Bud has a pot. Bud digs in the mud. The sun is hot. Bud sees a bug. A pot is a little cup. It holds soil. A plant can grow in it.
key: Read the four lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Ask: Who is the story about? (Bud)
Ask: Where does Bud dig? (in the mud)

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the sounds of letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: The student says the most common sound for each letter: b /b/, A as in apple, s /s/, r /r/, I as in itch, f /f/, h /h/, v /v/, k /k/, o as in otter. The letter name is not needed here.
The long sound for A or I is also fine. Write down any sounds that were missed.

title: Garden Words
desc: reading high-frequency words and short vowel words
dir: Read each word out loud.
text: me she to and you bud wet pot dig
key: High-frequency words the student should know by sight: me, she, to, and, you
Sounds out or reads: bud, wet, pot, dig

title: Listen to the Garden
desc: answering questions about key details in a text read aloud and asking for help
dir: Put your eyes on your teacher and listen. Then answer out loud.
text: Listening time. Your teacher will read you a report about how a seed grows.
key: Ask: What is folded up inside a seed? (a whole plant)
Ask: What two things does a seed need before it starts to swell? (soil covering it, and water)

title: Little Spring Book
desc: reading a short emergent-reader book with purpose and understanding
dir: Point to each word and read it out loud.
text: I see rain. I see sun. I see a seed. It is in a pot. The pot is big. I can dig. The sun is hot. I like the seed. A seed is small. A seed is dry. A plant starts
key: Count the words the student reads correctly, out of 30, and enter the number in the box. A word the student fixes without help counts. Write down the words that were missed.
Points or tracks under each word, left to right and top to bottom

title: Garden Talk
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, question words, position words in complete sentences)
dir: Look at the picture. Listen to your teacher. Say your answer out loud.
key: Say: One seed, two ____. (seeds)
Say: One bush, two ____. (bushes)

title: Spring Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write opinion piece about planting seeds or splashing in puddles
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Would you rather plant a row of seeds, or splash in the puddles after the rain? Draw the one you pick. Write or tell what you think and why.
key: Tells the reader what the choice is about: planting seeds or splashing in puddles (W.K.1)
States an opinion, which one the student would pick. Drawing, telling, or writing all count (W.K.1)

title: Spring Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write informative piece about a seed, a bird, or the rain
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Pick one: a seed, a bird, or the rain. Draw it. Write its name. Then write or tell one true thing about it. A seed is a small thing. It is dry. A plant starts f
key: Names what the drawing and writing are about: a seed, a bird, or the rain (W.K.2). The student may say it, label the picture, or write a letter or word for it
Gives at least one piece of true information about it, such as: A seed grows into a plant. A bird builds a nest. Rain makes the grass wet (W.K.2)

title: Garden Day List
desc: answering questions from a picture chart and from experience
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the chart. What grows into a plant?
Look at the chart. What gives the plants a drink?
key: The seed. Uses the chart to answer.
The watering can. Uses the chart to answer.

title: Tell Me More
desc: describing a familiar thing you do outside, with details
dir: Tell your teacher out loud. Use lots of details.
text: Tell me about something you like to do outside when it gets warm.
key: Names the thing and tells something about it
Adds a detail when you ask: Where do you do it?

title: Worms on the Path
desc: answering and asking questions about key details in an informational text read aloud
dir: Listen to your teacher read about worms. Then answer out loud.
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture first. Say: This is the garden path the morning after a long rain. Then read the facts out loud.

Ask: Why do the worms come up onto the path after it rains? (The top of the ground is damp everywhere, and that is the one time a worm can crawl a long way to a new patch of garden. A worm cannot trav

title: A Rainy Day Story
desc: a draw-and-tell story about one real thing that happened, in order, with a reaction
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Think of one time you were out in the rain, or one time you helped something grow. Draw what happened. Then tell it in order. Then tell how it felt.
key: Tells about one real thing that happened, using any mix of drawing, telling and writing (W.K.3)
Tells the parts in the order they happened. Look for at least two things in the right order, or for words like first, then, next, after (W.K.3)

title: Down the Path
desc: counting out loud by ones
dir: Count out loud. Start at 1. Go as high as you can.
text: The garden is planting a long row. Count out loud as the seeds go in.
key: Say: Start at 1 and count as high as you can. Check: counts 1 to 20 in order with no skips.
Keeps going from 20 to 40 and gets across each new ten (29 to 30, 39 to 40).

title: Ten to a Tray
desc: counting by tens
dir: Count by tens out loud.
text: Each tray holds 10 seeds. Count by tens to 100 as the trays are filled.
key: Say: Count the seeds by tens as each tray is filled. Check: says 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 with no help.
Keeps going: 60, 70, 80, 90, 100. Write the last number said in order.

title: How Many Seeds
desc: counting to tell how many, knowing the last number said is the answer, and knowing the count does not change when the things are moved
dir: Count each box out loud. Then answer out loud.
key: Box A. Say: Point to each seed and count out loud. How many seeds are in Box A? (8. Look for one number word per seed, touching each one once.)

Box A again. Do not let the student recount. Ask: How many seeds were in Box A? (8, said straight back. Knowing the last number said is the answer is the whole point here. Having to start over is wort

title: Count On
desc: counting on from a given number and telling the number that is one more
dir: Listen to your teacher. Count out loud.
text: Count with your teacher.
key: Say: Start at 6 and keep counting up. Stop at 11. (7, 8, 9, 10, 11. The student does not go back to 1.)
Say: Start at 11 and count up to 15. (12 to 15)

title: Seeds in the Row
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 10, with drawings
dir: Listen to each story. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer out loud.
text: You can draw a circle for each seed on your paper, then count or cross out.
key: Say: 4 seeds go in the first row. 3 more seeds go in the second row. How many seeds in all? (7. 4 + 3 = 7)
Say: 9 raindrops were on the window. 2 of them slid down. How many raindrops can you still see? (7. 9 - 2 = 7)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: putting numbers from 11 to 19 together as one ten and some more ones
dir: Look at the trays. Count out loud. You can draw on your paper.
qs: Look at the first picture. How many seeds are in the full tray?
In the first picture, how many loose seeds are there? How many seeds in all?
key: 10. A full tray always holds ten.
5 loose seeds. 15 seeds in all. Look for the student counting on from 10 (11, 12, 13, 14, 15) rather than starting over at 1.

title: Greater, Less, or Equal
desc: telling whether one group is greater than, less than, or equal to another group
dir: Count each box out loud. Then answer out loud.
key: Say: Count Box D and Box E. Which group is greater? How do you know? (Box D is greater. 9 sprouts in a line and 6 raindrops spread about. Counting both, or matching one raindrop to one sprout, both co
Say: Now say it the other way. Which group is less? (Box E. 6 is less than 9.)

title: Seven Seeds, Two Pots
desc: breaking 7 into two parts in more than one way and recording one way
dir: Look at the seeds and the two pots. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer out loud.
key: Say: You have 7 seeds and two pots. Show me one way to put all 7 seeds into the two pots. Draw it or tell me. (Any pair that makes 7: 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, 4 and 3, 5 and 2, 6 and 1. Putting all
Say: Now show me a different way. (A second pair that makes 7 and is not the one just given.)

title: Split It
desc: breaking a number up to 10 into two parts in more than one way and recording each way
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Here are 9.
key: Say: Show me one way to split these 9 into two groups. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 3 + 6 = 9. (a drawing with two groups, or an equation, that makes 9)
Say: Now show me a different way. (a second pair of parts that make 9. The same two numbers in the other order do not count as different.)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: showing a number from 11 to 19 as a ten and some more and recording it
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Look at the full ten frame and the extra ones.
key: Say: Show 14 as a ten and some more. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 14 = 10 + 4. (a drawing of a ten and 4 more, or the equation)
Ask: How many ones are left after the ten? (4)

title: Two Hoses
desc: comparing two objects directly by length and describing the difference
dir: Look at the two hoses. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Which hose is longer, A or B? (A)
Say: How do you know? (Both hoses start at the same post, so the one whose far end reaches farther is the longer one. Look for the student lining up the starts, not only pointing at the picture.)

title: Heavy or Light
desc: comparing two objects by weight to say which is heavier and which is lighter
dir: Look at the scales. Answer out loud.
text: A B
key: Ask: Look at scale A. Which one is heavier? (the wateringCan. It is on the side that goes down.)
Ask: Which one is lighter? (the sprout)

title: Sort the Garden Tray
desc: sorting into three given kinds, counting each kind, and putting the kinds in order by count
dir: Look at the tray. Answer out loud.
key: Say: This tray came in from the garden. Sort it into three kinds: leaves, carrots and flowers. How many of each? (7 leaves, 4 carrots, 5 flowers)
Say: Which kind has the most? Which kind has the fewest? (Leaves the most, with 7. Carrots the fewest, with 4.)

title: Shed Shapes
desc: naming shapes in a scene and telling where things are with position words
dir: Look at the potting shed. Answer out loud.
key: Say: The potting shed is built out of shapes. What shape is the roof? What shape is the big part under it? (A triangle. A square.)
Say: What shape is the door? What shape is the little window? (The door is a rectangle. The window is a square.)

title: Flat or Solid
desc: telling flat two-dimensional shapes from solid three-dimensional ones
dir: Look at the six tiles. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Some of these shapes are flat and some are solid. Which ones are flat? (1, 3 and 5: the circle, the triangle and the square.)
Say: Which ones are solid? (2, 4 and 6: the box, the ball and the can.)

title: What Living Things Need
desc: telling what plants and animals need to stay alive
dir: Look at each row. Answer out loud.
text: A tulip and a bee both live in the spring garden. Living things need certain things to stay alive.
qs: A tulip needs two of these to grow. Which two? Water, sunlight, or a ribbon?
A bee needs two of these. Which two? Food, water, or a bell?
key: water and sunlight. A ribbon is not something a tulip needs.
food and water. A bell is not something a bee needs.

title: A Week of Spring Weather
desc: describing a weather pattern from a week of observations
dir: Look at the week of weather. Answer out loud.
text: Here is one week of weather over the garden. Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat
qs: How many rainy days were there?
How many sunny days were there?

title: A Week of Spring Weather
desc: telling how a living thing changes its surroundings to get what it needs
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A squirrel comes into the garden bed carrying an acorn.
qs: The squirrel digs a hole in the soft dirt and buries the acorn to save it for later. Did the squirrel change the garden bed, or did the garden bed change the squirrel?
Tell me one way you change a yard or a garden to get what you need.
key: The squirrel changed the garden bed. There is a hole and a buried acorn that were not there before.
Any sensible answer about changing a space on purpose: pulling weeds out of a row, digging a hole for a seed, moving a pot into the sun, raking leaves off a path.

title: Homes, Reports and the Garden
desc: matching animals to the places that give them what they need
dir: Match each animal to the place it lives. Answer out loud.
text: Animals live in the garden. Each one lives in one place. It gets what it needs. Here are the places. A leaf. The pond. A burrow under the hedge.
qs: Where does the ladybug live?
Where does the frog live?
key: a leaf. Accept a plant or a stem.
the pond. Accept the water.

title: Homes, Reports and the Garden
desc: telling what a weather forecast is for
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The day before the class plants their seedlings outside, their teacher checks the weather report on her phone.
qs: Why does she check the weather report? To find out if a hard rain is coming so they can wait a day, or to find out what color the flowers will be?
What could the class do if a hard rain was coming?
key: to find out if a hard rain is coming so they can wait a day.
Any sensible answer: wait a day, cover the row, plant in the morning before it starts.

title: Homes, Reports and the Garden
desc: telling one way people can take better care of the land and water
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two children water the garden rows with a hose.
qs: One child turns the hose off as soon as the row is full. The other child leaves the hose running all afternoon. Which choice takes better care of the water?
Tell me one more way to take care of the land or the water.
key: turning the hose off as soon as the row is full
Any sensible answer: put a weed pile in the compost, do not pour paint water on the ground, use a watering can instead of a running hose, pick up the plastic pots, plant something.

title: Pushes and Pulls in the Garden
desc: telling a push from a pull, and comparing a strong push with a gentle one
dir: Answer out loud. Do not say push or pull for the student.
text: A push moves something away from you. A pull brings it toward you.
qs: You pull the garden gate toward you to open it. Is that a push or a pull?
You press a seed down into the soil with your thumb. Is that a push or a pull?
key: a pull
a push

title: Pushes and Pulls in the Garden
desc: deciding whether a change made a thing move farther or in a new direction
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The class let the wind carry the same paper kite across the lawn twice. The wind How far the kite moved a strong gust 9 steps a soft puff 2 steps
qs: Which wind moved the kite farther?
A ball is rolling straight down the garden path. You tap it on its side with a stick. Does it keep going straight, or does it turn?
key: the strong gust, 9 steps
It turns. The tap from the side changes the direction it was going.

title: Sun and Shade in the Garden
desc: telling what sunlight does to the ground and to the things on it
dir: Answer out loud. If you can, touch a sunny spot and a shady spot together first.
text: Two watering cans stand full of water all morning. One sits out in the open. One sits under a leafy bush.
qs: What warms the water in the can, sunlight or moonlight?
Which can of water is warmer by lunchtime, the one in the open or the one under the bush?
key: sunlight
the one in the open, because the sunlight reaches it

title: Sun and Shade in the Garden
desc: designing and drawing something that keeps a spot cooler
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: The new seedlings are here. They are in the garden. They droop in the hot sun. The afternoon sun is hot. Draw something to shade the row of seedlings, like a cl
qs: Draw your shade cover over the row of seedlings.
Tell me how your cover keeps the seedlings cooler.
key: Any cover drawn ABOVE the row. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one still counts. A cover drawn beside the row is partial: ask where the sun is coming from.
Something like: it blocks the sun, the sun cannot reach the leaves, it puts the row in a shadow.

title: Solving a Garden Problem
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking about it
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem? The rain soaks the bird seed, or the feeder is made of wood?
Ask me one question that would help you fix it.
key: The rain soaks the bird seed.
Any real question: how hard does it rain, how much seed is in there, is the top open, could we move the feeder. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Solving a Garden Problem
desc: drawing something whose shape would solve the problem
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would keep the rain off the bird seed, like a little roof, a lid, or an umbrella over the feeder.
qs: Draw your fix.
Tell me what you drew and how its shape keeps the rain out.
key: Any cover that would turn rain away: a roof, a lid, a wide hat shape, an upside down bowl, an umbrella. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one earns credit.
Naming it is what shows intent. Something like: the roof sends the rain off the side, the lid stops it getting in.

title: Solving a Garden Problem
desc: comparing test results from two fixes for the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The class tried two covers and measured the wet seed after one rainy afternoon. Cover Wet seed a slanted roof 1 spoon a flat lid laid on top 6 spoons
qs: Which cover worked better?
How do you know?
key: the slanted roof
Because only 1 spoon of seed got wet under the slanted roof and 6 spoons got wet under the flat lid. The reason has to come from the chart, not from liking roofs.

title: Garden Rules and Doing Right
desc: following rules, knowing what happens when they are broken, and naming an honest choice
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What did Tess choose to do? Tell the truth, or walk away and say nothing?
One garden rule is wait for your turn with the watering can. What might happen if nobody waited for a turn?
key: She told the truth.
Everybody grabs at once, the can gets spilled, and somebody never gets a turn. Any real consequence counts.

title: A Map of the Garden
desc: telling land from water on a map, using position words, and naming the jobs people do nearby
dir: Look at the map. Answer out loud.
text: Here is a map of the garden. the shed the flower beds the apple tree
qs: On this map, which color shows the water and which color shows the land?
The shed is behind the flower beds. The apple tree is in front of them. Which one is behind?
key: The blue part shows water and the green or brown part shows land.
the shed

title: Left and Right
desc: telling where things are with left and right, near and far, and in front and behind
dir: Look at each picture. Point or answer out loud.
text: A B C
key: Ask: Look at picture A. Point to the one on the left. (the tulip)
Ask: Point to the one on the right. (the sprout)

title: The Flag and Long Ago
desc: recognizing the flag as a symbol of the country
dir: Answer out loud.
text: California has state symbols too. They are its own. The state flower is a poppy. It is golden. The state animal is a bear. It is a grizzly. The state bird is a
qs: What do we call this, and what country is it for?
California has its own symbols as well. Name the state flower or the state animal of California.
key: the flag. Accept the American flag or the flag of the United States. Naming it as our flag counts.
the golden poppy for the flower, or the grizzly bear for the animal. Accept the California quail as the state bird. A state symbol is the other half of this standard. (HSS-K.2)

title: The Flag and Long Ago
desc: telling what a holiday honors and how life long ago was different from life today
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Long ago there were no garden hoses.
qs: How did people long ago bring water to a garden, by carrying it from a well in buckets or by turning on a hose?
How do you give a plant water today?
key: by carrying it from a well in buckets
Any real answer: a hose, a watering can, a cup, the rain. Naming today's way is the then-and-now half of this standard.

title: Spring Sound Check
desc: blending, segmenting, and isolating sounds, counting syllables, and telling long from short vowels in spoken words
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the sounds and words out loud.
text: Listen. Then say it.
key: Blend these sounds: /s/ /ee/ /d/ (seed)
Blend these sounds: /s/ /p/ /r/ /ou/ /t/ (sprout)

title: First Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the initial sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the first sound.
qs: What is the first sound in van?
What is the first sound in jam?
key: The sound /v/. Say the sound, not the letter name.
The sound /j/. Say the sound, not the letter name.

title: Middle Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the medial vowel sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the middle sound.
qs: What is the middle sound in map?
What is the middle sound in bed?
key: The short vowel sound /a/.
The short vowel sound /e/.

title: Seed Packet Words
desc: reading words with digraphs, blends, final e, vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, endings, and two syllables
dir: Read each word out loud. The last one is a silly word. Just sound it out.
key: Count each word read correctly. frean is a silly word: listen for the long e that the ea team makes.

Watch for: ch digraph plus ck ending (chick), nd ending (pond), bl blend plus a vowel team (bloom), double letters (well), final e (vine), igh (right), three-letter blend spr plus the ou diphthong (sp

title: How Many Parts?
desc: using the rule that every syllable has a vowel sound to find the number of syllables in a printed word
dir: Read the word to yourself. Tell how many syllables, or parts, it has. Clap it if that helps.
text: pencil sun window hen
key: Point to “pencil”. How many syllables? (2)
Point to “sun”. How many syllables? (1)

title: The First Row
desc: a 76-word spring garden story read aloud
dir: Look at the three pictures. Then read the story out loud in your best reading voice.
text: a bean seed the rain all night the sprout in the row The First Row Our class planted a row of beans. We did it last week. Every morning I check the soil. I want
key: 76 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Point to the three pictures first so seed, rain, and sprout are clear before the student reads.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: a bean seed the rain all night the sprout in the row The First Row Our class planted a row of beans. We did it last week. Every morning I check the soil. I want
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the story about? What happened first?” (a summary or answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Mina's Seed
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about a story the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: Mina's Seed Mina found one last seed. It lay at the packet bottom. The garden rows were already full. So she got an old cup. She filled it with soil. She plante
qs: What did Mina find at the bottom of the packet?
Why did she use a cup instead of the garden rows?
key: One last seed, down at the bottom
Because there was no room left: every row outside was full already

title: What a Seed Needs
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the facts. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: What a Seed Needs A seed is a tiny plant. It has its own lunch. The lunch is packed around it. The seed stays dry and still. It waits until three things reach i
qs: What three things does a seed need?
What does the water do to the hard coat?
key: Water, air, and warmth
It softens the coat

title: Sentence Spotter
desc: finding sentences by their first word, capital letter, and end mark
dir: Look at the sentences. Answer out loud.
text: The seeds are up. Can you see them?
qs: How many sentences do you see? How can you tell?
Read the first word of the second sentence. What kind of letter does it start with?
key: 2 sentences. Each one starts with a capital letter and ends with an end mark
The word is Can. It starts with a capital, or uppercase, C

title: Garden Fix It
desc: spoken grammar items (past tense, plural nouns, subject and verb match, joining two sentences, describing words, place words)
dir: Listen to your teacher read each one. Say your answer out loud.
qs: Today we water the row. Last week we ____.
One bush, two ____.
key: watered
bushes

title: Which Word Fits?
desc: using indefinite pronouns such as everyone, anyone, someone, something, and nothing
dir: Listen to the sentence. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? I have ___ to tell you. (something / anyone)
Which word fits? ___ is asleep. The room is quiet. (Everyone / Nobody)
key: something. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)
Nobody. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)

title: Whose Is It?
desc: using possessive nouns to show who owns something
dir: Listen. Say the answer. For the last one, you can point to the right one on paper.
qs: Lily has a ball. Whose ball is it?
The boy has a coat. Whose coat is it?
key: Lily’s ball. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)
the boy’s coat. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)

title: Commands and Big Feelings
desc: producing imperative (command) and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts
dir: Listen. Say your answer out loud in a full sentence.
qs: Tell me to sit down. Say it as a command.
Your team wins the game! Say one sentence that shows a big feeling.
key: A command such as “Sit down.”
An exclamation, for example “We won!” or “That was so fun!”

title: Print the Alphabet
desc: printing all upper- and lowercase letters
dir: On your paper, print each big letter and its small letter. Print them in order. Hold up your paper when you finish.
text: A a B b C c D d E e F f G g H h I i J j K k L l M m N n O o P p Q q R r S s T t U u V v W w X x Y y Z z
key: Look at the paper. Mark each letter pair where both the capital and the small letter are formed correctly and sit on the line. Letters may be uneven. Count a pair when each letter can be told from the
Check the tall letters (b, d, f, h, k, l, t), the letters that drop below the line (g, j, p, q, y), and the look-alikes (b and d, p and q).

title: Listen Up
desc: asking and answering questions about a text read aloud
dir: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about what happens in the garden after it rains. Then answer out loud.
text: Listen.
key: Ask: What did people think for a long time? (that the worms came up because their tunnels had filled with water)
Ask: How does a worm breathe? (through its skin)

title: Tell Me About It
desc: describing a thing with relevant details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about something you can watch growing or changing outside right now. What is it? What does it look like? How do you feel when you look at it?
key: Names the thing and gives 2 or more details about it (SL.1.4)
Gives 2 or more details about what it looks like now, and they stay on this one thing (SL.1.4)

title: Two-Step Directions
desc: giving, restating, and following simple two-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear, say it back, and give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do what your teacher says. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once, without repeating: “Point to the floor, then point to the ceiling.” (does both steps, in the right order)
Say once, without repeating: “Close your eyes, then count to three out loud.” (does both steps, in the right order)

title: Person, Place, Thing, Event
desc: describing a person, a place, a thing, and an event with relevant details, and saying ideas and feelings clearly
dir: Listen to your teacher. Tell about each one. Use lots of details.
text: Tell about a person, a place, a thing, and something that happened.
key: Say: “Tell me about a person who helps you.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the person, such as who they are, what they look like, or what they do)
Say: “Tell me about a place you go with your family.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the place, such as what is there or what you do there)

title: Garden Day Chart
desc: using a provided chart to answer a question in writing
dir: Look at the chart. Write 1 sentence on your paper and hold it up.
text: The class wants to find out how much the bean sprout grew this week. What will they take out to the row? Use the chart.
key: Finds the answer in the chart. Your help is fine: read the two columns out loud and point to the row headings
Writes a sentence drawn from the chart, such as: They will take the ruler

title: Remember and Tell
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question
dir: Think about what happened to you. Tell your teacher your answer out loud. You can draw it, too.
qs: Think about breakfast. What did you eat today or yesterday? Tell me about it.
Think about the weather today. What did you see or feel outside? Tell me.
key: Names a real food or meal from experience.
Gives one real detail about today’s weather from their own experience. (They may draw first, then tell. Write down what they say if you want a record.)

title: Spring Journal
desc: an informative piece about a spring thing, with facts and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Pick one spring thing: a seed, the rain, or a bird. Write its name. Then write 2 or 3 true facts about it. End with one last sentence that wraps it up. a seed t
key: Names the topic: the seed, the rain, or the bird (W.1.2)
Supplies at least 2 facts about it, such as: A seed needs water. A bird builds a nest out of grass (W.1.2)

title: Spring Journal
desc: a narrative about a rainy day or a day the student helped something grow, told in order
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about a day you were out in the rain, or a day you helped something grow. Tell two things that happened, in order. Use the words first and then. End by te
key: Tells about two or more things that happened, in an order that makes sense (W.1.3)
Includes some detail about what happened, not just a list (W.1.3)

title: The Best Part of Spring
desc: an opinion piece about the best part of spring, with a topic, an opinion, a reason, and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: What is the best part of spring in the garden: the rain, the first sprout, or the flowers? Name the one you pick. Write what you think. Give one reason. Then wr
key: Names the topic, which one of the three the writing is about (W.1.1)
States an opinion about it, such as: The rain is the best part of spring (W.1.1)

title: Count the Seeds
desc: counting, reading, and writing numerals to 120 and counting objects
dir: Count and read out loud. Write your numbers on your paper and hold it up.
text: The class counts every seed before it goes into the row.
qs: Count out loud from 94 to 110.
Read these numbers out loud: 73, 102, 118.
key: Seventy-three, one hundred two, one hundred eighteen

title: Garden Problems
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 20, with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen to each story problem. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer.
text: The class plants its seeds in long rows.
qs: One tray holds 8 seeds and another tray holds 9. How many seeds in all?
There were 15 sprouts in the tray. 6 of them were moved out to the big bed. How many sprouts are still in the tray?
key: 9 sprouts (15 - 6 = 9)

title: Trays of Ten
desc: place value in two-digit numbers (bundles of ten and leftover ones)
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud.
text: A full tray holds 10 seeds. A long block stands for one full tray of ten, and a small cube stands for one loose seed.
qs: Look at the picture. How many full trays of ten do you see, and how many loose seeds? What number is that?
In the number 28, what does the 2 stand for? What does the 8 stand for?
key: 4 trays of ten and 6 loose. That is 46
The 2 stands for two tens, which is twenty seeds. The 8 stands for eight ones

title: Add Up the Garden
desc: adding within 100 (a two-digit number plus a one-digit number and plus a multiple of ten)
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Say your answer and tell how you got it.
text: The class counts the garden row by row.
qs: Row A has 24 sprouts. 5 more come up. How many now?
Row B has 43 sprouts. The class plants 30 more. How many now?
key: 29 (24 + 5 = 29. Only the ones change)
73 (43 + 30 = 73. Adding tens to tens: 4 tens and 3 tens is 7 tens)

title: Explain Your Adding
desc: adding within 100 with a drawing, relating it to a written equation, and explaining the reasoning with tens and ones
dir: Solve on your paper. Draw tens and ones. Write the equation. Then tell how you added.
qs: Add 45 + 30. Draw tens and ones, write the equation, and tell how you added.
Why did you add the tens with the tens and the ones with the ones?
key: 45 + 30 = 75. The drawing shows tens and ones, the equation matches, and the explanation says tens were added to tens and ones to ones (and that ten ones were made into a new ten when needed).
Because tens are worth ten and ones are worth one. They are different amounts, so like parts go together.

title: Take Away Tens
desc: subtracting multiples of ten from multiples of ten within 100
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, tell how you know.
text: Every tray that gets planted takes ten seeds off the shelf.
qs: There are 80 seeds on the shelf. Three trays of ten get planted. 80 - 30 is what?
key: 50 (8 tens take away 3 tens is 5 tens)

title: Measure the Vine
desc: measuring length as a whole number of same-size units laid end to end
dir: Look at the blocks under the vine and the hose. Answer out loud.
qs: How many blocks long is the vine?
How many blocks long is the hose?
key: 6 blocks
4 blocks

title: Turn It Around
desc: using the order of addends and making a ten as strategies to add
dir: Look at the two frames. Answer out loud.
qs: 9 + 4 = 13. What is 4 + 9? How do you know that without adding it again?
Now use the frames. Move 2 of the pea seeds into the 2 empty boxes of the bean frame. What two numbers are you adding now, and what is 8 + 6?
key: 13. Turning the two numbers around does not change the total, so 4 + 9 has to be 13 too. Count it correct only when the student says the order does not matter, not just the answer
10 and 4, which is 14. So 8 + 6 = 14. The bean frame fills to 10 and 4 pea seeds are left over

title: Count On, Count Back
desc: counting on to add and counting back to subtract, and naming the matching fact
dir: Use the number line. Answer out loud.
qs: Start at 12 and count on 3. Where do you land? What addition fact did you just do?
Start at 16 and count back 4. Where do you land? What subtraction fact is that?
key: 15. The fact is 12 + 3 = 15
12. The fact is 16 - 4 = 12

title: Garden Clocks
desc: telling and writing time to the hour and the half hour on an analog clock
dir: Look at the two clocks. Answer out loud. Then write one time on your paper.
qs: What time does Clock A show? How do you know?
What time does Clock B show? How do you know?
key: 4 o'clock, or 4:00. The short hand is on the 4 and the long hand is straight up on the 12
Half past 7, or 7:30. The long hand points straight down at the 6, and the short hand sits halfway between the 7 and the 8

title: Seedling Chart
desc: reading a three-category chart for the total, for one category, and for how many more or fewer
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
qs: How many seedlings came up in all?
How many more bean seedlings are there than carrot seedlings?

title: Make a Graph
desc: organizing and representing data with up to three categories, and answering questions about the total and about how many more or less
dir: Look at the list. Make a tally chart or a picture graph on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: Ten kids told us their favorite colors. blue red blue green blue red blue green blue red
key: A chart or graph with red 3, blue 5, green 2. Each item is counted once. Tally marks, pictures, or squares all work. Labels are on each group.
10 (the total of all three groups)

title: Share the Beds
desc: naming halves and fourths, telling how many shares make the whole, and knowing more shares means smaller shares
dir: Look at the round tray and the long bed. Answer out loud.
qs: The round tray is cut into 2 equal shares. What is each share called, and how much of the tray is shaded?
The long bed is cut into 4 equal shares. What are those called, how much is shaded, and how many of them make the whole bed?
key: Halves. One half of the tray is shaded, which is 1 of the 2 equal shares
Fourths, or quarters. One fourth of the bed is shaded, which is a quarter of it. Four fourths make the whole bed

title: Copy a Maple Seed
desc: naming the job a plant part does, then designing a tool that copies it to solve a human problem
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer the first out loud. Draw the second on your paper and hold it up.
text: A maple seed has a wing. The wing is flat and papery. It is on one side. It comes off the tree. The wing makes it spin. The spin holds it in the air. It stays u
qs: How does a flat papery wing get a maple seed further away from its parent tree?
Draw something the gardener could drop her seed in that copies the maple seed's wing.
key: The wing makes the seed spin, the spin keeps it up in the air longer, and while it is up there the wind carries it sideways. Any answer about staying up longer or catching the wind counts.
Any design that catches air: a paper wing or blade on each seed packet, a spinner, a little parachute, a wide flat scoop the wind can take the seed off, a fan to blow it out.

title: Robin Parents
desc: finding a pattern in what a parent animal does and what the young do in answer, and saying how it helps the young
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What do the young robins do every single time a parent lands on the rim of the nest?
What does the parent do differently once the young are bigger?
key: They throw their heads back and open their beaks as wide as they can. Every single time is what makes it a pattern.
It stops landing on the rim and pulls worms up on the grass below where the young can watch.

title: Robin Parents
desc: making observations that young plants and animals are like their parents but not exactly like them
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
text: Three seedlings came up. They came from one packet of seeds. All were saved from the same plant. It was the parent plant. A puppy and a dog. The dog is its pare
qs: The three seedlings came from the same parent plant but they are not the same height. Does that mean one of them is a different kind of plant? Say why.
Name one way all three seedlings are like the parent plant they came from.
key: No. Plants grown from one parent are like it and like each other, but not exactly the same. Being a different height is one of those differences.
Same kind of leaf, same green colour, same shape of stem, all come out of the ground the same way. Any likeness counts.

title: Earlier Every Week
desc: finding a pattern in a log of sky observations and using it to predict what comes next
dir: Look at the log. Answer out loud.
text: The gardener wrote down the time the sun came up, once a week for four weeks. Week Time the sun came up first week 6:50 second week 6:40 third week 6:30 fourth
qs: Is the sun coming up earlier or later as the weeks go by?
How many minutes earlier does it come up each week?
key: earlier each week
10 minutes earlier each week

title: Earlier Every Week
desc: relating the number of hours of daylight to the time of year from observations made across a year
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Hours of daylight on the first day of three spring months. Month Hours of daylight March 12 April 13 May 14
qs: Are the hours of daylight going up or down as spring goes on?
How many more hours of daylight does May have than March?
key: going up, one hour more each month
2 more hours. 14 take away 12

title: A Blade of Grass
desc: planning an investigation showing that a shaking material makes sound and that a sound can make a material shake
dir: If you can find a wide blade of grass, try the first part. Either way, answer out loud.
text: Hold a wide blade of grass tight between your two thumbs and blow hard across the edge of it. Now stretch plastic wrap over the top of a jar and tape it down. P
qs: What has to happen to the blade of grass before you hear the squeak?
Let one thumb go slack so the grass is loose. What happens to the sound, and why?
key: It has to shake. The air rushing past the edge makes the blade shake very fast, and the shaking makes the sound.
The sound stops or goes dull. A loose blade cannot shake the same way, and no shaking means no sound.

title: The Dark Potting Shed
desc: accounting for why an object in darkness can be seen only when light shines on it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The potting shed has one small window. A heavy cover goes over it. The cover is down. The door is shut. No light gets in at all.
qs: A packet of seeds is on the bench inside the dark shed. Can you see it? Say why or why not.
What would have to get into that shed before you could see the packet?
key: No. No light gets into the shed, and a thing can only be seen when light shines on it and comes back to your eyes.
Light has to reach it: a flashlight, a lamp, the door opened, or the window cover lifted.

title: The Dark Potting Shed
desc: using test results to tell what happens when different materials are put in the path of a beam of light
dir: Look at the test results. Answer out loud.
text: One flashlight beam was pointed at four things in the shed and what it did was written down. What was put in the beam What the beam did a glass jar over a seedl
qs: Which thing let all the light through?
Which thing let a little light through?
key: the glass jar
the thin cloth row cover

title: Across the Field
desc: designing a device that uses light or sound to send a message over a distance too far to shout
dir: Draw your answer on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: The far end of the field is a long walk from the house, and a shout does not carry that far over open ground.
qs: Draw a device at the house that tells the person at the far end of the field that it is time to come in. It has to use light or sound.
Explain what you drew and say which of the two, light or sound, it uses.
key: Any device that carries light or sound across the field: a bell, a horn, a whistle, a drum, a bright lamp on a pole, a lamp flashed on and off.
Names it and says which one it uses.

title: Fix the Falling Seedlings
desc: naming a problem people want to change, asking a question about it, and saying what to observe first
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem the gardener wants to change?
What is one question you would ask the gardener before you built anything?
key: Tall thin seedlings bend over in the wind and lie flat on the soil.
Any real question: how tall are they, how strong is the wind, which way does it come from, how many fall, is the end row worse than the others. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Fix the Falling Seedlings
desc: making a simple drawing of a fix and explaining how the shape of the object makes it work
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
text: Draw something that keeps the tall seedlings standing up in the wind.
qs: Draw your fix on the row of seedlings.
Point to the part that holds the stem up and tell me its shape.
key: Any real fix: a stick beside each stem with a loose tie, a low fence along the row, a wind break at the end of the row, a cage round each plant, a string between two posts the plants lean on.
Names a shape: a straight upright stick, a ring round the stem, a long low wall, a flat panel standing on its edge.

title: Which Support Worked
desc: comparing the data from tests of two objects built to solve the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two supports were tried on the same windy day, fifteen seedlings with each. Support Seedlings that bent over, out of 15 a stick and a loose tie 2 extra soil rou
qs: Which support worked better in the test?
Point to the numbers that show it and tell me what they are.
key: the stick and the loose tie
Only 2 seedlings out of 15 bent over with the stick, and 10 out of 15 bent over with the extra soil. The numbers have to be in the answer.

title: The Town Library
desc: telling a right from a responsibility and explaining why a shared service has rules
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: Anybody who lives in the town may get a card. Is that a right or a responsibility?
Bringing the books back in three weeks is something you must do. Is that a right or a responsibility?
key: a right
a responsibility

title: The Field Map
desc: giving an exact grid location, describing a relative location, and telling a physical feature from a built one
dir: Look at the map grid. Answer out loud.
text: A map of the farm field, drawn on a grid. 1 2 3 A B C the farmhouse the hedge the seedling rows the stream the plank bridge
qs: Find the farmhouse. Give its exact spot on the grid, the letter and the number.
Where is the stream compared to the farmhouse? Use words like above, below, left of, or right of.
key: A1. Both parts are needed.
Below the farmhouse and to the right of it. Down and over counts too.

title: The Field Map
desc: naming built features of a familiar place and recognizing that people in one place come from many different places
dir: Answer out loud.
text: On market day there are fourteen stalls. They line the main street. People are running them. They grew up in nine different places. Three of the stalls sell foo
qs: Do all the people running stalls on one street come from the same place? Say how you know.
Name three things people built in your own town, and say what one of them does for the people there.
key: No. They grew up in nine different places.
Any three built things with a use for one: a school teaches children, a hospital takes care of people, a road lets people travel, a store sells things, a library lends books.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: telling what a national memorial is for and naming a tradition people keep over many years
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Washington, D.C. has a long building. It is white marble. It has wide steps. Inside is a huge stone statue. It is Abraham Lincoln. He is sitting in a chair. It
qs: Who is the statue inside the Lincoln Memorial?
A memorial is built to remember somebody. Why would a whole country build one instead of just writing the person's name down somewhere?
key: Abraham Lincoln, a president of the United States.
Because a big building that people can visit together keeps the memory alive for everybody, not just for the people who read one page. Any answer about remembering together counts.

title: Symbols, Then and Now
desc: comparing everyday life long ago with life today and telling what changed from what stayed the same
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Getting a field ready for planting. Long ago Today what pulled the plough two horses in harness a tractor with an engine how long one field took three days two
qs: Long ago, what pulled the plough across a field?
What pulls it today?
key: Two horses in harness.
A tractor with an engine.

title: Spring Word Flip
desc: reading words with vowel teams, blends, r-controlled vowels, two syllables, a prefix, a suffix, and an irregular spelling
dir: Read each word out loud. The last two are made-up words. Just sound them out.
key: Read each word in order. drean and blork are made-up words: listen for the ea team sound and the or sound.
Watch for: the -ed ending said as /d/ (bloomed), the spr blend with the ou diphthong (sprout), r-controlled ir plus the y ending (thirsty), a three-letter blend with the -le ending (sprinkle), the ow

title: Two-Part Long Vowel Words
desc: decoding regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels
dir: Read each word out loud. Each word has two parts.
key: Mark each word read correctly. Each word has two syllables and at least one long vowel sound, such as pa-per, mu-sic, o-pen.
If the student breaks the word into syllables and then says it smoothly, count it correct.

title: Read the Story
desc: a 105-word grade-level story read aloud
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: On the last Saturday of the month the whole block meets. They gather at the empty lot on the corner. Somebody brings a wheelbarrow. Somebody else brings a crate
key: 105 words. Mark each missed word and each self-correction on the passage in the record sheet.
Note pace and expression in your notes.

title: Story Questions
desc: asking and answering who, what, why, and how questions about key details in a story
dir: Look back at the story if you need to. Then answer each question out loud.
text: The Corner Lot (click to open or close the story) On the last Saturday of the month the whole block meets. They gather at the empty lot on the corner. Somebody
qs: Who meets at the empty lot?
When do they meet?
key: The whole block, everyone who lives there
The last Saturday of the month

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: On the last Saturday of the month the whole block meets. They gather at the empty lot on the corner. Somebody brings a wheelbarrow. Somebody else brings a crate
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the text about? Tell me two things you remember.” (an answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Why It Rains
desc: asking and answering what, where, why, and how questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about rain. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Why It Rains Every day the sun warms the top of the ocean. Some of that water turns into a gas you cannot see. The gas rises with the warm air. High up, the air
qs: What does the sun do to the top of the ocean?
Where does the gas turn back into tiny drops?
key: It warms it, and some of the water turns into a gas you cannot see
High up, where the air is cold

title: Say It Right
desc: spoken grammar items (irregular past tense, irregular plural, reflexive pronoun, adverb, word order, joining two sentences)
dir: Say each answer out loud.
qs: This summer the beans grow fast. Last summer they ____.
One leaf, two ____.
key: grew
leaf

title: Write It Right
desc: written conventions (capital letters in place names, an apostrophe for a possessive and a contraction, a comma in a letter greeting, spelling two patterns)
dir: Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Fix this sentence: we walked down maple street to the river garden
The trowel belongs to the class. Write the missing word: the ____ trowel
key: We walked down Maple Street to the River Garden. (capital W to start, capital M and capital S in the street name, capital R and capital G in the garden name, and a period)
class’s (apostrophe before the s)

title: Capital Letters
desc: capitalizing holidays, product names, and geographic names
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each sentence. Write it again with the right capital letters. Hold up your paper when you finish.
qs: Fix the capital letters: people clean up on earth day.
Fix the capital letters: we drove through texas.
key: People clean up on Earth Day.
We drove through Texas.

title: Use a Dictionary
desc: using a beginning dictionary and ABC order to check and correct spellings
dir: Listen. Answer out loud. If you have a beginning dictionary, you may use it.
qs: Put these words in ABC order: zebra, lion, bear.
The guide words are map and net. Would the word moon be on this page? Tell why.
key: bear, lion, zebra
Yes. moon comes after map and before net.

title: Group Words
desc: using collective nouns
dir: Listen. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? A group of players on a ball field is called a ___. (team / flock)
Which word fits? A group of wolves is called a ___. (pack / school)
key: team. (A collective noun names a group.)
pack. (A collective noun names a group.)

title: The Two Rows
desc: recounting a story in order and telling its lesson
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then answer each question out loud.
text: The Two Rows Ravi was given a packet of bean seeds. He planted them in two short rows. He watered both rows the same. But he could not stop wondering about the
qs: Tell me this story again in your own words. What happened first, next, and last?
What did Ravi do every afternoon?
key: Recounts the main events in order: Ravi planted two rows and watered them the same, every afternoon he dug a seed up out of the fence row to look at it, after two weeks one row was knee high and the f
He dug a seed up out of the fence row, brushed it off, looked at it, and pushed it back in

title: Listen Up
desc: recounting and describing key ideas and details from a text read aloud
dir: Listen first. Then answer your teacher's questions out loud.
text: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read a report about flowers and bees.
key: Ask: What does a bee come to the flower for? (a drop of sweet nectar, deep inside the petals)
Ask: Describe how the pollen gets from one flower to another. (the bee brushes past the powdery yellow pollen going in, and some of it rubs off on the next flower of the same kind)

title: Tell Me About It
desc: telling about an experience in order, with facts and details, in clear complete sentences
dir: Tell about it out loud. Say what happened first, next, and last.
text: Tell me about a time you planted something, or a time you got caught out in the rain. Where were you? What did you do? What did you see or hear? First Next Last
key: Tells what happened in an order that makes sense
Gives facts that fit (where, when, who, or what)

title: Longer Directions
desc: following three- and four-step oral directions, requesting clarification when something is not understood, and giving multi-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear. Ask a question if you are not sure what to do. Then give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do the steps in order. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once: “Draw a tree, draw a sun above it, and color the sun yellow.” (does all three steps in order)
Say once: “Hold up your hand, count to five out loud, wave, and put your hand down.” (does all four steps in order)

title: Plan and Tell a Story
desc: planning and delivering a short narrative presentation that recounts an event with details, a logical sequence, and a conclusion
dir: Pick one idea. Plan what you will say: the start, the middle, and the end. Then tell your story out loud.
text: Pick one: a day at the park or the beach, a time you learned a skill, or a time you were proud. Beginning Middle End
key: Plans first: says or draws what will happen at the start, the middle, and the end before telling (give about one minute to plan)
Tells one event with enough detail (who, where, and what happened)

title: The Garden Log
desc: gathering information from a provided log and recalling information from experience to answer questions
dir: Use the log to answer. Say the first two answers out loud. Write number 3 on your paper and hold it up. Then say number 4.
text: The garden crew writes down how many new sprouts came up each day, and what the weather was like.
qs: Use the log. Which day had the most new sprouts?
Which days were sunny?
key: Thursday, with 31 sprouts
Tuesday and Wednesday

title: Spring Writing
desc: an opinion piece about the better job on garden day, with reasons, linking words, and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: On garden day there are two jobs: digging the beds, or filling the watering cans and watering the rows. Which job is the better one? Write what you think. Give
key: Introduces the topic: which garden day job is better (W.2.1)
States a clear opinion, naming one of the two jobs (W.2.1)

title: Spring Writing
desc: an informative piece explaining how a seed turns into a plant, with facts, a definition, and a closing
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Explain how a seed turns into a plant. Start by telling the reader what your writing is about. Use facts. Somewhere in it, tell the reader what the word sprout
key: Introduces the topic in the first sentence, so the reader knows what the writing is about (W.2.2)
Uses facts to develop the points, such as: a seed needs water, a root goes down first, leaves catch the sunlight (W.2.2)

title: Spring Writing
desc: a short narrative with events in order, details about actions and feelings, time words, and an ending
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: You are on the garden crew. You have one row left to plant, and the first fat raindrops start to fall. Write a story about what happens next. Tell it in order.
key: Tells about one event or a short set of events in order (W.2.3)
Includes details about actions, thoughts, or feelings (W.2.3)

title: Read the Rows
desc: applying grade-level phonics and word-analysis skills to decode words in text
dir: Read each line out loud. Sound out any word that is tricky.
text: The bright green shoots pushed through the crumbly brown soil. We unpacked eight flats and replanted every seedling. A light rain sprinkled the thirsty rows all
key: Line 1: listen for igh in bright, the ee team in green, the oo team in shoots, ough in through, and the -ly ending in crumbly.
Line 2: listen for the prefix un in unpacked, the -ed ending said as /t/ in unpacked, the irregular eigh in eight, and the prefix re in replanted.

title: Fill the Trays
desc: one-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100 with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen while your teacher reads each problem. Solve it on your paper. You can draw or write a number sentence. Say your answer.
text: The garden crew fills trays of seedlings and plants them out in long rows.
qs: A tray has 48 cells. So far 29 of them are filled. How many cells are still empty?
The bean row got 36 seeds and the pea row got 27. How many seeds is that in all?

title: Odd or Even Seeds
desc: telling odd from even for a group of up to 20 and writing an even number as a sum of two equal addends
dir: Count each pile. Say your answer out loud. Write the doubles on your paper and hold it up.
qs: Count Pile A. How many? Is it odd or even? Write it as a double.
Count Pile B. How many? Is it odd or even? How do you know?
key: 14 seeds. Even, because they pair up with none left over. 7 + 7 = 14
11 raindrops. Odd, because when you pair them up one is left over with no partner. Counting by 2s also lands on 10 and then one more.

title: Seedling Trays
desc: finding the total of a rectangular array and writing it as a sum of equal addends
dir: Look at the tray. Write your adding sentence on your paper and hold it up.
text: A seedling tray holds its sprouts in even rows.
qs: How many sprouts are in the tray in all?
Write an adding sentence for the tray, using equal addends.
key: 20 sprouts
5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 (one addend for each row), or 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20 (one addend for each column). Either one counts.

title: Greenhouse Math
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with a place value strategy and relating it to a written method
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Show your work and hold it up. Say your answer.
text: The greenhouse keeps a count of every seedling it starts.
qs: The greenhouse started 348 bean seedlings and 276 pea seedlings. How many is that in all? Show how you added.
The crew wants 500 seedlings ready by May. So far 237 are ready. How many more are needed?
key: 624 seedlings (348 + 276 = 624). Listen for hundreds with hundreds, tens with tens, ones with ones, and for making a new ten and a new hundred.
263 more (500 - 237 = 263). This one needs two decomposes, so watch the work.

title: Why Regroup?
desc: adding and subtracting within 1000 with place value, and explaining why a ten or hundred is composed or decomposed
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work. Then tell why you had to regroup.
qs: Solve 258 + 167. Tell why you had to regroup.
Solve 413 - 156. Tell why you had to regroup.
key: 425. 8 + 7 = 15 ones, so 10 ones became 1 ten. 5 + 6 + 1 = 12 tens, so 10 tens became 1 hundred.
257. Not enough ones or tens at first, so a ten was broken into 10 ones and a hundred into 10 tens.

title: The Seed Shop
desc: money word problems with quarters, dimes, nickels, pennies, and dollars, using the cent sign and the dollar sign
dir: Look at the coins. Write each answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: The seed shop opens the first week of spring.
qs: Nel has these coins in her pocket. How much money does she have? Write it with the right symbol.
A packet of bean seeds costs 45¢. Nel buys one. How much money does she have left?
key: 67¢ (25 + 25 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 67). $0.67 is also correct, but 67¢ is the grade 2 target.

title: Garden Graph
desc: reading a bar graph with four categories and a single-unit scale, solving compare and put-together problems from it, and drawing a new bar
dir: Look at the graph. Say the first four answers out loud. Draw the last one on your paper and hold it up.
text: The crew counted the sprouts in each row and made this graph. The numbers up the side go up by one.
qs: How many sprouts are up in the corn row?
Which row has the fewest sprouts, and how many?
key: 9 sprouts
Peas, with 5

title: Draw a Picture Graph
desc: drawing a picture graph from a data set with four categories and solving put-together, take-apart, and compare problems
dir: Look at the table. Draw a picture graph on your paper. Use one picture for each 1. Then answer out loud.
text: Ways to get to school: number of kids Choice Number of kids Walk 3 Bus 7 Car 5 Bike 2
qs: Draw a picture graph of the table. Give it a title and label each row.
How many kids chose Walk and Bus together?
key: A picture graph with 3 symbols for Walk, 7 symbols for Bus, 5 symbols for Car, 2 symbols for Bike. Each symbol stands for 1, the symbols are the same size and lined up, and the rows are labeled.

title: Two Rows at Once
desc: two-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100
dir: Each problem takes two steps. Solve it on your paper and say your answer.
text: On planting day the crew works two rows at a time, so most counts take two steps.
qs: The shed had 64 seed packets. 18 went to one class and 23 went to another. How many packets are left in the shed?
One flat holds 9 pots and a second flat holds 7 pots. The crew plants 5 of those pots out in the garden. How many pots are still in the flats?

title: The Seedling Count
desc: reading hundreds, tens and ones off a block model, and writing a number in numerals, words and expanded form
dir: Look at the blocks. Say the first two answers out loud. Write the last one on your paper.
text: The greenhouse counted this spring's seedlings with blocks. A flat is a hundred, a stick is a ten, and a cube is a one.
qs: How many hundreds, how many tens, and how many ones are on the mat? What number is that?
In that number, what does the 4 stand for? How many tens would it take to make that same amount?
key: 4 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones. The number is 406 (2.NBT.A.1). The empty tens place is the part to listen for: a student who says 46 read the mat as two piles instead of three places
The 4 stands for 4 hundreds, which is 400. It takes 40 tens to make 400, because 10 tens make one hundred (2.NBT.A.1)

title: Count the Rows
desc: counting on within 1000 and skip counting by 5s, 100s and 2s
dir: Count out loud. Your teacher will tell you where to start and where to stop.
text: The crew counts the whole lot out loud while they plant.
qs: Start at 596 and count on to 605.
Skip count by 5s, starting at 60 and stopping at 100.
key: 596, 597, 598, 599, 600, 601, 602, 603, 604, 605. Crossing 599 to 600 is the part that trips students up

title: Measure the Seedling
desc: reading a length off a ruler, knowing why a measure starts at zero, choosing the right tool for a long object, and measuring a real object with a ruler
dir: Look at the seedling lined up on the ruler. Answer out loud. For the last one, get a real ruler and measure.
text: The ruler is marked in inches. The gold bar is the seedling, laid along it.
qs: How long is the seedling, and in what unit?
Why does the end of the seedling have to line up with the 0 and not with the 1?
key: 7 inches. The bar starts at 0 and ends at 7
Because the measure counts the units the object actually covers. Starting at the 1 would leave out the first inch and the answer would come out one short

title: Garden Day Clock
desc: telling time to the nearest five minutes with a.m. and p.m., and knowing time relationships
dir: Look at the two clocks. Answer out loud.
qs: What time does Clock A show? The crew arrives in the morning, so say it with a.m. or p.m.
What time does Clock B show? The crew packs up in the afternoon.
key: 7:15 a.m. The long hand is on the 3, which is 15 minutes past
3:50 p.m. The long hand is on the 10, which is 50 minutes past. The short hand sits very close to the 4, so watch for 4:50

title: Time Facts
desc: knowing relationships of time such as minutes in an hour, days in a month, and weeks in a year
dir: Listen. Answer out loud.
qs: Which month has fewer days: February or July?
How many minutes are in half an hour?
key: February (28 or 29 days; July has 31)
30 minutes

title: Shapes in the Garden
desc: naming shapes by their number of sides and angles, identifying a cube, and drawing a shape to a given attribute
dir: Look at the five tiles. Say the first two answers out loud. Draw the last one on your paper.
qs: Name tiles 1, 2, 3 and 4. For each one, say how many sides it has.
Which tile is a cube? How can you tell?
key: 1 is a triangle with 3 sides. 2 is a quadrilateral with 4 sides. 3 is a pentagon with 5 sides. 4 is a hexagon with 6 sides. Calling tile 2 a trapezoid is right too, and a trapezoid is one kind of quad
Tile 5. It is solid, not flat, and it is built from 6 square faces that are all the same size

title: Three Trays of Radish Seed
desc: reading the results of a plant test and planning a fair test of one thing a plant needs
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Then answer out loud.
text: Three trays of radish seeds were sown on the corner lot on the same spring morning, 30 seeds in each tray. Tray What it got After twelve days 1 out in the open,
qs: Which tray did best, and what did it get?
Tray 2 and tray 3 each went wrong, but for different reasons. Say what each one was missing.
key: Tray 1, 27 short dark green seedlings. It got both sunlight and water.
Tray 2 was missing water, because the plank kept the rain off. Tray 3 was missing sunlight, because the pail kept the light off. Both have to be named for full credit.

title: Three Trays of Radish Seed
desc: making a simple model that does the job an animal does when it moves seeds
dir: Draw your model on your paper. Then tell your teacher about it.
text: Ants on the lot pick up small seeds. They carry them down into their tunnels. They leave some behind in the soil. Those seeds grow in spring. Draw a model you c
qs: Draw your model. Label the part that grips the seed and the part that gets it under the soil.
Which animal job does your model copy, and why does getting the seed under the soil help the plant?
key: Any model with a gripping part and a digging or pushing part: a peg, a bent paper clip, tweezers and a small spoon, a straw with a plunger. The two labelled parts are what to look for.
It copies an ant carrying seeds down into its tunnels. Under the soil the seed is damp and safe from birds, so it can sprout, while a seed left on a hard path dries out or gets eaten.

title: The Wet Ditch and the Gravel Strip
desc: comparing the kinds of living things found in two different habitats
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both lists. Answer out loud.
text: Two children spent twenty minutes in each of two places on the lot and wrote down every kind of living thing they could find. The wet ditch at the back The dry
qs: How many kinds of living things are on the wet ditch list?
Name one living thing from the ditch that would not last long in the gravel strip, and say why.
key: 11. Four rushes and weeds, two worms, one frog, one water snail and three flies or midges.
Any sensible pick with a reason: a worm would dry out in the gravel because it needs damp soil, a frog needs water to keep its skin wet, a water snail needs water to live in.

title: One Day, or Twenty Years
desc: using two sources as evidence that some Earth events happen quickly and some happen slowly
dir: Listen while your teacher reads both notes. Answer out loud.
text: Two notes about this corner of the city, from two different places. Where it came from What it says a city street repair report In one day of heavy spring rain,
qs: Which note tells about a change that happened in one day?
Which note tells about a change that took twenty years?
key: The street repair report, the gravel carried across the lot in one day of rain.
The pair of photographs, the clay bank worn back the width of a doorway over twenty years.

title: One Day, or Twenty Years
desc: telling where water is found on Earth and whether it is solid or liquid
dir: Answer out loud.
text: In spring the water on this lot is easy to find.
qs: Name three places on or near this lot where you would find water.
Most of the water on Earth is in the ocean and it is salty. Name a place nearby where the water is fresh instead.
key: Any three: the puddles, the rain barrel, the ditch, the creek two streets away, the tap, clouds, in the soil, inside the plants.
The creek, the ditch, the rain barrel, a pond, or the tap. Fresh water is the kind plants can be watered with.

title: Holding the Beds, and a Map of the Block
desc: comparing two things put in place to stop water from washing the soil away
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Spring rain washes soil off the new beds, which sit on a gentle slope. Two ways of holding it were tried and the soil caught in a tray at the bottom was weighed
qs: Which one kept the most soil on the beds?
How do you know, using the numbers in the chart?
key: the layer of straw over the soil
Only 1 kilogram washed off under the straw, 2 kilograms washed off with the boards, and 6 kilograms washed off the bare soil. The reason must come from the numbers.

title: Holding the Beds, and a Map of the Block
desc: making a model of an area that shows the shapes of the land and the bodies of water in it
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Make your own model map of the block. Put in the slope the lot sits on, the flat ground by the gate, the creek two streets over, and the pond in the park. Add a
qs: Draw your model map with the slope, the flat ground, the creek and the pond on it.
Show me your key. Which parts are land and which parts are water?
key: All four on the page and told apart by shape or colour: the slope as a bump or as rings, the flat ground left flat, the creek as a line, the pond as a closed shape.
Points to each part and reads the key. The key is what makes this a model and not just a picture.

title: Sorting the Seed Shop Shelf
desc: describing materials by properties you can see or feel and sorting them into groups
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Four things off the seed shop shelf, and what was noticed about each one. Item Material What was noticed a seed packet paper thin, bends easily, soaks water up,
qs: Sort the four items into a group that soaks water up and a group that does not.
Which two bend easily, and which one is hard?
key: Soaks water up: the paper packet, the wooden label and the cotton twine. Does not: the plastic tray.
Bend easily: the paper packet and the cotton twine. Hard: the wooden label. The plastic tray is stiff and bends only a little, so either group can be argued for it as long as the student says why.

title: Sorting the Seed Shop Shelf
