desc: using test data to choose the material that suits a job
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The club needs little covers to put over young seedlings on cold spring nights. Three materials were tried over three nights and the trays were checked each mor
qs: Which cover should the club use?
Which two pieces of the chart make you sure?
key: the clear plastic cloche
Nearly every seedling was still standing, 23 of 24, and nearly all the light still got through. Both columns have to be used, not just one.

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: telling how a thing built from a few pieces can be taken apart and built into something new
dir: Answer out loud. You may draw if it helps.
text: The tray stand is on the lot. It is made of 6 bricks and 3 boards. They are just stacked. Nothing is holding it. The club took it down. They wanted to move it.
qs: The stand is gone. Are the bricks and boards gone too? What is lying on the ground?
Build something new in your head out of those 6 bricks and 3 boards. What is it, and how do the pieces go together?
key: No. All 6 bricks and all 3 boards are still there. They are the same pieces, just not stacked as a stand any more.

Any real thing from 6 bricks and 3 boards: a step, a bench, a path edge, a low wall, a cold frame, a ramp for a wheelbarrow. Listen for how the pieces sit on each other, because that is the evidence t

title: Taken Apart, Heated, Cooled
desc: arguing with evidence that some heating and cooling changes can be undone and some cannot
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two things happened in the kitchen next to the lot on the same morning. What happened A knob of butter was put in a warm pan and spread out into a thin yellow l
qs: Put the pan of melted butter in the refrigerator. What happens to it?
Put the cooked egg in the refrigerator. Does the white part go clear and runny again?
key: It goes hard again and is butter, in the shape of the pan.
No. It stays white and firm. Cold does not turn it back into the clear runny part.

title: The Trays That Blow Off
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking a question about it
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the note. Answer out loud.
text: The seedling trays sit on a long shelf. The shelf is against the fence. So they catch the morning sun. Spring wind comes along the fence line. It lifts the ligh
qs: What is the problem the club wants to fix? Say it in one sentence.
Ask one question that would help you fix it.
key: The wind lifts the light trays off the shelf and tips them onto the gravel. Naming the trays blowing off, not the repotting, is the problem.
Any real question: how light is a full tray, how wide is the shelf, which way does the wind come along the fence, how many trays are there, is there a lip on the shelf. A statement is not a question,

title: The Trays That Blow Off
desc: drawing a design and telling how its shape does the job
dir: Draw on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would keep the trays on the shelf in a spring wind. Still let the sun reach them. Think hard about its shape.
qs: Draw your fix.

steadfast. Accept strong or loyal with the same reasons. Any reason taken from the text: he stood calmly by what he believed and kept saying it for years, he held his people together.

-ful: full of thanks.

Nonliteral. The new bean leaves are small, green, and opening up out of the soil, so they look like little hands. (RL.3.4, nonliteral language)

1/8. One part of this row is 1/8, because the whole from 0 to 1 is cut into 8 equal parts. Partial: the fraction right with no name for one part is approaching. (3.NF.A.2)

key: 3/4. The top numbers are the same, so compare the piece sizes: fourths are bigger pieces than eighths, so 3 fourths is more than 3 eighths. Partial: naming 3/4 with no reason about the size of the pie
5/6. The pieces are the same size, so the one with more pieces is more. Partial: naming 5/6 with no reason is approaching. (3.NF.A.3)

2 1/2 inches. The strip ends halfway between 2 and 3, which is two quarter ticks past the 2. Partial: 2 inches or 3 inches rounds to a whole and is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)

Four sixths, 4/6 (3.NF.A.1). It means 4 parts, each one of size 1/6. Listen for parts of size 1/6, not just the name of the fraction. Saying it is also 2/3 is correct but is a grade 4 move and is not

title: Area of the Bed

How did it travel in observation 2?

dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: The garden has room for the long trial bed or for the square plots by the gate, but not for both. Write to the garden committee and tell them which one to keep.
key: Introduces the topic and states an opinion clearly (W.5.1a)
Creates an organizational structure in which the ideas are logically grouped and support the writer's purpose (W.5.1a)

title: Garden Writer
desc: an informative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write to teach a new gardener why one garden can hold more than one climate, and what that means for where things get planted. Use facts from the text. Write 8
key: Introduces the topic clearly and gives the reader a general observation of what is coming (W.5.2a)
Groups related information logically, with each cause developed on its own (W.5.2a)

title: Garden Writer
desc: a narrative writing piece
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: You have been watching one bed all spring and it has done nothing. This morning you get there before anybody else, and something has changed. Write the story of
key: Orients the reader by establishing a situation and introducing a narrator and characters (W.5.3a)
Organizes an event sequence that unfolds naturally (W.5.3a)

title: Ten Times and One Tenth
desc: how a digit's value changes from one place to the next in a multi-digit number
dir: Answer out loud. Say the value of the digit, not just its name.
text: The rain gauge is read to the nearest thousandth of an inch, so the chart is full of decimals. Every place on that chart is worth ten times the place on its rig
qs: In the March storm reading 3.440, the 4 in the tenths place is worth how many times the 4 in the hundredths place?
In 55.500, what is the 5 in the ones place worth compared with the 5 in the tens place?
key: 10 times. The tenths place is 0.4 and the hundredths place is 0.04, and 0.04 × 10 = 0.4. Partial: naming the two values with no comparison is approaching. (5.NBT.A.1)
One tenth as much. The ones 5 is worth 5 and the tens 5 is worth 50, and 50 ÷ 10 = 5. Partial: 10 times as much reverses the comparison and does not count. (5.NBT.A.1)

title: Unlike Pieces
desc: adding and subtracting fractions and mixed numbers with unlike denominators
dir: Work on your paper and hold it up. Show the equivalent fractions you used.
text: Every answer on this stop needs the two fractions written over the same denominator first.
key: 13/15. In fifteenths, 2/3 = 10/15 and 1/5 = 3/15, and 10/15 + 3/15 = 13/15. Or: thirtieths work too, 20/30 + 6/30 = 26/30 = 13/15. Partial: 3/8 comes from adding across and does not count. (5.NF.A.1)
17/24. In twenty-fourths, 7/8 = 21/24 and 1/6 = 4/24, and 21/24 − 4/24 = 17/24. Partial: subtracting across, numerator from numerator and denominator from denominator, does not count. (5.NF.A.1)

title: Does That Answer Make Sense?
desc: fraction word problems with unlike denominators, with benchmark estimates to check the answer
dir: For each one, say your estimate first, then work it out on your paper and hold it up.
text: Estimate before you compute. Compare each fraction to 0, to 1/2, and to 1, and say what the answer should be near.
qs: A bed is 3/4 full of compost. The class adds another 1/8 of a bed. How full is it now? Estimate first.
The gauge held 1 1/2 inches after the first storm of the week and 3/5 of an inch after the second. What is the total for the two storms? Estimate first.
key: 7/8 of a bed. Estimate: 3/4 is near 1 and 1/8 is small, so the answer should be just under 1. In eighths, 3/4 = 6/8, and 6/8 + 1/8 = 7/8. Partial: 7/8 right with no estimate made first is approaching.

2 1/10 inches. Estimate: 1 1/2 plus a bit over 1/2 should be a little over 2. In tenths, 1 1/2 = 15/10 and 3/5 = 6/10, and 15/10 + 6/10 = 21/10 = 2 1/10. Partial: 21/10 right with no mixed number give

title: A Fraction of a Fraction
desc: multiplying a fraction or whole number by a fraction, including the area of a rectangle with fractional sides
dir: Use the picture for number 4. Work the rest on your paper and hold it up.
text: The square below is one square yard, cut into fourths across and thirds down. The shaded block is the corner the class planted.
key: 8/15. Multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms: (2 × 4)/(3 × 5) = 8/15. Or: an area model of 15 parts with 8 of them shaded. (5.NF.B.4a)
9. 3/4 × 12 = 36/4 = 9. Also 12 ÷ 4 = 3, and 3 × 3 = 9. Partial: 36/4 left unsimplified is approaching. (5.NF.B.4a, a whole number times a fraction)

title: Tell a Story for the Product
desc: creating a story context for a product of a fraction and a whole number or of two fractions
dir: Tell your teacher a story that fits the multiplication. Then solve it. Show your work on paper.
qs: Tell a short story that fits (1/4) × 8. Then solve it.
Tell a short story that fits (3/5) × (1/2).
key: A story about 1/4 of 8 things. The answer is 2.
A story such as 3/5 of half a pie. The answer is 3/10.

title: Counting Cubes
desc: understanding volume as the number of unit cubes that fill a solid with no gaps or overlaps
dir: Use the picture. Answer out loud and say the unit every time.
text: The model below is built from cubes that measure 1 foot on every edge. One of those cubes is called a unit cube.
qs: What is a unit cube, and how much volume does one of them have?
How many cubes are in one layer of the model, and how many layers are there?
key: A cube that measures 1 unit on every edge. It has a volume of 1 cubic unit, and here that is 1 cubic foot. Partial: defining the cube with no volume given is approaching. (5.MD.C.3a)
12 cubes in one layer, because the base is 4 cubes by 3 cubes, and there are 2 layers. Partial: one of the layer count and the number of layers is approaching. (5.MD.C.3b)

title: Soil to Order
desc: finding volume with length times width times height, with base area times height, and for a solid made of two boxes
dir: Work on your paper and hold it up. Say the unit in every answer.
text: The long bed is being rebuilt out of two rectangular boxes that sit end to end and do not overlap.
qs: A seed box is 6 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. What is its volume?
A planter has a base area of 35 square feet and is 4 feet deep. What is its volume?
key: 72 cubic centimeters. 6 × 4 × 3 = 72. Or: 6 × 4 = 24 for the base, then 24 × 3. (5.MD.C.5a)
140 cubic feet. Volume is the base area times the height, so 35 × 4 = 140. Partial: 140 with no unit named is approaching. (5.MD.C.5b)

84 cubic meters

What are the two lines through the gate called, and what is the gate point itself called?

The horizontal line is the x-axis and the vertical line is the y-axis. The point where they meet is the origin, written (0, 0). Partial: two of the three names given is approaching. (5.G.A.1)

title: Inside the Brackets

Evaluate 2 x [15 + (9 - 4)].
key: 48. Inside the parentheses first: 14 + 6 = 20. Then 3 x 20 = 60, and 60 - 12 = 48. A student who works left to right gets 3 x 14 = 42 and lands somewhere else. Partial: 60 found by stopping before the
40. The innermost group first: 9 - 4 = 5. Then 15 + 5 = 20 inside the brackets, and 2 x 20 = 40. Partial: 20 found by stopping inside the brackets is approaching.

Write the pea weight in expanded form.
key: Four and seventy-five thousandths. The radish weight in words is four and five hundred seven thousandths. Reading 4.075 as four point zero seven five is a description of the digits, not the number nam
4.57 is 4 + 0.5 + 0.07. Writing it as (4 x 1) + (5 x 1/10) + (7 x 1/100) is correct too. Partial: one of the two places written is approaching.

Nine people share a 50 pound sack of seed potatoes equally by weight. How many pounds does each person get? Between which two whole numbers does your answer lie?
key: 3 / 4, that is 3 divided by 4. Each bed gets 3/4 of a tray. Check it the other way: 4 beds with 3/4 of a tray each is 4 x 3/4 = 3 trays, which is what there was to share. Partial: the division right w

50 / 9 = 5 and 5/9 pounds each. It lies between 5 and 6, because 9 x 5 = 45 and 9 x 6 = 54, and 50 sits between them. An answer of 5 remainder 5 is not finished: the leftover has to be shared too. Par

title: In the Watering Can
desc: using a model of particles too small to be seen to explain what happens to matter
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A scoop of blue plant food goes into a watering can. Within a minute the water is a faint even blue with no grains left at the bottom, and every bed watered fro
qs: No grains are left and the colour is even everywhere. Explain that using particles too small to see.
Why does an even mix matter to the gardener pouring from the can?
key: The grains broke apart into particles far too small to see and spread out evenly among the water particles, so the plant food is everywhere in the can at the same concentration. (5-PS1-1)
Because every bed then gets the same dose. If the plant food sat in one spot, the first bed would get too much and the last none, even though the gardener poured the same amount. (5-PS1-1)

title: In the Watering Can
desc: identifying materials from measured properties rather than from appearance
dir: Read the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Four soil samples came from different corners of the garden. The same dry amount of each was tested. Sample Mass of 100 ml, dry Holds its shape when rolled wet?
qs: Which sample is the clay? Name two results that point to it.
Which sample is the sand, and which result is the clearest giveaway?
key: B. It rolls into a firm ring and takes over five minutes to drain, both of which fit clay with its very fine particles packed close together. (5-PS1-3)
A. Water drained through it in 8 seconds, far faster than any other, which is what coarse sand grains with big gaps between them do. (5-PS1-3)

title: The Sealed Terrarium
desc: using measurements to show that total weight is conserved through heating, cooling, and mixing
dir: Read the chart. Answer out loud.
text: A class sealed three jars in March and weighed them every week until May. No jar was ever opened. Sealed jar What was inside March May 1 damp soil and two seedl
qs: The seedlings in jar 1 tripled in size. What does the jar weigh in May? Explain.
What does jar 2 weigh in May, and where is the missing pool water?
key: 655 g. The plants built themselves out of the carbon dioxide, water, and minerals already inside the sealed jar, so matter was rearranged, not added. (5-PS1-2)
390 g. The water that left the pool is on the glass as drops and in the air inside the jar as vapour, all still sealed in. (5-PS1-2)

title: The Sealed Terrarium
desc: deciding from evidence whether mixing two substances made a new substance
dir: Read the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Three mixings tried in the potting shed. Mixing What was seen a copper coin in vinegar with a pinch of salt, left two days a blue green crust on the coin that w
qs: Which two mixings made a new substance? Give the evidence for each.
Which one is only a mixture, and what is the evidence?
key: The coin in vinegar and salt, because a blue green substance formed that cannot be rinsed off and the liquid changed colour, and the baking powder in water, because a gas bubbled off and the powder wa
The sand and seeds. A sieve returned every seed whole and the sand was unchanged, so they were only mixed. (5-PS1-4)

title: Lettuce in Water
desc: arguing from measurements that plants get their material for growth from air and water
dir: Read the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Two trays of lettuce were grown side by side on the classroom bench. One sat in weighed compost, the other had its roots in plain water with a measured trace of
qs: Both trays gained about the same dry weight. What does that tell you about whether soil is needed?
The compost tray gained 93 g and lost only 4 g of compost. Where did the rest of the material come from?
key: Soil is not where the material comes from. A tray with no soil at all grew almost as much dry material as the one in compost. (5-LS1-1)
From air and water. Carbon dioxide taken in through the leaves and water taken up by the roots are built into the plant using energy from sunlight. (5-LS1-1)

title: Lettuce in Water
desc: using a model to trace the energy in an animal's food back to the sun
dir: Look at the chain. Answer out loud.
text: One path energy takes through the spring garden. → → → Caterpillars eat the new leaves. A bird feeds the caterpillars to its chicks.
qs: Trace the energy in a chick's meal back to its source.
A bird brings hundreds of caterpillars to the nest over two weeks. Explain why so many are needed.
key: From the caterpillar, which got it from the new leaves, which captured energy from sunlight and stored it in the food they made. (5-PS3-1)

Most of the energy in each caterpillar was already used up by the caterpillar itself for its own living and growing, and the chick uses most of what is left for growing, moving, and keeping warm. Only

title: The Spring Bed
desc: describing with a model how matter moves among plants, animals, decomposers, and the environment
dir: Look at the model. Answer out loud.
text: A model of one garden bed. Clover was grown over the winter and dug in before planting. From To How air and soil clover and vegetables taken in through leaves a
qs: Clover roots host bacteria that capture nitrogen from the air. Explain why a gardener would grow clover and then dig it in rather than harvest it.
Name the decomposers in this model and say what they do.
key: The nitrogen captured by the bacteria is in the clover plant. Digging it in hands that nitrogen to the decomposers, who release it into the soil where the next crop's roots can take it up. Harvesting
Worms, fungi, and bacteria in the soil. They break down dead plant material and waste into simpler substances that plants can take up again. (5-LS2-1)

title: Up and Down in the Garden
desc: arguing that the gravitational force Earth exerts on objects is directed down
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Water poured from a can falls to the bed. A string with a stone on the end hangs beside a new bean trellis so it can be set upright.
qs: Which way does the poured water travel, and which way does the stone on the string point?
A bean shoot grows upward even in the dark, away from the pull. Does that mean the pull is not acting on it? Explain.
key: Both go straight down toward the ground. (5-PS2-1)

No. The pull is still acting on it. The plant senses which way down is and grows its shoot the opposite way on purpose, using energy to do it. Growing against a force does not mean the force has gone.

title: Up and Down in the Garden
desc: describing with an example how the geosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere interact
dir: Read the story. Answer out loud.
text: The Earth system has four parts. The geosphere is rock and soil. The biosphere is living things. The hydrosphere is all the water. The atmosphere is air. A spri
qs: Name the two spheres interacting when rain carries topsoil into the ditch.
Clover was growing on one plot and the ditch beside it stayed clear. Explain that as an interaction between spheres.
key: The hydrosphere and the geosphere. Water moving across the land picks up soil and carries it somewhere else, which is erosion. The atmosphere delivered the rain. (5-ESS2-1)
Living clover, the biosphere, held the geosphere in place with its roots and slowed the rain with its leaves, so the hydrosphere soaked in rather than running off with soil in it. (5-ESS2-1)

title: Spring Sky
desc: arguing that the sun looks brightest because of how near it is, not because it gives off the most light
dir: Read the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Three stars easily seen in spring, with the light each gives off and its distance. Star Light it gives off Distance from Earth the sun 1 unit 8 light-minutes Ar
qs: Rank the three by light given off, then by how bright they look from the garden. What do you notice?
Spica gives off more than ten times the light of Arcturus but looks fainter. Explain using the distance column.
key: By light given off: Spica, then Arcturus, then the sun. By how bright they look: the sun by an enormous margin, then Arcturus, then Spica. The order is almost reversed, because of distance. (5-ESS1-1)
Spica is 250 light-years away and Arcturus is 37, so Spica is nearly seven times further. Light spreads out as it travels, and that difference in distance outweighs the difference in light given off.

title: Spring Sky
desc: finding patterns in graphed data about shadows, day length, and the night sky
dir: Read the chart. Answer out loud.
text: A 1 m stake in the bed had its noon shadow measured on the twenty-first of four months, and the sunrise direction was noted. Date Noon shadow Hours of daylight
qs: Describe the pattern across the four dates, using both the shadow and the daylight columns.
The sun rises due east on only two of these dates. What is special about those two dates?
key: As the daylight hours rise the noon shadow shortens, and they move together. The extremes are December, with the longest shadow and shortest day, and June, with the shortest shadow and longest day, an
They are the equinoxes, when day and night are about equal everywhere. On those two dates the sun rises due east and sets due west, and the daylight hours in the chart are both about 12. (5-ESS1-2)

title: Water for Growing
desc: describing the amounts and percentages of water and fresh water in Earth's reservoirs
dir: Read the charts. Answer out loud.
text: Where Earth's water is, and what the fresh part of it gets used for. All of Earth's water Share salty ocean about 97% frozen in ice and glaciers about 2% ground
qs: About what percentage of all Earth's water is fresh and liquid? Which row of the first chart is it?
Growing food takes about 70% of the fresh water people use. Why would farming need so much more than homes?
key: About 1%, which is the third row, groundwater, lakes, rivers, soil, and air together. The 2% in ice is fresh but frozen. (5-ESS2-2)
Every crop takes up and loses enormous amounts of water as it grows, far more than a person drinks or washes with, and fields cover huge areas. Food is where almost all the water goes. (5-ESS2-2)

title: Water for Growing

qs: Mowing once in late autumn instead of often gave four times as many species. Explain why the timing matters.

The hedge gives pollinating insects food and shelter close to the crop, so more flowers get pollinated and more fruit sets. It also slows the wind at the field edge, so less soil is picked up and blow

Any three criteria from the story: keeps the trays watered for seven days with nobody there, fits a windowsill forty centimetres deep, and does not leak onto the sill. (3-5-ETS1-1)

Electric light let a factory run after dark. Name one gain and one cost of that.

title: Find the Letter
desc: matching a spoken letter name to its printed form (12 cards, 6 uppercase and 6 lowercase)
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
key: Say: Here are twelve letter cards from the camp box. I will say a letter name. Point to the card with that letter.
Say: Point to the letter e. (top row, fourth card)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: First Sound Check
desc: saying the first sound of a pictured word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the first sound.
key: Model first: Lake. The first sound in lake is /l/. Now you try.
Point to the deer. Say: Deer. What is the first sound in deer? (/d/)

title: Rhyme Time
desc: making a rhyme for a given word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say a word that rhymes.
key: Model first: Camp, lamp, stamp. They rhyme. They sound the same at the end.
Point to the tent. Say: Tell me a word that rhymes with tent. (bent, went, sent, dent, zent)

title: Put It Together
desc: blending syllables and sounds into a word with picture support
dir: Listen to the slow, sleepy voice. Say the whole word.
key: Say: I am going to talk very slowly out here on the water. Put the parts together and tell me the word. The pictures can help you, but they are mixed up.
Say with a pause between the parts: ca ... noe. (canoe, the little boat in the first picture)

title: Mira Walks to the Dock
desc: questions about the character, the order of three events, and what happens next in a story read aloud
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Mira Walks to the Dock
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: This is a camp beside a lake. A dock is a wooden walkway that goes out over the water. The girl in the picture is Mira, and she i
Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Mira comes to the dock.

title: How a Pine Tree Plants Itself
desc: making an inference, making a connection, and asking a question about an informational text read aloud
dir: Listen to your teacher read about pine cones. Then answer out loud.
key: If picture supports are on, point to the picture first. Say: This shows what happens to a pine cone, in order. Top left: the cone is shut tight in the snow. Top right: the sun is out, the cone opens,

Ask: A squirrel buries more seeds than it can eat, and it does not dig up every hole again. What do you think happens to the seeds that stay in the ground? (They grow into new pine trees. The text doe

title: Sound Letters
desc: writing the letter for a beginning sound (l, t, p, b)
dir: Listen for the sound. Write the letter on your paper and hold it up.
key: Point to the first picture. Say: This is a log. Log starts with /l/. Write the letter that makes the /l/ sound. Hold it up. (l or L)
Point to the tent. Say: Tent starts with /t/. Write the letter for /t/. (t or T)

title: Label Your Pack
desc: writing letters to label a drawing
dir: Draw one thing you would pack for camp. Write letters to tell what it is. Hold it up.
key: If picture supports are on, the tent, backpack, and boots are only ideas for what to bring. The child can draw anything.
Say: Draw one thing you would put in your pack for camp. Then write a word or some letters to tell what it is. Hold it up and tell me what you wrote.

title: Name It
desc: naming objects, actions, and describing words from pictures
dir: Look at each picture. Answer out loud.
key: Picture 1. Say: What is this? (a canoe or a boat. Both count.)
Picture 2. Say: What is this? (a backpack, a pack, or a bag.)

title: Mystery Pack
desc: asking questions and follow-up questions to find out information
dir: Something is packed in the backpack. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
key: Your secret: an apple is in the pack. Do not tell.
Say: One thing is packed in this backpack. Ask me questions to find out what it is. You can ask things like: Is it alive? What do you do with it?

title: Lake or Trail
desc: sharing an opinion with a reason and details
dir: Pick one. Tell your teacher why.
key: Say: This afternoon you can paddle the canoe out on the lake, or you can hike up the trail through the pine trees. Which one would you pick? Tell me why.
Look for: tells an opinion (picks one).

title: Count the Camp
desc: counting 10 or more real objects one by one where the teacher can see, then counting groups of 11, 13, 15, and 12 objects one by one on the screen
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
key: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one

Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down

title: Number Cards
desc: naming the numerals 1 to 10
dir: Say the name of each number.
key: Say: The camp counts everything. What number is this? Click Next after each one.
Correct means the child says the number name. Write down the ones missed. Watch for 6 and 9 mixed up.

title: More or Fewer
desc: comparing two groups by counting (more, same, fewer)
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
key: Box 1. Say: Are there more logs or more fish? How do you know? (More logs. 7 logs and 4 fish.)
Box 2. Say: Are there more tents, more canoes, or the same number of each? (The same. 5 tents and 5 canoes.)

title: Sort the Stones
desc: sorting and classifying objects by color, by size, by two attributes at once, and making a rule
dir: Look at the tree stump and the pile. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the tree stump. Say: Here are the stones we picked up along the lake. How many stones are on the tree stump in all? (8)
Say: Sort them by color in your head. How many grey? How many tan? (4 grey and 4 tan)

title: Camp Chart
desc: reading, copying, and adding to a picture chart with two groups
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud. Then make marks on your paper.
key: Say: The children at camp picked what they like best, paddling the canoe or swimming at the dock. Each face is one child. How many children picked the canoe? (6)
Say: Did more children pick the canoe or swimming? (The canoe. 6 is more than 4.)

title: Name the Shapes
desc: naming, describing, and drawing circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud. Then draw a shape on your paper.
key: Say: Here is the camp, drawn with shapes. What shape is the green tent? (triangle)
Say: What shape is the blue window on the cabin? (square)

title: Where at Camp?
desc: position words (on, next to, in, above, between, near and far)
dir: Look at the camp. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Here is the whole camp. Look at the wooden dock. What is on the dock? (the canoe)
Say: What is next to the tent? (the backpack, or the pack)

title: Tallest Tree
desc: ordering five objects by height
dir: Look at the trees. Answer out loud.
key: Point to the trees. Say: Five pine trees grow along the camp trail. Which tree is the tallest? (B)
Say: Which tree is the shortest? (A)

title: What Comes Next?
desc: extending repeating patterns and naming the part that repeats
dir: Look at each row. Say what comes next.
key: Row 1. Say: Tent, pine, tent, pine, tent, pine, tent. What comes next? (a pine tree)
Row 2. Say: Look at this row. What comes next? (a fish. The pattern is fish, fish, frog, frog, and the row ends with the second frog.)

title: Uppercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 uppercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts.

title: Lowercase Letters
desc: naming all 26 lowercase letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly.
b, d, p and q are the ones to watch. Write down which way a mix-up went, such as said d for b.

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the most common sound for all 26 letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: Show one letter at a time and ask: What sound does this letter make? Mark each correct sound.
For a, e, i, o and u the short sound is what is expected. The long sound is also correct.

title: Two Lines
desc: print concepts (where to start, where to go at the end of a line, counting words and letters)
dir: Look at the two lines. Answer out loud.
text: We hike up the trail. The lake is cold. The four pictures are a boot, a pine tree, a hat, and a fish.
key: Say: I want to read this. Ask: Where do I start, at the boot, the pine tree, the hat, or the fish? (the boot. Reading starts at the top on the left.)
Say: I read the top line and I stop at the pine tree. Ask: Where do I go next? (to the hat, the start of the next line)

title: Book Parts
desc: print concepts (finding the title, where to start, which way to read, and the first and last word of a line)
dir: Look at the page. Point or answer out loud.
text: The Camp Trip We sit by the lake The sun is warm
key: Say: This is a page from a book. Point to the title. (the big words in the banner at the top: The Camp Trip. If the student cannot point on the screen, they can tell you where it is.)
Ask: Where do I start reading? Point to it. (the first word of the top line, on the left: We)

title: Rhyme and Clap
desc: hearing rhymes, making a rhyme, and clapping syllables
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
text: A dock is a wooden walkway out over the water.
key: Ask: Do lake and cake rhyme? (yes)
Ask: Do tent and pine rhyme? (no)

title: Put It Together
desc: blending spoken sounds and saying the first, last, and all sounds in a word
dir: Listen to your teacher. Answer out loud.
key: Say: Put these sounds together: /l/ /o/ /g/. (log)
Say: Put these sounds together: /t/ /e/ /n/ /t/. (tent)

title: Rosa and the Frog
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in a story read aloud to the student
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: Rosa has a map. Rosa sits on a log. The sun is up. Rosa sees a big frog. A log comes from a tree. It fell down. Then it was cut.
key: Read the four lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Ask: Who is the story about? (Rosa)
Ask: What does Rosa sit on? (a log)

title: Letter Sounds
desc: saying the sounds of letters
dir: Say the sound each letter makes.
key: The student says the most common sound for each letter: r /r/, A as in apple, s /s/, k /k/, o as in otter, N /n/, f /f/, b /b/, i as in igloo, p /p/. The letter name is not needed here.
The long sound for A, o or i is also fine. Write down any sounds that were missed.

title: Lake Words
desc: reading high-frequency words and short vowel words
dir: Read each word out loud.
text: we go see at is log pan fin hut
key: High-frequency words the student should know by sight: we, go, see, at, is
Sounds out or reads: log, pan, fin, hut

title: Listen Up
desc: answering questions about key details in a text read aloud and asking for help
dir: Put your eyes on your teacher and listen. Then answer out loud.
text: Listening time. Your teacher will read you a report from the lake camp.
key: Ask: What goes up first at camp? (the tents)
Ask: How are the tents set up? (in a half circle facing the water)

title: Tell Me More
desc: describing a familiar thing you do outside, with details
dir: Tell your teacher out loud. Use lots of details.
text: Tell me about something you like to do outside when it is warm.
key: Names the thing and tells something about it
Adds a detail when you ask: Where do you do it?

title: Little Camp Book
desc: reading a short emergent-reader book with purpose and understanding
dir: Point to each word and read it out loud.
text: I see the lake. The sun is hot. I see a log. The log is big. I see a fish. The fish can swim. I sit on the log. I like the lake.
key: Count the words the student reads correctly, out of 33, and enter the number in the box. A word the student fixes without help counts. Write down the words that were missed.
Points or tracks under each word, left to right and top to bottom

title: Frogs at the Lake
desc: asking and answering questions about key details in an informational text about frogs
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the lines. Then answer out loud.
text: A frog can hop. A frog can swim. A frog has long legs. A frog eats bugs. A frog is wet. A frog naps in the sun.
key: Read the six lines on the screen out loud to the student two times. Point under each word as you read. The student does not read them. Ask: What are two things a frog can do? (hop and swim. Lines 1 an
Ask: What kind of legs does a frog have? (long legs. Line 3.)

title: Camp Talk
desc: spoken grammar items (plural nouns, question words, position words in complete sentences)
dir: Look at the picture. Listen to your teacher. Say your answer out loud.
key: Say: One tent, two ____. (tents)
Say: One dish, two ____. (dishes)

title: Camp Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write opinion piece about sleeping in a tent or paddling a canoe
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Would you rather sleep in a tent or paddle a canoe on the lake? Draw the one you pick. Write or tell what you think and why.
key: Tells the reader what the choice is about: the tent or the canoe (W.K.1)
States an opinion, which one the student would pick. Drawing, telling, or writing all count (W.K.1)

title: Camp Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write informative piece about a frog, a deer, or a pine tree
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Pick one: a frog, a deer, or a pine tree. Draw it. Write its name. Then write or tell one true thing about it. A pine tree stays green. It is green all year. It
key: Names what the drawing and writing are about: a frog, a deer, or a pine tree. The student may say it, label the picture, or write a letter or word for it (W.K.2)
Gives at least one piece of true information about it, such as: A frog hops. A deer eats grass. A pine tree is tall (W.K.2)

title: Camp Notebook
desc: a draw-and-write story about a time outside on a warm day, told in order with a reaction
dir: Draw and write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Think of a time you were outside on a warm day. Draw what happened. Then tell what happened first and what happened next. Tell how you felt.
key: Tells about one real thing that happened, not a list of facts (W.K.3)
Tells two parts, a first and a next, in the order they happened (W.K.3)

title: The Pack List
desc: answering questions from a picture chart and from experience
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the chart. What do we use to see the trail at night?
Look at the chart. What do we cook over the fire with?
key: The flashlight. Uses the chart to answer.
The pan. Uses the chart to answer.

title: Count Out Loud
desc: counting out loud by ones and by tens
dir: Count out loud for your teacher. Start at 1.
text: Counting time. There is nothing on the screen. You cannot count it. Just count out loud for your teacher.
key: Say: Start at 1 and count as high as you can. Check: counts 1 to 20 in order with no skips.

Keeps going from 20 to 40 and gets across each new ten (29 to 30, 39 to 40). Keeps going past 50. Stop the student at 100 and write the highest number said before a mistake. The end of year goal is 10

title: How Many Logs
desc: counting objects, telling one more, and counting on from a given number
dir: Point to each log and count out loud.
qs: How many logs? Count them.
If one more log is tossed on the pile, how many will there be?
key: 8, touching or pointing to each log once. The last number said is the answer to how many.
9, said without counting the whole pile again

title: Teen Logs
desc: teen numbers as ten ones and some more ones
dir: Look at the counters. Answer out loud.
qs: How many counters in all?
This number is ten and how many more?
key: 14. The first frame is full, which is ten, and the second frame holds 4 more.
4. 14 is ten and 4 more.

title: Count On
desc: counting on from a given number and telling the number that is one more
dir: Listen to your teacher. Count out loud.
text: Count with your teacher.
key: Say: Start at 7 and keep counting up. Stop at 12. (8, 9, 10, 11, 12. The student does not go back to 1.)
Say: Start at 12 and count up to 16. (13 to 16)

title: More or Fewer
desc: comparing two groups of objects (more, fewer, the same)
dir: Look at the two groups. Answer out loud.
key: Card 1. Ask: Are there more logs or more acorns? (acorns. 8 is more than 6.)
Card 2. Ask: Which group has fewer, the frogs or the fish? (the fish. 5 is fewer than 7.)

title: One for Each
desc: matching and counting to tell which group has more, fewer, or the same
dir: Look at the boxes. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the top box. Is there an acorn for every log?
In the top box, which has more: the logs or the acorns?
key: Yes. There are 5 logs and 7 acorns, so 2 acorns are left over.
The acorns (7 is more than 5)

title: Logs on the Fire
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 10, with drawings
dir: Listen to each story. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer out loud.
text: Listening time. There is nothing on the screen. You cannot count it. You can draw a circle. Draw one for each log. Use your paper. Then count or cross out.
key: Say: 4 logs are stacked by the fire ring. 3 more get carried up. How many logs are there now? (7. 4 + 3 = 7)
Say: 9 frogs sat on the bank. Then 2 of them hopped into the water. How many frogs are still on the bank? (7. 9 - 2 = 7)

title: Two Packs
desc: breaking numbers up to 10 into two parts in more than one way
dir: Look at the logs. Put some in each pack. Answer out loud.
qs: Look at the first picture. There are 5 logs and 2 packs. Say one way to put them in the two packs. Say it like this: ____ and ____ makes 5.
Now tell me a different way to make 5.
key: Any true pair for 5: 4 and 1, 3 and 2, 2 and 3, 1 and 4, 5 and 0. The student has to say both parts.
A different true pair for 5 than the first one. Saying the same pair backwards (3 and 2, then 2 and 3) counts as different only if the student points to which pack each part goes in.

title: Split It
desc: breaking a number up to 10 into two parts in more than one way and recording each way
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Here are 7.
key: Say: Show me one way to split these 7 into two groups. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 3 + 4 = 7. (a drawing with two groups, or an equation, that makes 7)
Say: Now show me a different way. (a second pair of parts that make 7. The same two numbers in the other order do not count as different.)

title: Ten and Some More
desc: showing a number from 11 to 19 as a ten and some more and recording it
dir: Look at the picture. Draw or write on your paper. Hold it up when you finish.
text: Look at the full ten frame and the extra ones.
key: Say: Show 16 as a ten and some more. Draw it or write it with numbers, such as 16 = 10 + 6. (a drawing of a ten and 6 more, or the equation)
Ask: How many ones are left after the ten? (6)

title: Tall and Long
desc: comparing two objects to tell which has more or less of an attribute and describing the difference
dir: Look at the two trees and the two paddles. Answer out loud.
text: Both trees stand on the same ground line, and both paddles start at the same dotted line, so you can see which one is bigger.
key: Ask: Which pine tree is taller? (Tree 2)
Ask: Which pine tree is shorter? (Tree 1)

title: Heavy or Light
desc: comparing two objects by weight to say which is heavier and which is lighter
dir: Look at the scales. Answer out loud.
text: A B
key: Ask: Look at scale A. Which one is heavier? (the bear. It is on the side that goes down.)
Ask: Which one is lighter? (the frog)

title: Sort and Count
desc: sorting objects into groups, counting each group, and comparing the counts
dir: Look at the forest finds. Count out loud.
qs: How many acorns? How many pine cones? How many leaves?
Which group has the most?
key: 4 acorns, 3 pine cones, 2 leaves
The acorns (4)

title: Where Is It
desc: naming shapes and telling where they are (above, below, beside)
dir: Look at the shapes. Answer out loud.
qs: Name each shape.
Which shape is above the square?
key: Circle, square, triangle, rectangle
The red circle

title: Flat or Solid
desc: telling flat shapes from solid shapes
dir: Look at each card. Say flat or solid.
qs: Is card 1, the acorn, flat or solid?
Is card 2, the triangle, flat or solid?
key: Solid. You could pick it up and hold it.
Flat. It is drawn on the card.

title: What Living Things Need
desc: telling what plants and animals need to stay alive
dir: Look at each row. Answer out loud.
text: A pine tree and a turtle both live at the lake. Living things need certain things to stay alive.
qs: A pine tree needs two of these to live. Which two? Water, sunlight, or a whistle?
A turtle needs two of these. Which two? Food, water, or a flashlight?
key: water and sunlight. A whistle is not something a pine tree needs.
food and water. A flashlight is not something a turtle needs.

title: A Week of Summer Weather
desc: describing a weather pattern from a week of observations
dir: Look at the week of weather. Answer out loud.
text: Here is one week of weather at the lake camp. Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri Sat
qs: How many days were sunny?
How many days were not sunny?
key: 2, the cloudy day and the rainy day

title: A Week of Summer Weather
desc: telling how a living thing changes its surroundings to get what it needs
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The campers find a scooped hollow in the sandy bank by the water.
qs: A turtle dug the hollow in the sand and laid her eggs in it, then covered them over. Did the turtle change the sandy bank, or did the sandy bank change the turtle?
Tell me one way you change the ground or the sand when you play outside.
key: The turtle changed the sandy bank. There is a hollow full of eggs that was not there before.
Any sensible answer about changing a space on purpose: digging a hole, piling sand into a wall, clearing sticks off a spot to sit, making a path with stones.

title: Homes, Reports and the Lake
desc: matching animals to the places that give them what they need
dir: Match each animal to the place it lives. Answer out loud.
text: Animals live at the camp. Each one lives in one place. It gets what it needs. Here are the places. A hollow in a tall tree. It is up high. A nest under the wood
qs: Where does the owl live?
Where does the mouse live?
key: a hollow high in a tall tree. Accept a hole in a tree.
a nest under the woodpile. Accept under a log or in the ground.

title: Homes, Reports and the Lake
desc: telling what a weather forecast is for
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Every morning the camp leader reads the weather report out loud before anyone takes a canoe onto the lake.
qs: Why does she read the weather report first? To find out if a thunderstorm is coming so the group can stay off the water, or to find out how deep the lake is?
What should the group do if a thunderstorm is coming?
key: to find out if a thunderstorm is coming so the group can stay off the water.
Any sensible answer: stay on shore, wait until it passes, keep the canoes in.

title: Homes, Reports and the Lake
desc: telling one way people can take better care of the land and water
dir: Answer out loud.
text: After lunch the camp pans have to be washed.
qs: One camper tips the soapy dishwater straight into the lake. Another camper carries it over to the drain by the camp sink. Which choice takes better care of the lake?
Tell me one more way to take care of the lake or the woods.
key: carrying it to the drain by the camp sink
Any sensible answer: pack the trash out, keep soap out of the water, stay on the trail so plants are not trampled, put the fire all the way out, do not pick every flower.

title: Pushes and Pulls at Camp
desc: telling a push from a pull, and comparing a strong push with a gentle one
dir: Answer out loud. Do not say push or pull for the student.
text: A push moves something away from you. A pull brings it toward you.
qs: You pull the tent rope tight before you tie it. Is that a push or a pull?
You throw the beach ball across the water to a friend. Is that a push or a pull?
key: a pull
a push

title: Pushes and Pulls at Camp
desc: deciding whether a change made a thing move farther or in a new direction
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The campers gave the same beach ball the same push in two places and counted the steps it rolled. Where it rolled How far it rolled the smooth dock 10 steps the
qs: Which place let the ball roll farther?
A canoe is drifting away from the dock. You catch the rope and pull it toward you. Which way does the canoe move now?
key: the smooth dock, 10 steps
toward you, back to the dock. The pull changes the direction it was drifting.

title: Sun and Shade at the Lake
desc: telling what sunlight does to the ground and to the things on it
dir: Answer out loud. If you can, touch a sunny spot and a shady spot together first.
text: Two flat stones sit by the water all afternoon. One is out in the open. One is under the pine trees.
qs: Which stone is warmer by the end of the afternoon, the one in the open or the one under the pines?
What made that stone warm?
key: the one in the open
the sun. Accept sunlight or the sun shining on it.

title: Sun and Shade at the Lake
desc: designing and drawing something that keeps a spot cooler
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: The camp water jug is here. It sits in the open sun. The water inside turns warm. It is warm by noon. Draw something to put the jug in the shade, like a canvas
qs: Draw your shade cover over the water jug.
Tell me how your cover keeps the water cooler.
key: Any cover drawn ABOVE the jug. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one still counts. A cover drawn beside the jug is partial: ask where the sun is coming from.
Something like: it blocks the sun, the sun cannot shine on the jug, it keeps the jug in a shadow.

title: Solving a Camp Problem
desc: naming a problem people want to fix and asking about it
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem? The wind blows the loose pages out, or the pencils are yellow?
Ask me one question that would help you fix it.
key: The wind blows the loose pages out of the book.
Any real question: how strong is the wind, how many loose pages are there, does the pocket close, could the book go inside the tent. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Solving a Camp Problem
desc: drawing something whose shape would solve the problem
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up.
text: Draw something that would keep the pages from blowing away, like a smooth stone laid on top, a clip on the edge, or a pack that zips shut.
qs: Draw your fix.
Tell me what you drew and how it holds the pages down.
key: Anything that would hold paper against wind: a stone or other weight, a clip, a band, a zipped bag or pack, a lid, a box. The three examples are in the direction, so copying one earns credit.
Naming it is what shows intent. Something like: the stone is heavy so the wind cannot lift the page, the zipper closes the wind out.

title: Solving a Camp Problem
desc: comparing test results from two fixes for the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: The campers tried two fixes and counted the pages that blew away each afternoon. Fix Pages that blew away a stone laid on top 2 a band around the book 7
qs: Which fix worked better?
How do you know?
key: the stone laid on top
Because only 2 pages blew away with the stone and 7 blew away with the band. The reason has to come from the chart, not from liking stones.

title: Camp Rules and Doing Right
desc: following rules, knowing what happens when they are broken, and naming a fair choice
dir: Listen, then answer out loud.
qs: What did Lena choose to do? Take an extra turn, or wait because it was not her turn?
One camp rule is stay with a buddy at the water. What might happen if a camper did not follow that rule?
key: She waited, because it was not her turn.
Nobody would know where that camper was, and a leader would have to stop the swim to go look. Any real consequence counts.

title: A Map of the Camp
desc: telling land from water on a map, using position words, reading a map symbol, and planning a map of a familiar place
dir: Look at the map. Answer out loud.
text: Here is a map of the lake camp. the tents the pine woods the lake
qs: Which part of this map is water? How can you tell?
The tents are on the left side of the map. The pine woods are on the right side. Which one is on the right?
key: The blue part. Maps show water in blue.
the pine woods

title: Left and Right
desc: telling where things are with left and right, near and far, and in front and behind
dir: Look at each picture. Point or answer out loud.
text: A B C
key: Ask: Look at picture A. Point to the one on the left. (the tent)
Ask: Point to the one on the right. (the fish)

title: The Flag and Long Ago
desc: recognizing the flag as a symbol of the country
dir: Answer out loud.
qs: Point to our country's flag and tell me what we call it.
A flag is a symbol. That means it stands for something. What does our flag stand for?
key: the flag. Accept the American flag or the flag of the United States.
our country. Accept the United States or America. Accept all of us or everybody here if the student explains it means the country.

title: The Flag and Long Ago
desc: telling what a holiday honors and how life long ago was different from life today
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Long ago there were no electric lights at a camp.
qs: What did people long ago use to see after dark, a lantern with a flame or a light switch on the wall?
What do you use to see after dark today?
key: a lantern with a flame. Accept a candle or a campfire.
Any real answer: a lamp, a light switch, a flashlight, a phone. Naming today's way is the then-and-now half of this standard.

title: Lake Sound Check
desc: blending, segmenting, and isolating sounds, counting syllables, and telling long from short vowels in spoken words
dir: Listen to your teacher. Say the sounds and words out loud.
text: Listen. Then say it.
key: Blend these sounds: /d/ /o/ /k/ (dock)
Blend these sounds: /p/ /ie/ /n/ (pine)

title: First Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the initial sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the first sound.
qs: What is the first sound in zip?
What is the first sound in dog?
key: The sound /z/. Say the sound, not the letter name.
The sound /d/. Say the sound, not the letter name.

title: Middle Sound
desc: isolating and pronouncing the medial vowel sound in spoken single-syllable words
dir: Listen to the word. Say just the middle sound.
qs: What is the middle sound in pin?
What is the middle sound in hot?
key: The short vowel sound /i/.
The short vowel sound /o/.

title: Camp Words
desc: reading words with digraphs, blends, final e, vowel teams, r-controlled vowels, endings, and two syllables
dir: Read each word out loud. The last one is a silly word. Just sound it out.
key: Count each word read correctly. blape is a silly word: listen for the long a that the final e makes.

Watch for: ch digraph (chip), nk ending (bunk), blend plus a vowel team (float), blend plus double letters (grill), final e (pine), igh (high), blend plus ee team (creek), blend plus r-controlled ar (

title: How Many Parts?
desc: using the rule that every syllable has a vowel sound to find the number of syllables in a printed word
dir: Read the word to yourself. Tell how many syllables, or parts, it has. Clap it if that helps.
text: napkin map happy jump
key: Point to “napkin”. How many syllables? (2)
Point to “map”. How many syllables? (1)

title: Morning on the Lake
desc: a 70-word lake camp story read aloud
dir: Look at the three pictures. Then read the story out loud in your best reading voice.
text: ducks on the water the camp pan your boots Morning on the Lake The lake is flat and still when I wake up. I pull on my boots. I walk down to the dock. No one el
key: 70 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Point to the three pictures first so ducks, pan, and boots are clear before the student reads.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: ducks on the water the camp pan your boots Morning on the Lake The lake is flat and still when I wake up. I pull on my boots. I walk down to the dock. No one el
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe
After the second reading ask: “What was the story about? What happened first?” (a summary or answer that matches the text on the screen)

title: Teo's Paddle
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about a story the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the story. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: Teo's Paddle Teo made a paddle. He made it in the camp workshop. He used a flat board. He added a long handle. He sanded the edges. Soon they were smooth. He ca
qs: What did Teo make?
What was it made of?
key: A paddle
A flat board and a long handle

title: Sentence Spotter
desc: finding sentences by their first word, capital letter, and end mark
dir: Look at the sentences. Answer out loud.
text: The canoe is ready. Can you carry the paddle?
qs: How many sentences do you see? How can you tell?
Read the first word of the second sentence. What kind of letter does it start with?
key: 2 sentences. Each one starts with a capital letter and ends with an end mark
The word is Can. It starts with a capital, or uppercase, C

title: Camp Fix It
desc: spoken grammar items (past tense, plural nouns, subject and verb match, joining two sentences, describing words, place words)
dir: Listen to your teacher read each one. Say your answer out loud.
qs: Today we hike up the trail. Last night we ____.
One tent, two ____.
key: hiked
tents

title: Which Word Fits?
desc: using indefinite pronouns such as everyone, anyone, someone, something, and nothing
dir: Listen to the sentence. Say the word that fits.
qs: Which word fits? ___ in the bag is red. (Everything / Someone)
Which word fits? ___ came to the party, so the room was empty. (Nobody / Everybody)
key: Everything. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)
Nobody. (Say the whole sentence with the word. Other correct pronouns that make sense also count.)

title: Whose Is It?
desc: using possessive nouns to show who owns something
dir: Listen. Say the answer. For the last one, you can point to the right one on paper.
qs: Ben has a kite. Whose kite is it?
The teacher has a pen. Whose pen is it?
key: Ben’s kite. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)
the teacher’s pen. (an apostrophe and s shows ownership)

title: Commands and Big Feelings
desc: producing imperative (command) and exclamatory sentences in response to prompts
dir: Listen. Say your answer out loud in a full sentence.
qs: Tell a friend to wash their hands. Say it as a command.
You get a surprise present! Say one sentence that shows a big feeling.
key: A command such as “Wash your hands.”
An exclamation, for example “Wow, I love it!”

title: Print the Alphabet
desc: printing all upper- and lowercase letters
dir: On your paper, print each big letter and its small letter. Print them in order. Hold up your paper when you finish.
text: A a B b C c D d E e F f G g H h I i J j K k L l M m N n O o P p Q q R r S s T t U u V v W w X x Y y Z z
key: Look at the paper. Mark each letter pair where both the capital and the small letter are formed correctly and sit on the line. Letters may be uneven. Count a pair when each letter can be told from the
Check the tall letters (b, d, f, h, k, l, t), the letters that drop below the line (g, j, p, q, y), and the look-alikes (b and d, p and q).

title: Listen Up
desc: asking and answering questions about a text read aloud
dir: Listen carefully. Your teacher will read about how people made canoes long ago. Then answer out loud.
text: Listen.
key: Ask: What did people make a canoe out of? (one single tree, a big straight log)
Ask: What did they do to the log? (hollowed out the middle, a little at a time, until the walls were thin and even)

title: Tell Me About It
desc: describing a thing with relevant details
dir: Talk for about one minute. Speak clearly.
text: Tell me about something you can see or hear outside early in the morning. What is it? What does it look like? What does it sound like? How do you feel when you
key: Names the thing and gives 2 or more details about it (SL.1.4)
Gives 2 or more details about what it looks like or sounds like, and they stay on this one thing (SL.1.4)

title: Two-Step Directions
desc: giving, restating, and following simple two-step directions
dir: Listen to your teacher. Do what you hear, say it back, and give a direction of your own.
text: Listen carefully. Do what your teacher says. You need a pencil and paper.
key: Say once, without repeating: “Stomp your feet three times, then sit down.” (does both steps, in the right order)
Say once, without repeating: “Put your hand on your head, then hop one time.” (does both steps, in the right order)

title: Person, Place, Thing, Event
desc: describing a person, a place, a thing, and an event with relevant details, and saying ideas and feelings clearly
dir: Listen to your teacher. Tell about each one. Use lots of details.
text: Tell about a person, a place, a thing, and something that happened.
key: Say: “Tell me about someone you like to play with.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the person, such as who they are, what they look like, or what they do)
Say: “Tell me about a store or a park near your home.” (gives at least 2 relevant details about the place, such as what is there or what you do there)

title: Why Pines Stay Green
desc: asking and answering key detail questions about an informational text the student read
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about pine trees. Then answer out loud.
text: Why Pines Stay Green Most trees drop all their leaves. They do it when the cold comes. A pine tree does not. Its leaves are thin, hard needles. Each needle has
qs: What do most trees do when the cold comes?
What are a pine tree's leaves like?
key: They drop all their leaves
Thin, hard needles with a waxy coat

title: Pack for the Lookout
desc: using a provided chart to answer a question in writing
dir: Look at the chart. Write 1 sentence on your paper and hold it up.
text: The group wants to hike up to the lookout and walk back after the sun goes down. What will they take? Use the chart.
key: Finds the answer in the chart. Your help is fine: read the two columns out loud and point to the row headings
Writes a sentence drawn from the chart, such as: They will take the flashlight

title: Remember and Tell
desc: recalling information from experiences to answer a question
dir: Think about what happened to you. Tell your teacher your answer out loud. You can draw it, too.
qs: Think about a time you helped someone. Tell me what you did.
Think about getting ready for bed. Tell me two things you do.
key: Tells one real time and what they did.
Gives two real things the student does at bedtime. Any true answer counts. (They may draw first, then tell. Write down what they say if you want a record.)

title: Camp Journal
desc: an opinion piece about how to spend an afternoon at camp
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Would you rather spend the afternoon swimming at the dock, or hiking up to the lookout? Write what you think and tell why. swimming at the dock hiking to the lo
key: Names the topic: swimming at the dock or hiking to the lookout (W.1.1)
States an opinion, which one the student would pick (W.1.1)

title: Camp Journal
desc: an informative piece about one thing at camp
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Pick one: a canoe, a campfire, or a pine tree. Write what it is and tell a reader two true things about it. a canoe a campfire a pine tree Write 2 or 3 sentence
key: Names the topic: the canoe, the campfire, or the pine tree (W.1.2)
Gives at least one true fact about it (W.1.2)

title: Camp Journal
desc: a narrative about a day the student spent outside, told in order
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up and tell your teacher what you wrote.
text: Write about a day you spent outside. Tell two things that happened, in order. Use the words first and then. End by telling how it felt. the day where you went h
key: Tells about two or more things that happened, in an order that makes sense (W.1.3)
Includes some detail about what happened, not just a list (W.1.3)

title: Count the Woodpile
desc: counting, reading, and writing numerals to 120 and counting objects
dir: Count and read out loud. Write your numbers on your paper and hold it up.
text: The camp counts every log before it goes on the rack.
qs: Count out loud from 95 to 112.
Read these numbers out loud: 73, 106, 119.
key: Seventy-three, one hundred six, one hundred nineteen

title: Log Hops
desc: counting on and counting back or up to add and subtract
dir: Count out loud like you are hopping from log to log. Say each answer.
text: There is nothing on the screen. You cannot count it. Every hop is one number you say out loud.
qs: Start at 9. Count on 5. Where do you land? What adding sentence is that?
Start at 16. Count back 4. Where do you land? What take away sentence is that?

title: Smart Adding
desc: using turn-around facts and making ten as strategies to add
dir: Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: Nothing here to count. Every number you need is in the question.
qs: 7 + 8 = 15. So what is 8 + 7?
Luz says 5 + 9 is easier if she turns it around and thinks 9 + 5. Is that OK? What is the total?
key: 15. Knows it without counting because the two numbers just switch places
Yes, that is fine. The order does not change the total. Both make 14

title: Camp Problems
desc: addition and subtraction word problems within 20, with the unknown in different places
dir: Listen to each story problem. You can draw on your paper. Say your answer.
text: Listen to each problem. There is nothing to count on the screen, so use your paper.
qs: The woodpile had 7 logs. Teo carried up 6 more. How many logs are there now?
16 frogs sat on the bank. Then 7 of them hopped into the water. How many frogs are still on the bank?

title: Bundles of Ten
desc: place value in two-digit numbers (bundles of ten and leftover ones)
dir: Look at the blocks. Answer out loud.
text: A full bundle holds 10 logs. A long block stands for one full bundle of ten, and a small cube stands for one loose log.
qs: Look at the picture. How many full bundles of ten do you see, and how many loose logs? What number is that?
In the number 18, what does the 1 stand for? What does the 8 stand for?
key: 4 bundles of ten and 2 loose. That is 42
The 1 stands for one ten, which is ten logs. The 8 stands for eight ones

title: Add Up the Camp
desc: adding within 100 (a two-digit number plus a one-digit number and plus a multiple of ten)
dir: Solve each one on your paper. Say your answer and tell how you got it.
text: The crew counts the logs rack by rack.
qs: The first rack holds 34 logs. The crew adds 5 more. How many now?
The second rack holds 52 logs. The crew adds 30 more. How many now?
key: 39 (34 + 5 = 39. Only the ones change)
82 (52 + 30 = 82. Adding tens to tens: 5 tens and 3 tens is 8 tens)

title: Take Away Tens
desc: subtracting multiples of ten from multiples of ten within 100
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, tell how you know.
text: Every bundle that comes off the rack takes ten logs away.
qs: There are 80 logs on the rack. Three bundles of ten come off. 80 - 30 is what?
key: 50 (8 tens take away 3 tens is 5 tens)

title: Explain Your Adding
desc: adding within 100 with a drawing, relating it to a written equation, and explaining the reasoning with tens and ones
dir: Solve on your paper. Draw tens and ones. Write the equation. Then tell how you added.
qs: Add 52 + 9. Draw tens and ones, write the equation, and tell how you added.
Why did you add the tens with the tens and the ones with the ones?
key: 52 + 9 = 61. The drawing shows tens and ones, the equation matches, and the explanation says tens were added to tens and ones to ones (and that ten ones were made into a new ten when needed).
Because tens are worth ten and ones are worth one. They are different amounts, so like parts go together.

title: Measure the Paddle
desc: measuring length as a whole number of same-size units laid end to end
dir: Look at the blocks under the paddle and the log. Answer out loud.
qs: How many blocks long is the paddle?
How many blocks long is the log?
key: 6 blocks
4 blocks

title: Camp Clock
desc: telling and writing time to the hour and the half hour
dir: Look at each clock. Say the time out loud. Write the last one on your paper.
text: The clock in the camp kitchen keeps everyone on time.
key: Clock A: 3:00, said as three o'clock. The minute hand is on the 12.
Clock B: 7:30, said as seven thirty or half past seven. Watch for a student who says eight thirty because the hour hand has moved halfway to the 8.

title: Fair Shares
desc: halves and fourths of circles and rectangles, and knowing that equal shares must be the same size
dir: Look at the three shapes. Answer out loud.
qs: Shape A is cut into 2 equal parts. What do we call one of those parts?
Shape B is cut into 4 equal parts. What do we call one of those parts?
key: A half, or one half. Two of them make the whole circle
A fourth, or a quarter. Four of them make the whole square

title: Log Tally
desc: reading a graph with three categories and answering how many more and how many in all
dir: Look at the graph. Answer out loud.
text: The crew counted the logs they carried up on three mornings and made this graph.
qs: How many logs were carried on Tuesday?
Which morning had the fewest logs?
key: Wednesday, with 5

title: Make a Graph
desc: organizing and representing data with up to three categories, and answering questions about the total and about how many more or less
dir: Look at the list. Make a tally chart or a picture graph on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: Ten kids told us their ways kids get to school. bus car walk bus bus car bus walk bus car
key: A chart or graph with walk 2, bus 5, car 3. Each item is counted once. Tally marks, pictures, or squares all work. Labels are on each group.
10 (the total of all three groups)

title: Copy a Crab Claw
desc: naming the job an animal body part does, then designing a tool that copies it to solve a human problem
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer the first out loud. Draw the second on your paper and hold it up.
text: A crab has a claw. It is made of two curved halves. They close on each other. It can pick up something small. The thing may be slippery. It can hold on to it. I
qs: How do two curved halves closing on each other hold something better than one flat spoon does?
Draw a tool for the cook that copies the crab's claw.
key: They close from both sides at once, so the thing is held between them and cannot slide out. Any answer about gripping from both sides counts.
Any two sided gripping tool: tongs, pincers, two sticks joined at one end, a clamp, a clip. One flat spoon is partial, so ask how many sides a claw grips from.

title: Duck and Ducklings
desc: finding a pattern in what a parent animal does and what the young do in answer, and saying how it helps the young
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What do the ducklings do every single time the duck stops walking?
In what order do the ducklings go into the water?
key: They stop too. Every single time is what makes it a pattern.
The same order they walked in, one after another behind her.

title: Duck and Ducklings
desc: making observations that young plants and animals are like their parents but not exactly like them
dir: Look at the pictures. Answer out loud.
text: Two sunflowers grown from seed off the same parent plant. A young turtle and the turtle that is its parent.
qs: Both sunflowers came from the same parent plant, but one grew much taller. Are they both still sunflowers? Say why.
Name one way both sunflowers are like the plant they came from.
key: Yes. Plants from the same parent are like it and like each other, but not exactly the same, and height is one of the things that can differ.
Both have a tall stem, big leaves, and a round yellow flower head. Any likeness counts.

title: Sunset at the Lake
desc: finding a pattern in a log of sky observations and using it to predict what comes next
dir: Look at the log. Answer out loud.
text: The camp keeper wrote down the time the sun went behind the far shore, once a week for four weeks in late summer. Week Time the sun went down first week 8:41 se
qs: Is the sun going down earlier or later as the weeks go by?
How many minutes earlier does it go down each week?
key: earlier each week
8 minutes earlier each week

title: Sunset at the Lake
desc: relating the number of hours of daylight to the time of year from observations made across a year
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
text: Hours of daylight at the lake, counted on one day in each of four months. Month Hours of daylight June 15 August 13 October 11 December 9
qs: Which month on the chart had the longest daylight?
What is happening to the hours of daylight as the months go from June to December?
key: June, 15 hours
They are going down, two fewer hours each time.

title: Sound at the Water
desc: planning an investigation showing that a shaking material makes sound and that a sound can make a material shake
dir: If you have an empty bottle, try the first part. Either way, answer out loud.
text: Blow hard across the open top of an empty bottle until it hoots. Then put your hand flat on your own throat and hum a long low note. Now stand a cup of water on
qs: When the bottle hoots, what is shaking to make that sound: the glass, or the air inside it?
What do you feel under your hand while you hum, and what happens to it when you stop?
key: The air inside it. Blowing across the top sets the air shaking, and the shaking air makes the hoot.
A buzzing or a tickle. It stops the moment the humming stops, which shows the shaking and the sound go together.

title: The Dark Boathouse
desc: accounting for why an object in darkness can be seen only when light shines on it
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The boathouse has no window. When both doors are pulled shut, it is completely dark inside.
qs: A big striped beach ball is sitting in the middle of the dark boathouse. Can you see it? Say why or why not.
What would someone have to do before the ball could be seen in there?
key: No. No light gets into the boathouse, and a thing can only be seen when light shines on it and comes back to your eyes.
Light has to reach it: a flashlight, a lamp, or a door opened so daylight comes in.

title: The Dark Boathouse
desc: using test results to tell what happens when different materials are put in the path of a beam of light
dir: Look at the test results. Answer out loud.
text: One flashlight beam was pointed at four things in the boathouse and what it did was written down. What was put in the beam What the beam did a jar of clear lake
qs: Which thing stopped the beam altogether?
Which thing let a soft coloured light through?
key: the thick dock board
the cloth of the beach umbrella

title: Dock to Raft
desc: designing a device that uses light or sound to send a message over a distance too far to shout
dir: Draw your answer on your paper. Then answer out loud.
text: The swimming raft is far out. It sits on the lake. A shout comes from the dock. It is swallowed up. That happens before it gets there. Waving an arm is easy to
qs: Draw a device on the dock that tells the swimmers on the raft that it is time to come in. It has to use light or sound.
Point to your drawing and tell me if it signals with light or with sound.
key: Any device that carries light or sound out over the water: a whistle, a horn, a bell, a bright lamp, a lamp flashed on and off.
Names it and says which one it uses.

title: Fix the Blowing Cups
desc: naming a problem people want to change, asking a question about it, and saying what to observe first
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then answer out loud.
qs: What is the problem the camp wants to change?
Ask me one question that would help you understand the problem better.
key: The breeze blows the empty paper cups off the picnic table.
Any real question: how strong is the breeze, which way does it come from, are the cups empty or full, how heavy is a cup, how many blow off. A statement is not a question, so ask once more.

title: Fix the Blowing Cups
desc: making a simple drawing of a fix and explaining how the shape of the object makes it work
dir: Draw your answer on your paper and hold it up. Then answer out loud.
text: Draw something that keeps the empty cups on the table in the breeze.
qs: Draw your fix on the picnic table.
Point to the part that holds the cup and tell me its shape.
key: Any real fix: a tray with round holes the cups drop into, a rack, a lid that clips on, a weight dropped in each cup, a rim round the edge of the table, a box the cups sit in until they are filled.
Names a shape: a round hole the cup sits in, a deep box, a rim along the edge, a clip.

title: Which Holder Worked
desc: comparing the data from tests of two objects built to solve the same problem
dir: Look at the chart. Answer out loud.
