qs: How long is Ribbon A?
How long is Ribbon B?
key: 2 1/2 inches. The ribbon ends on the half-inch mark between 2 and 3. Partial: 2 inches or 3 inches rounds to a whole and is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)
3 3/4 inches. The ribbon ends on the last small mark before 4. Partial: 4 inches rounds to a whole and is approaching. (3.MD.B.4)

title: Plot It
desc: showing measurement data on a line plot marked in fourths of an inch, and reading the plot
dir: Tell your teacher where each X goes. Your teacher will click for you.
text: Four more ribbons were measured. Put all six ribbons on the line plot. Ribbon C D E F Length in inches 3 2 1/4 3 3
qs: Where does the X go for each ribbon: A, B, C, D, E, and F?
Which length has the most Xs above it? How many ribbons were that long?
key: How to mark: click above a number on the line plot to add an X as the student tells you. Use Undo last X to fix a click.

Six Xs in all: one above 2 1/4 for Ribbon D, one above 2 1/2 for Ribbon A, three stacked above 3 for Ribbons C, E, and F, and one above 3 3/4 for Ribbon B. If A or B was measured wrong, count the X as

title: Tile the Display Floor
desc: relating the area of a rectangle to multiplication and addition
dir: Answer out loud. For numbers 3 and 6, write your work on your paper and hold it up.
text: The crew lays square tiles under the display tables so the showcase has a dry floor. Every tile is 1 square meter.
qs: Look at the tiled corner. How many tiles cover it? Write the multiplication equation that matches the picture.
A banner is 4 meters tall and 9 meters long. What is its area? Say the unit.
key: 35 tiles. 5 × 7 = 35, or 7 × 5 = 35. The picture shows 5 rows of 7 tiles. Partial: the count right with no multiplication equation written is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)
36 square meters. 4 × 9 = 36. The unit has to be square meters, not meters. Partial: 36 with no square unit named is approaching. (3.MD.C.7)

title: Cut the Panels
desc: cutting shapes into parts with equal areas and naming one part as a unit fraction of the whole
dir: Look at the panels. Answer out loud. Tell how you know.
text: The art class paints flat panels for the gate. Each panel is cut into parts. Every painter gets the same amount of panel to work on.
qs: Panel A is cut into 8 parts with equal areas. What fraction of the whole panel is one part?
Panel B is cut into equal strips. What fraction of the whole panel is one strip?
key: 1/8. The panel is cut into 8 parts with the same area, so one part is 1 of 8 equal parts of the whole. Partial: 8 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.G.A.2)
1/3. There are 3 equal strips, so one strip is 1/3 of the panel. Partial: 3 given with no fraction form is approaching. (3.G.A.2)

title: What a Product Means
desc: interpreting a product as a number of equal groups and describing a context for one
dir: Look at the array. Answer out loud.
text: The felt squares for the tables are laid out in rows on the gate table.
qs: Write a multiplication for this array and tell me what each number stands for.
What does 5 x 7 mean? Tell a showcase story for it.
key: Say: Write a multiplication for this array and tell me what each number stands for. (6 x 4 = 24. The 6 is the number of rows and the 4 is how many squares are in each row. 4 x 6 = 24 is right too if t
Say: What does 5 x 7 mean? Tell me a showcase story for it. (5 groups of 7, such as 5 boxes with 7 programs in each box, 35 programs in all. The story has to have equal groups.)

title: What a Quotient Means
desc: interpreting a quotient as the size of each share and as the number of shares

qs: The 48 name cards are shared out equally among the 6 tables. What does 48 divided by 6 tell you here?
Here is a different story with the same numbers. The 48 cards go into piles of 6. Now what does 48 divided by 6 tell you?
key: Say: The 48 name cards are shared out equally among the 6 tables. What does 48 divided by 6 tell you here? (8, and here the 8 is how many cards go on each table. The number of shares is given and the

Say: Here is a different story with the same numbers. The 48 cards go into piles of 6. Now what does 48 divided by 6 tell you? (8 again, but now the 8 is the number of piles. The size of each share is

title: Two Step Problems
desc: two-step word problems written as equations with a letter, checked for reasonableness
dir: Write an equation with a letter for the unknown. Solve it and hold up your paper.
text: Use a letter for the number you do not know yet.
qs: The crew printed 120 programs. They handed out 45 in the morning and 38 in the afternoon. How many are left?
Round each number to the nearest ten and check that your answer is reasonable.
key: Say: The crew printed 120 programs. They handed out 45 in the morning and 38 in the afternoon. How many are left? (p = 37. One equation: 120 - 45 - 38 = p. Adding first, 45 + 38 = 83 and 120 - 83 = 37

Say: Round each number to the nearest ten and check that your answer is reasonable. (120 - 50 - 40 = 30. The exact answer 37 is close to 30, so it is reasonable. An answer like 137 or 7 would not be.)

title: Round It
desc: rounding whole numbers to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Round in your head. Say the number you land on.
qs: Round 347 to the nearest ten.
Round 347 to the nearest hundred.
key: Say: Round 347 to the nearest ten. (350. 347 is between 340 and 350, and the 7 ones carry it up.)
Say: Round 347 to the nearest hundred. (300. 347 is between 300 and 400, and 47 is less than 50.)

title: Parts of One Banner
desc: naming a unit fraction and reading a fraction as a number of copies of the unit fraction
dir: Look at the bar. It is one whole banner. Answer out loud.
qs: How many equal parts is the banner cut into, and what do we call one of those parts?
What fraction is shaded? Say it as a number of copies of one eighth.
key: Say: How many equal parts is the banner cut into, and what do we call one of those parts? (8 equal parts, and one part is 1/8 of the banner.)
Say: What fraction is shaded? Say it as a number of copies of one eighth. (3/8, which is three copies of 1/8.)

title: Find It on the Line
desc: locating a unit fraction and a fraction a/b on a number line from 0 to 1
dir: Look at the number line from 0 to 1. Answer out loud.
qs: The space from 0 to 1 is cut into equal parts. How many parts, and what fraction is one of those parts?
What fraction does the dot stand for?
key: Say: The space from 0 to 1 is cut into equal parts. How many parts, and what fraction is one of those parts? (6 equal parts, and one part is 1/6.)
Say: What fraction does the dot stand for? (4/6. It sits 4 parts along from 0, so it is 4 copies of 1/6. Saying 2/3 is also correct and worth a note.)

title: Same Size or Not
desc: equivalent fractions and comparing fractions with the same numerator
dir: Look at the two bars. They are the same whole banner. Answer out loud.
qs: Bar A shows 1/2 and Bar B shows 2/4. Are they equal? How do you know?
Which is greater, 3/4 of a banner or 3/8 of the same banner? Why?
key: Say: Bar A shows 1/2 and Bar B shows 2/4. Are they equal? How do you know? (Yes. Both bars are the same whole and the shaded part reaches exactly the same place, so 1/2 = 2/4.)
Say: Which is greater, 3/4 of a banner or 3/8 of the same banner? Why? (3/4. Fourths are bigger pieces than eighths when the whole is the same, so three fourths cover more than three eighths.)

title: Compare With Symbols
desc: comparing fractions with the same numerator or denominator, recording the results with the symbols >, =, or <, and justifying the conclusion
dir: Write each comparison with >, = or < on your paper. Tell how you know. You can draw a model.
qs: Compare 7/8 and 5/8 with >, = or <.
Compare 2/6 and 2/3 with a symbol. Tell how you know.
key: 2/6 < 2/3. Same numerator, so the fraction with the bigger denominator (sixths) is smaller.

title: Sense, Brain, Act
desc: using a model to show how an animal takes in information, processes it, and responds
dir: Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your model on your paper and hold it up.
text: A dog waits at the yard gate while the showcase is set up. Dishes clatter, a chair scrapes, and then someone calls his name. He lifts his head only at his name
qs: Which body part took in all those sounds?
Three sounds reached him and he answered only one. What does that tell you about the work his brain was doing?
key: His ears. Every one of those sounds reached them. (3-LS1-1)
His brain was sorting the information, not just receiving it: it recognized one sound as his name and chose to respond to that one and ignore the rest. (3-LS1-1)

title: The Flock in the Yard
desc: building an argument from data that forming a group helps animals survive
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.

qs: Which sparrows ate more crumbs each in five minutes?
Make an argument that feeding in a flock helps a sparrow survive. Use a number from the table.
key: the ones in the flock, 14 crumbs each against 6 (3-LS2-1)

The claim yes, with the numbers attached: a bird in the flock ate 14 crumbs instead of 6, and the cat only got close once in eight tries instead of five, so a bird in a flock eats more and is caught o

title: Passed Down and Shaped
desc: reading trait data for parents and offspring, naming the variation, and telling when the surroundings shaped a trait
dir: Look at both tables. Answer out loud.
text: Table 1: a pair of speckled hens from the school coop, and their five chicks grown out. Bird Feathers Comb height in mm parent 1 speckled 31 parent 2 speckled 2
qs: Every chick has speckled feathers, like both parents. Where did that trait come from?
The comb heights are all a little different. What is that difference called. Does it mean one of them is not theirs?
key: It was inherited from the parents. A trait both parents have and every offspring has is passed down. (3-LS3-1)
Variation. They are all still their chicks: inherited traits vary from one offspring to the next, so a group of similar organisms is not identical. (3-LS3-1)

title: Clues from the Quarry Trip
desc: reading fossil data to say which organisms lived in a place and what the place was like
dir: Look at the table of rock layers. Answer out loud.
text: On the last field trip of the year the class visited a quarry and recorded the fossils in three layers of the quarry wall. The top layer is the youngest. Layer
qs: Name two organisms that once lived where this quarry is now.
Was the bottom layer salt water, fresh water, or dry land? Use the fossils as your evidence.
key: Any two the table names: a pine, a land snail, a fern, a frog, a pond snail, coral, a sea urchin, a clam. (3-LS4-1)
Salt water, the sea. Coral, sea urchins and clams live in the ocean, and naming them is the evidence. An answer with no fossil named is not yet using the data. (3-LS4-1)

title: A Useful Difference
desc: explaining how a variation among individuals of one species gives an advantage
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Fence lizards sun themselves on the yard wall, and cats hunt them. A class measured tails and watched what happened in a chase. Lizards Tail length Turns made i
qs: Which lizards escaped more often?
Explain why a longer tail is an advantage for a lizard being chased along a wall. Use the table.
key: the long-tailed lizards, 15 escapes out of 18 against 6 (3-LS4-2)
A long tail helps the lizard swing and turn sharply, 7 turns in a chase against 2, so it can dodge into a crack, and 15 of 18 got away against 6. The explanation has to lean on the data. (3-LS4-2)

title: Who Survives, and What Would Help
desc: arguing from data who can survive in a changed habitat, then judging the merit of a solution
dir: Read the table. Answer out loud.
text: The big oak at the far end of the yard was taken out to make room for a new building. The corner it shaded is now bare and sunny all day. A class surveyed it be
qs: Which living thing survived well after the oak came down? Give the evidence.
Which one was gone from the corner entirely. Which one survived less well?
key: The crabgrass. It went from a few blades to covering the whole corner, so full sun suited it. (3-LS4-3)
The owls could not survive there at all, none seen since. The ferns survived less well, from 22 plants down to 4 with browned leaves. (3-LS4-3)

title: A Season of Weather
desc: reading and making a graphical display of typical weather for one season
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud. For the last one, draw your graph on your paper and hold it up.
text: The class weather station recorded the highest temperature on the first day of each week of the last month of school. Week Highest temperature Rain that week 1
qs: What are the two things changing together across these four weeks?
The showcase is in week 5. What would you expect the weather to be, and why?
key: The temperature is rising, 22 to 32 C, while the rain is falling, 14 mm to none. (3-ESS2-1)
Hot and dry, probably above 30 C with little or no rain, because that is where both trends in the table are heading. The reason has to come from the table. (3-ESS2-1)

title: Two Parts of the World
desc: combining information to describe the climates of two different regions of the world
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: The same month, the last month of this school year, in two regions of the world. Region Average temperature that month Rain that month What people are doing out
qs: Which region is warmer in this month, and by how many degrees?
In one region people are watering and in the other they are only now planting. How does the table explain that difference?
key: the dry region with hot summers, 28 C against 11 C, a difference of 17 degrees (3-ESS2-2)

The warm dry region is already deep into its growing season and the rain has stopped, so gardens need watering, while the cool region is only just warm enough at 11 C for crops to start. The table has

title: Ready for the Heat
desc: making a claim about the merit of a design that reduces the impact of a weather hazard
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The showcase runs from noon to three. It is the hottest day of the year so far. The yard has no shade. The crew strings a wide cloth cover on wires above the ta
qs: Which weather hazard are the cover and the water meant to reduce?
Make a claim. Does the cover and the water have merit? Give your reason.
key: extreme heat in an unshaded yard in the middle of the day (3-ESS3-1)

Yes, with a reason attached: the cover blocks the direct sun over the tables so the air under it is cooler, and water at both ends keeps people from getting overheated. A yes with no reason is not yet

title: Balanced or Not
desc: planning an investigation of balanced and unbalanced forces acting on an object
dir: Answer out loud.
text: A loaded table cart stands in the sloped lane behind the yard. One helper holds the handle and another pushes gently from the front. The cart does not move.
qs: Are the forces on the cart balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
The helper at the front steps aside. What happens, and what changed about the forces?
key: Balanced. The hold and the push are equal and opposite, and the cart staying still is the evidence. (3-PS2-1)
The cart starts to roll down the lane. Nothing balances the downhill pull and the pull of the handle now, so the forces are unbalanced. (3-PS2-1)

title: Predict the Next Chalk Mark
desc: using a pattern in motion data to predict where an object will be later
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: Chalk marks are drawn every meter down the middle of the lane. A cart is given one push and the class records where it is at the end of each second. Seconds Dis
qs: Is the cart covering the same distance each second, or less each time? Use the numbers.
Look at how much is added each second: 4, then 3, then 2. What would you predict for the fifth second, and what happens after that?
key: Less each time. The gaps shrink: 5, then 4 more, then 3 more, then 2 more. The cart is slowing down. (3-PS2-2)
About 1 m more, so around 15 m, and then it stops, because the next step in the pattern would add nothing. Accept any answer the student reaches by continuing the pattern and explaining it. (3-PS2-2)

title: Ask About the Pull
desc: asking questions about cause and effect in electric or magnetic interactions between objects not touching
dir: Answer out loud. Your two questions have to be questions, not statements.
text: A paper sign is held onto the steel gate post. A magnet behind it holds the sign. A second magnet is brought near the first. The sign slides sideways on its own
qs: The two magnets never touch, yet one moves the other. What does that tell you about this force?
Say two questions about it that you could check for yourself.
key: The force acts across a distance, with no contact between the objects. (3-PS2-3)
Any two real investigable questions: how close do the magnets have to be, does a bigger magnet move the sign further, does the thickness of the post matter, how heavy a sign can one magnet hold, does

title: A Problem for a Magnet
desc: defining a design problem that magnets can solve, with criteria for success and constraints
dir: Answer out loud. For the third one you may write your two sentences on your paper.
text: Last year the signs for the showcase were taped to the steel posts. By noon every one of them had peeled off in the heat. They had blown into the lane.
qs: Give the problem in one sentence that opens with: The problem is.
Why is a magnet a sensible idea here? Would a magnet hold a sign onto a wooden post?
key: A problem statement about holding signs on the posts all day without tape peeling in the heat. The problem has to be about the signs staying up, not about the heat in general. (3-PS2-4)

The posts are steel, and a magnet pulls steel without touching the sign to anything sticky, so heat cannot peel it loose. A wooden post would not work, because a magnet does not pull on wood. (3-PS2-4

title: Three Ways to Do It
desc: comparing several possible solutions against stated criteria and constraints
dir: Look at the table and the three rules. Answer out loud.
text: The long cloth banner across the yard sagged into the lane last year. Three ways to hold it up are tried. Design Sag in the middle Minutes to put up Cost one ro
qs: Which design sags the least?
Which way of holding it meets all three rules? Explain using the table.
key: the wire with a tightener, 6 cm of sag (3-5-ETS1-2)

The two ropes with a pole in the middle. It sags 9 cm, goes up in 25 minutes, and costs 4 dollars. Another choice counts only if the student argues it against all three rules using the table. (3-5-ETS

title: Make the Test Fair
desc: judging whether a test is fair, naming controlled variables, and identifying a failure point
dir: Answer out loud.
text: Two ropes were tested to see which one sags less under the banner. Rope Banner hung on it Distance between the posts Weather on the test day thin cotton rope th
qs: Can this test tell you which rope is better? Say why.
Name two things that have to be the same for a fair test.
key: No. Three things were different at once, the banner, the span and the weather, so less sag cannot be pinned on the rope. (3-5-ETS1-3)
Any two controlled variables: the same banner, the same distance between posts, the same weather, the same knot, the same height, the same time left hanging. (3-5-ETS1-3)

title: Maps and Places
desc: using a map grid and a table to describe physical and human features and where they sit
dir: Use the map grid and the table. Answer out loud.
text: A map grid of the school and the blocks around it. North is the top row. west middle east north city park library shops middle low ridge school yard school gard
qs: What lies directly east of the school yard?
Which two directions do you walk to get from the school yard to the shops?
key: the school garden (HSS-3.1)
north and east, in either order. The shops sit in the north row and the east column. Partial: one of the two directions is approaching. (HSS-3.1)

title: The First Nations Here
desc: describing what the American Indian nations of California do in the state today and how they lived here long ago
dir: Answer out loud. Use what is on the screen and what you have learned.
text: California nations are not only part of history. Nations across the state hold yearly gatherings. They run cultural centers and language programs. They send mem
qs: The screen says nations send members to meetings where decisions are made. What are those decisions about. What does that tell you about whether nations belong only to history?
Think of that nation, or of California nations. Name one thing people did long ago. It helped them live well in this place.
key: The decisions are about land and water. It tells you nations do not belong only to history, because they are taking part in decisions being made now. Partial: naming land and water with nothing said a

Any true answer the student has studied: gathering and preparing acorns, fishing and drying fish, weaving baskets, building with tule, using fire to care for the land, trading with other nations, movi

title: A Town Over Time
desc: sequencing local historical events and describing the mark each period left on the land
dir: Look at the timeline. Answer out loud.
text: A timeline for the town of Oak Landing. Year What happened 1856 a landing is built where the creek meets the river 1881 the oak grove on the ridge is cut and th
qs: Put these three in order, earliest first: the first school, the freeway, the landing.
Which event changed the ridge, and what did it do to it?
key: landing, first school, freeway. Partial: two of the three in the right order is approaching. (HSS-3.3)

the cutting in 1881, which took the oak grove off the ridge and put wheat in its place. Accept the 1958 freeway or the 2015 replanting as further answers, since both changed the same ridge again. Part

title: Rules, Laws and Government
desc: telling rules from laws and naming the basic parts and levels of United States government
dir: Answer out loud.
text: The school has a rule. Walk in the lane, do not run between the tables. The state has a law about school. Every child must be in school or in a school program.
qs: What is the difference between the school’s rule and the state school law?
How does a person get a say in the laws their state makes?
key: The school rule is set by the school and applies at school. The state law is made by a government, applies to every child in the state, and the government decides what happens when it is not followed.

By voting for the lawmakers who represent them, and by speaking at meetings or writing to those lawmakers. Accept voting, speaking up, or contacting a representative. Partial: saying people can compla

title: Choices and the Local Economy
desc: basic economic reasoning about producers and consumers, cost, price and scarcity
dir: Look at the table. Answer out loud.
text: A class runs a table at the showcase. They made bookmarks out of card and they also offer to letter a name on any bookmark while you wait. Item Amount what the
qs: All forty bookmarks sell. How much comes in? How much is left after the 14 dollars of costs?

Twenty people want a lettered name but the class can only letter twelve before the showcase ends. What do we call it when there is not enough to go around. Then name one fair way to decide who gets one?
key: 40 dollars comes in from the bookmarks, since 40 times 1 is 40, and 26 dollars is left after the 14 dollars of costs. Partial: the 40 dollars right with no amount left over is approaching. (HSS-3.5)

That is scarcity: less of something than people want. Any fair method named: first in line, a sign-up list, drawing names, charging more for the lettering, or taking orders to finish later. Partial: n

title: Read the Field
desc: a 168-word grade-level text read aloud
dir: Read the text out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Setting the Field The Juniper Bend fair takes over the back field for one afternoon in June, and the field does not give it up easily. The grass has to be cut t
key: 168 words, not counting the title. Time 1 minute and mark errors and self-corrections on your own copy. Let the student finish the passage.

Spring grade 4 benchmark: about 133 words correct per minute (Hasbrouck and Tindal 2017, spring 50th percentile). 25th percentile is about 105. This is the last check of the year, so the spring column

title: Read the Poem
desc: reading on-level poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression
dir: Read the poem out loud. Use your best reading voice. Let the rhythm and the rhymes show.
text: Winter Fields The fields lie quiet under snow, Where only the footprints of foxes go. The fence posts wear their caps of white, And the sky grows pink in the fa
key: 46 words, not counting the title. Mark each word read wrong or skipped. A word the student fixes alone counts as correct.
Listen for rhythm, pauses at the end of lines or punctuation, and a voice that fits the mood of the poem.

title: Read It Again
desc: reading the same on-level text orally a second time with accuracy, rate, and expression
dir: Read the same text one more time. Make it smoother and more expressive.
text: Setting the Field The Juniper Bend fair takes over the back field for one afternoon in June, and the field does not give it up easily. The grass has to be cut t
key: Second reading of the same text. Count the words read correctly again and compare with the first reading. More words read correctly, fewer stops and rereads, and smoother phrasing show growth on succe

title: Long Word Cards
desc: decoding unfamiliar multisyllabic words using syllable patterns and word parts
dir: Read each word out loud. Break it into chunks you already know before you say the whole word.
key: Read each word in order: rehearsal, assemble, decorate, admission, generous, individual, temporary, arrangement, contribute, incredible, approximately, souvenir.

Word parts to listen for: the prefixes re-, ad-, con-, in- (rehearsal, admission, contribute, incredible) and the endings -al, -ate, -ous, -ment, -ible, -ary, -ly (rehearsal, decorate, generous, arran

title: Read the Sentences
desc: reading multisyllabic words accurately in context using letter-sound correspondences, syllable patterns, and word parts
dir: Read each sentence out loud. Take your time with the long words.
text: The architect designed a spectacular library with enormous windows. Our neighborhood celebrated the beginning of the harvest festival.
key: Listen for these six words read correctly in the sentences: architect, spectacular, library, neighborhood, celebrated, harvest. Mark each one.
A word that is self-corrected on a second try counts as correct. Note words the student breaks into syllables to decode.

title: The Cash Box
desc: referring to details and examples in a story and drawing inferences from them
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud. Use details and examples from the story in every answer.
text: The Cash Box Ibrahim's job at the fair was the cash box, and he had asked for it. He liked numbers, and he liked being the one who knew the total. At two o'cloc
qs: What was Ibrahim's job at the fair, and did he want it? Read the words that tell you.
How much did he count at two o'clock, and how much at four o'clock?
key: The cash box, and he asked for it. Reads “Ibrahim's job at the fair was the cash box, and he had asked for it,” and “He liked numbers, and he liked being the one who knew the total.” (RL.4.1, explicit
Ninety-four dollars at two o'clock and eighty-six dollars at four o'clock. (RL.4.1, explicit details)

title: Why a Cake Rises
desc: referring to details and examples in an informational text and drawing inferences from them
dir: Read the article. Then answer out loud. Use details and examples from the article in every answer.
text: Why a Cake Rises A cake starts out as a thin batter that you could pour. Twenty-five minutes later it is tall and springy. The thing that changes it is gas. Mos
qs: What gas makes a cake rise? Read the words that tell you.
What does baking powder need before it starts to work? Find the details in the article.
key: Carbon dioxide. Reads “it begins to make carbon dioxide, the same gas that makes the bubbles in soda water.” (RI.4.1, explicit detail)
It has to be wet and then warmed. Reads “As soon as it is wet, and then warmed, it begins to make carbon dioxide.” (RI.4.1, explicit details)

title: Give It Room
desc: the meaning of words and phrases in a story, including figurative language and a reference to a figure from mythology
dir: Read the story. Then answer out loud. Use the story to explain each answer.
text: Give It Room Teo had been told to carry the cake table out on his own, and he was no Hercules. He got it as far as the doorway, where one leg caught the frame a
qs: The story says Teo “was no Hercules.” Hercules is a hero from Greek myths. What is the writer telling you about Teo?
“The whole thing stopped dead.” What does stopped dead mean here?
key: Hercules was famous for enormous strength, so saying Teo was no Hercules means Teo was not especially strong and the table was too heavy for one person. (RL.4.4, a word or phrase that alludes to a cha
It stopped suddenly and completely, all at once, with no drifting to a halt. (RL.4.4, meaning of a phrase as used in the text)

title: One Mistake Each
desc: relative pronouns, modal auxiliaries, ordering adjectives, confused words, and run-on sentences
dir: Each line from the fair notice has one mistake. Say the whole line out loud the right way.
qs: The booth who sold lemonade ran out of cups.
We should of counted the chairs first.
key: The booth that sold lemonade ran out of cups. Accept which. A booth is a thing, so it takes that or which, not who. (L.4.1a, relative pronouns)
We should have counted the chairs first. (L.4.1c, modal auxiliaries, and a common usage error)

title: Build a Line
desc: progressive verb tenses, relative adverbs, prepositional phrases, and confused words
dir: Answer out loud. Say whole sentences.
qs: Change this sentence so it tells what was happening: Rosa counts the tickets.
Which word fits? This is the field ____ the fair is held. Is it where or when?
key: Rosa was counting the tickets. (L.4.1b, past progressive verb tense)
where (L.4.1a, relative adverb)

title: Cursive Writing
desc: writing fluidly and legibly in cursive or joined italics
dir: Write this sentence on your paper in cursive or joined writing. Write smoothly and keep it neat.
text: Write this sentence: The old lighthouse stood bravely against the storm.
key: Letters are joined within words (cursive or joined italics)
Writing is legible: another reader can read each word

title: Say It Your Way
desc: paraphrasing parts of a text read aloud and information shown in a table
dir: Listen while your teacher reads. Then say each answer in your own words, not the words you heard.
text: Your teacher will read you a short report about how the school pays for the fair. Listen carefully. Then put what you heard into your own words. After that, loo
qs: Put the first part of the report into your own words. What does the fair cost, and where does the money come from?
Say the school's one rule about spending in your own words.
key: Paraphrase, not a repeat: the fair costs around six hundred dollars a year, and the money comes from more than one place. Half is put aside in September and half is raised during the year, mostly at t
Paraphrase: the school will not order anything until it already has the money for it. (SL.4.2)

title: Two Sources
desc: taking notes from two sources, sorting them into categories, and listing the sources
dir: Read both sources. Write your notes and your source list on your paper, then hold it up.
text: Here are two more sources about cakes. Take notes from both. Source 1: Bubbles in the Batter a chapter from the book Kitchen Science at Home by Delia Marchetti,
key: Gas box: at least two notes drawn from the sources, such as baking powder holds an acid and a base kept dry (Source 1), water lets them react (Source 1), heat speeds the reaction up (Source 1), one te

Sinking box: at least two notes, such as opening the oven door too early (Source 2), too much baking powder (Source 2), bubbles so large the walls tear before the batter sets (Source 2). (W.4.8, categ

title: Two Minutes at the Microphone
desc: a short spoken report on one topic, organized, with facts and descriptive details
dir: Plan for 1 minute. Then talk for 1 to 2 minutes. Look at the camera and speak clearly.
text: At the end of the fair, every class sends one person to the microphone for two minutes. Report on one thing you worked on this year. Say what it was, how you we
key: Reports on one topic and stays with it for the whole turn, rather than listing several things (SL.4.4)
The report is organized: what it was, then how it was done, then the hard part, then the change, in an order a listener can follow (SL.4.4)

title: Two Sources, One Subject
desc: integrating information from two texts on the same topic to speak knowledgeably about it
dir: Read both sources again. Then answer out loud, using both of them.
text: These are the same two sources about cakes. This time do not take notes. Put them together and talk. Source 1: Bubbles in the Batter a chapter from the book Kit
qs: Using both sources, tell me in two or three sentences. Baking powder makes a cake rise. How? What can make one sink?
Which part of what you just said came from Source 1, and which came from Source 2?
key: Say: Using both sources, tell me in two or three sentences. Baking powder makes a cake rise. How? What can make one sink? (An answer that holds facts from both: the acid and the base in the powder rea
Say: Which part of what you just said came from Source 1, and which came from Source 2? (Names the right source for each fact. This is the check that the student knows the two texts apart.)

title: Fair Writing
desc: a short opinion piece with reasons and supporting information
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Should the fair stay on the back field, or move into the gym where the weather cannot reach it? Write your opinion. Write 4 or 5 sentences. Open by naming the q
key: Introduces the topic and states an opinion clearly (W.4.1)
Supplies at least two reasons for that opinion (W.4.1)

title: Fair Writing
desc: a short informative piece that develops a topic with facts and definitions
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Explain to someone who has never been how a school fair gets set up. Write 4 or 5 sentences. Open by naming what you are explaining Group the facts so one idea
key: Introduces the topic clearly in the opening sentence (W.4.2)
Develops the topic with facts, such as cutting the grass twice, staking the holes, fourteen tables, or the curve that slows the crowd (W.4.2)

title: Fair Writing
desc: a short narrative with a clear sequence, dialogue or description, and an ending
dir: Write on your paper. When you finish, hold it up or read it to your teacher.
text: Write a short scene about something going wrong at a fair and getting fixed. It can be real or made up. Write 4 or 5 sentences. Set it up: who is there and wher
key: Orients the reader: establishes a situation and at least one character (W.4.3)
Organizes the events in a sequence that unfolds naturally (W.4.3)

title: Times as Many
desc: reading a multiplication equation as a comparison and writing comparison statements as equations
dir: Answer out loud. Write each equation on your paper and hold it up.
text: The fair keeps a tally of everything it sells and everything it uses. Many of the notes are written as comparisons.
qs: The lemonade table sold 7 times as many cups of lemonade as cups of tea. It sold 6 cups of tea. How many cups of lemonade did it sell? Write the equation.
Say what 35 = 5 × 7 means as a comparison. Use the words “times as many.”
key: 42 cups of lemonade. 42 = 7 × 6, or 7 × 6 = 42. Partial: the answer right with no equation written is approaching. (4.OA.A.1, a comparison written as a multiplication equation)
35 is 5 times as many as 7. Accept 35 is 7 times as many as 5. Partial: 35 is 5 more than 7 reads it as an addition and does not count. (4.OA.A.1, reading an equation as a comparison)

title: Same Amount, Different Pieces
desc: explaining why two fractions are equivalent and generating equivalent fractions
dir: Look at the bars. Answer out loud and explain how you know. You can write on your paper.
text: The two bars below are exactly the same size. They stand for two cakes of the same size, cut in two different ways.
qs: How much of Cake 1 is shaded? How much of Cake 2? Are the two shaded amounts equal?
Use the picture to explain why 3/4 and 6/8 name the same amount.
key: 3/4 of Cake 1 and 6/8 of Cake 2, and yes, the shaded amounts are equal. The bars are the same size and the shading reaches the same place. Partial: both fractions right with no answer about the amount
Every fourth is cut in half, so there are twice as many pieces and each piece is half as big. 3 fourths becomes 6 eighths, and the amount does not change: 3/4 = (2 × 3)/(2 × 4) = 6/8. Partial: naming

title: Which Slice Is Bigger?
desc: comparing fractions with different numerators and denominators, using benchmarks or common denominators
dir: Answer out loud and tell how you know. Write the comparisons on your paper.
text: The food table writes down how much of each tray is left at the end of the afternoon. Compare them. Every tray is the same size.
qs: Look at Tray P and Tray Q. Which has more left, 2/3 or 3/4? Show it with a common denominator.
Which is greater, 3/5 or 5/8? Show how you know.
key: 3/4 has more. In twelfths, 2/3 is 8/12 and 3/4 is 9/12, and 9/12 is greater than 8/12. The picture agrees: the shading on Tray Q reaches further. Partial: naming 3/4 with no common denominator shown i
5/8 is greater. In fortieths, 3/5 is 24/40 and 5/8 is 25/40. Partial: naming 5/8 with no common denominator shown is approaching. (4.NF.A.2, comparing by making a common denominator)

title: Measure the Field
desc: knowing the relative sizes of measurement units and expressing a larger unit in terms of a smaller one
dir: Answer out loud. Fill in the table on your paper and hold it up.
text: The crew writes every measurement down twice, once in the bigger unit and once in the smaller one, so that nobody has to work it out twice.
qs: Finish the table. How many inches are in 2 feet, in 3 feet, and in 5 feet?
A display table is 2 meters long. How many centimeters is that?
key: 24 inches, 36 inches, and 60 inches. 1 foot is 12 inches, so multiply the number of feet by 12: 2 × 12 = 24, 3 × 12 = 36, 5 × 12 = 60. Partial: two of the three rows right is approaching. (4.MD.A.1, r
200 centimeters. 1 meter is 100 centimeters, so 2 × 100 = 200. Partial: 20 uses tens instead of hundreds and does not count. (4.MD.A.1)

title: Pounds and Ounces
desc: knowing the relative sizes of pounds and ounces, converting a larger unit to a smaller unit, and recording equivalents in a table
dir: Solve on your paper. Show your work.
qs: A puppy weighs 5 pounds. How many ounces is that?
How many ounces are in 2 pounds?
key: 80 ounces (5 × 16)
32 ounces

title: Decimal Ribbons
desc: comparing two decimals to hundredths and recording the result with the greater than, less than, or equals sign
dir: Look at the two grids. Answer out loud and write each comparison on your paper.
text: Each grid below is one whole, cut into 100 small squares. The shaded part is written as a decimal.
qs: Which is greater, 0.4 or 0.37? Use the grids to explain, then write it with a sign.
Write >, <, or = to make this true: 0.7 ____ 0.70
key: 0.4 is greater. 0.4 is 40 of the 100 squares and 0.37 is 37 of them, so Grid 1 has more shaded. Written with a sign: 0.4 > 0.37. Partial: naming 0.4 with no sign written is approaching. (4.NF.C.7)

0.7 = 0.70. Seven tenths is the same as seventy hundredths, because each tenth is ten hundredths. Partial: making one of them the greater counts digits instead of places and does not count. (4.NF.C.7)

title: Sort the Sign Shapes
desc: classifying two-dimensional figures by parallel and perpendicular sides and by angle size, and recognizing right triangles
dir: Look at the five shapes. Answer out loud. Use the corner of a card to test any angle you are not sure about.
text: The sign crew cut five flat shapes out of board for the gate. The letter under each one is its name.
